rows.notes: African Pompano in Alabama state waters has a 24-inch fork length minimum size and a bag limit of 2 fish per person per day OR 2 per vessel per day (not both) under Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-3-.30. No closed season identified for this species; regulation is size/bag limited only. Spearing of this species is prohibited in Alabama state waters.

Albacore tuna is a federally-managed Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS); NOAA Fisheries recreational regulations apply in all waters, including Alabama state waters, and are not overridden by state rules. Per NOAA/HMS compliance guidance, there is currently no recreational minimum size and no bag limit for albacore (longfin) tuna — the fishery is open year-round. Anglers must hold a valid HMS Angling or HMS Charter/Headboat permit to target/retain albacore, and tunas cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded.

Alligator gar are regulated under Alabama's general public waters fishing code (Rule 220-2-.35), which applies statewide including Mobile Delta/coastal waters where the species occurs. No minimum size limit for recreational harvest. Any alligator gar caught with commercial fishing gear must be immediately returned to the water unharmed. Season is open continuously year-round unless otherwise noted.

Atlantic Angel Shark is a federally and state-designated prohibited shark species. Recreational and commercial harvest is banned in Alabama state waters year-round; any caught must be released immediately with minimal injury. This mirrors NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited species rules (50 CFR 635), which apply consistently across all US Atlantic/Gulf jurisdictions.

Alabama Admin Code 220-3-.30 (amended effective June 17, 2025) sets a daily recreational bag limit of 1 for Atlantic sharpnose shark, with no minimum size limit specified for this species (Atlantic sharpnose and bonnethead sharks are listed as 'no minimum size'). No recreational closed season is published for this species; state waters shark fishing is otherwise year-round subject to gear rules (non-offset, non-stainless circle hooks with natural bait) and prohibitions on chumming/bloodbaiting near shore.

Banded Rudderfish (Seriola zonata) is regulated by Alabama DCNR/Marine Resources Division as a Gulf Reef Fish species (Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-3-.46). It has a 14"-22" fork length slot limit, and no size within the slot may be exceeded. There is no species-specific daily bag limit; it falls under the statewide 20-fish aggregate reef fish creel limit that applies to reef species without their own individual bag limit. No closed season is currently listed for this species (unlike Red Snapper or Groupers, which have specific open-season windows tied to federal dates).

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Basking shark is on Alabama's prohibited species list for both recreational and commercial harvest. Must be released immediately if caught; retention is illegal. This aligns with NOAA HMS federal prohibited shark species list as well.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species - no open season)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sand Tiger Shark (Odontaspis noronhai) is on Alabama's prohibited species list. Recreational and commercial harvest is prohibited; any specimen caught must be released and cannot be retained, landed, or possessed. This mirrors the federal NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited shark species list.

rows.season: Closed year-round — prohibited species (no open season)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus nakamurai) is on Alabama's prohibited species list — recreational and commercial harvest is banned in Alabama state waters. Any specimen caught must be released immediately; no possession, size, or bag limit applies because retention is illegal at all times.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season, harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Bigeye Thresher Shark is a Prohibited Species under Alabama regulations — recreational AND commercial harvest, retention, and possession are unlawful in Alabama state waters. This mirrors the federal NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited shark species list. Fish must be released; anglers should consult NOAA's 'Handling and Release of Prohibited Species' guidance.

Bigeye tuna is a federally-managed Highly Migratory Species (HMS); NOAA Atlantic HMS rules apply in ALL waters (state and federal) and override Alabama state regulations. Minimum size is 27 inches curved fork length (measured along the body contour from tip of upper jaw to fork of tail). There is currently NO recreational bag limit for bigeye tuna (bagLimit set to null to represent 'no numeric cap', not 'unknown') — multiple sources confirm no daily retention limit is imposed on bigeye, unlike yellowfin (3/angler) or bluefin (permit/size-class based, per vessel). A valid federal HMS Angling or HMS Charter/Headboat permit is required to target/retain bigeye tuna, and the fish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded. Fishery status (open/closed) for this species has not changed from year-round open as of search date.

Bignose Shark is a federally and state-listed prohibited shark species. Alabama Admin. Code r. 220-3-.30 explicitly prohibits recreational and commercial harvest of the Bignose shark in Alabama state waters year-round, with no possession or size limit applicable since retention is not allowed at all. This aligns with NOAA HMS prohibited species list.

Black drum is not listed among the species with specific size/creel limits on Alabama's official saltwater regulations. Alabama's regulation (220-3-.30) states there is no possession or size limit on species not specifically listed in the creel limit table, and black drum does not appear in that table (unlike red drum, spotted seatrout, etc., which do have explicit slot/bag limits). Multiple secondary sources corroborate that Alabama currently imposes no size limit and no bag limit on black drum, making it one of the most permissive states for this species. No closed season is published for black drum in AL state waters, so harvest is year-round.

Black grouper counts within Alabama's 4-fish mixed-species grouper aggregate (no more than 2 red grouper and 2 gag grouper may be included in that aggregate). Alabama's Admin Code Rule 220-3-.30 sets a 24-inch total length minimum and no closed season for black grouper in state waters. The federal Feb 1–Mar 31 shallow-water-grouper closure (red, black, scamp, yellowfin, yellowmouth) applies only seaward of the 20-fathom break in the Gulf EEZ, outside Alabama's state-water boundary (9 nm for reef fish), so it does not close the state-water season.

Bigeye Tuna is an HMS species. Federal NOAA HMS rules apply and supersede state rules. Under NOAA HMS regulations, the recreational retention limit is 3 fish per person per day with a 27-inch curved fork length minimum. Alabama state waters regulations do not independently govern HMS species. Verify current NOAA HMS rules directly as these regulations change frequently.

Blackfin tuna is not listed on Alabama's official saltwater size/creel limit chart, meaning no state size or bag limit is currently established. Blackfin tuna is also explicitly exempt from the federal NOAA HMS Angling permit requirement (unlike other Atlantic tunas), and NOAA/Gulf federal-water summaries confirm no established bag or size limit for this species. Under Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-3-.30(7), fish harvested elsewhere without a limit must follow Alabama's own limit for that species — but since Alabama itself sets none for blackfin tuna, there is currently no minimum size, bag, or boat limit and no closed season; harvest is open year-round.

rows.season: Year-round (2026), subject to closure if adjacent federal Gulf shark season closes
rows.notes: Blacknose shark is not individually listed or prohibited under Alabama's shark rules, so it falls under the 'All other shark species' category: 54-inch minimum fork length (30 inches dressed), 1 shark per person per day. Alabama state waters open/close in tandem with federal Gulf shark season closures (Rule 220-3-.30 / Outdoor Alabama commercial license page). No specific closed season is currently in effect for 2026. Chumming/bloodbaiting to target sharks from shore or piers is prohibited within 300 feet of shoreline.

rows.season: Year-round (federal HMS recreational shark season; no closed season for blacktip shark, but valid HMS Angling/Charter-Headboat permit with shark endorsement required)
rows.notes: Blacktip shark (Carcharhinus limbatus) is an Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) — NOAA federal rules govern recreational retention in ALL U.S. Atlantic/Gulf waters, including Alabama state waters; Alabama does not set its own separate blacktip limits. Blacktip falls in NOAA's 'non-ridgeback large coastal shark' group (with tiger, bull, lemon, nurse, spinner, hammerheads, etc.), minimum size 54 inches fork length, retention limit ONE shark of that combined group per VESSEL per trip (not per angler) — so bagLimit is null and boatLimit=1 is the operative cap. Non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hooks required when using natural bait; shark must be landed with fins naturally attached. NOTE: NOAA published a proposed rule (Jan 5, 2026, comment period extended to May 29, 2026) that would create species-specific size groups and could lower the blacktip/spinner minimum size to as low as 48 in or raise it to 70 in, and could change the per-angler vs per-vessel bag structure for some species — but as of this search (Jul 22, 2026) no final rule adopting those changes had been published, so the longstanding 54 in / 1-per-vessel rule remains in effect. Alabama does prohibit possession of several other shark species (e.g., sandbar, dusky, shortfin mako) but blacktip is NOT on Alabama's prohibited list.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational retention open; may be closed to catch-and-release only if the annual U.S. combined landing limit of 250 blue marlin/white marlin/roundscale spearfish is reached — check NOAA HMS status page before keeping a fish)
rows.notes: Blue Marlin is a federal Highly Migratory Species (HMS); NOAA Atlantic HMS rules apply in ALL waters, including Alabama state waters, and are NOT overridden by Alabama DCNR regs. Minimum size is 99 inches lower-jaw fork length (LJFL). The 1-fish limit is PER VESSEL PER TRIP and is shared between blue marlin and white marlin combined (i.e., 1 total marlin of either species, not 1 of each). Vessel must hold a valid HMS Angling or HMS Charter/Headboat permit. Billfish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is already aboard or has been offloaded from the vessel that trip.

rows.season: Closed for retention - Year-round in Gulf of America (Alabama state waters): targeted fishing for Atlantic Bluefin Tuna is never permitted, and the incidental 'trophy' (73"+) fishery has been closed since May 2026 through Dec 31, 2026
rows.notes: Atlantic Bluefin Tuna is a federal HMS species; Alabama defers entirely to NOAA HMS regulations (tuna 'may be landed in the form permitted by Federal Fisheries Regulations'). Alabama's saltwater waters fall within the Gulf of America, which NOAA designates as bluefin spawning grounds where targeted BFT fishing is never allowed for any size class. The only allowance is incidental retention of one trophy-sized (≥73" curved fork length) BFT per vessel/year while targeting other HMS species when that subquota fishery is open — but NOAA closed the Angling category Gulf of America trophy fishery effective May 2026 through Dec 31, 2026 after the subquota was exceeded. Net effect: zero legal retention of Atlantic Bluefin Tuna in Alabama state waters currently. Catch-and-release/tag-and-release of all sizes remains allowed under HMS rules. HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit and 24-hr NOAA catch reporting required for any BFT interaction.

Blueline Tilefish in Alabama state waters may fall under NOAA/SAFMC federal management for South Atlantic or Gulf reef fish; state-specific limits for this species were not confirmed in training data. Verify current regulations at the Alabama DCNR saltwater fishing page and cross-reference with NOAA HMS or NOAA SERO Gulf reef fish regulations as applicable. Do not rely on this record for compliance.

Bonnethead (listed with Sharpnose) has no minimum size limit under Alabama regulations; daily creel limit is 1 per person per day. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks required when using natural bait for sharks. Bonnethead is not on Alabama's prohibited shark species list, so it remains open year-round in state waters (unlike large coastal sharks subject to federal quota closures).

Bull shark is not on Alabama's prohibited species list and has no species-specific limit, so it falls under the 'All Other Shark Species' category: 54 in. minimum fork length (or 30 in. dressed length), 1 shark per person per day. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when using natural bait for sharks, and shark chumming/bloodbaiting is prohibited within 300 ft of shoreline/piers.

rows.season: Closed year-round — no open season (prohibited species)
rows.notes: Caribbean Reef Shark is a prohibited species in Alabama state waters — recreational and commercial harvest is banned outright. Alabama's official creel limit page lists it explicitly among prohibited sharks (with Nassau/Goliath grouper, sawfishes, etc.), and this is corroborated by NOAA Atlantic HMS rules, which also classify Caribbean reef shark as a federally prohibited species that must be released with minimal injury and without removing it from the water. Any Caribbean reef shark caught must be released immediately.

Caribbean Sharpnose Shark is on Alabama's prohibited species list under Rule 220-3-.30 — recreational and commercial harvest/possession is banned in Alabama state waters; must be released if caught. This is a state-specific prohibition (note: NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations classify sharpnose sharks generally as retainable in federal waters, but Alabama state waters explicitly prohibit this species).
Minimum 36 in fork length; 1 per person, not to exceed 2 per vessel.

rows.season: Year-round in Alabama state waters (2026) — subject to closure if adjacent federal Gulf shark season closes
rows.notes: Finetooth shark is not individually listed by Alabama DCNR and is not among prohibited species (e.g., sandbar, silky, dusky, etc.), so it falls under the 'All Other Shark Species' category: 54 inches fork length minimum size, 1 shark per person per day. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks required when using natural bait for sharks. State waters shark season automatically closes if adjoining federal Gulf waters close to shark harvest.
Minimum 12 in total length.

rows.season: September 1 - September 30, 2026 (Alabama state waters open when adjacent Gulf federal waters are open)
rows.notes: 24-inch total length minimum. The 2-fish gag limit is part of a 4-fish mixed grouper aggregate per person, with no more than 2 red grouper and no more than 2 gag grouper in that aggregate. Charter/headboat captain and crew have a 0-fish bag limit. Alabama does not independently set a gag season — it mirrors the Gulf federal recreational season, which NOAA Fisheries/Gulf Council set for 2026 as opening Sept 1 and closing at 12:01 a.m. Oct 1, 2026.

Galapagos Shark is a prohibited species in Alabama state waters — no recreational or commercial harvest, possession, or landing is allowed at any time; must be released immediately with minimal harm. This matches the federal NOAA HMS prohibited shark species list, which also bans retention of Galapagos shark in all U.S. Atlantic/Gulf waters regardless of permit.

Goldface tilefish is classified as a Gulf Reef Fish species under Alabama Rule 220-3-.46 but has no species-specific size or bag limit. It falls under Alabama's 20-fish aggregate reef fish creel limit that applies to reef fish species with no other stated limit. No minimum size is set (consistent with Gulf Council federal management, which also lists no minimum size for this species). Alabama state waters for reef fish generally track federal open/closed status, but no federal closed season currently applies specifically to goldface tilefish (unlike red snapper/grouper), so it is treated as open year-round within the aggregate limit.

Gray snapper (mangrove snapper) in Alabama state waters. 10-inch minimum total length; 10-fish aggregate bag limit per angler per day. Verify whether this bag limit is standalone or part of a snapper aggregate with other species.

rows.season: Open August 1 – December 31, 2026 (or until the federal quota is met); closed annually in January/February and June/July
rows.notes: Alabama state waters for gray triggerfish open concurrently with federal Gulf waters. Per Outdoor Alabama's official season page: recreational harvest of gray triggerfish in state waters is open when federal waters are open, and the fish is closed annually in January/February and June/July, corresponding to a spring (Mar 1–May 31) and fall (Aug 1–Dec 31, or until quota met) structure. As of Aug 21, 2026 the fall season window is active. Minimum size is 15 inches fork length, bag limit 1 per person/day; a 20-fish aggregate reef-fish creel limit also applies if not otherwise capped. All harvested gray triggerfish must be reported through Alabama's Snapper Check system.

rows.season: Year-round (open recreationally; subject to in-season federal HMS shark closures)
rows.notes: Great hammerhead is not on Alabama's prohibited-shark list and is treated as a federally-managed HMS 'hammerhead' species (with smooth and scalloped hammerhead). Alabama state waters mirror NOAA Atlantic HMS shark rules; state season closes automatically when the adjacent federal season/quota closes. Minimum size is 78 inches fork length, and the recreational bag limit is 1 hammerhead shark per vessel per trip (not per angler) — hammerheads cannot be retained if any tuna, swordfish, or billfish is aboard, and a valid HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement plus non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks (with natural bait) are required. Great hammerhead retention is prohibited only in the U.S. Caribbean, not in the Gulf/Alabama waters.

White Shark (Carcharodon carcharias) is a federally protected prohibited species under NOAA's Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan (no retention allowed in any U.S. waters) and is separately named on Alabama's own prohibited species list. Catch-and-immediate-release only; must not be removed from the water. No harvest, possession, or landing permitted under any circumstances.

rows.season: Closed — 2026 season was September 1, 2026 - October 14, 2026 (Alabama state waters open concurrently with federal Gulf waters); season now closed and will not reopen until September 1, 2027
rows.notes: Alabama state-water greater amberjack season tracks the federal Gulf season exactly. NOAA/Gulf Council set the 2026 recreational season for September 1 – October 14, 2026 (43 days); as of today (Oct 18, 2026) that season has closed and harvest/possession is zero until it reopens September 1, 2027. Minimum size is 34 inches fork length, daily bag/possession limit is 1 fish per person (recreational); commercial minimum size is 36 inches FL. No separate vessel/boat limit applies to greater amberjack in Alabama rules.

rows.season: Closed Nov 1 - Nov 30; open the rest of the year
rows.notes: Minimum 14 in total length. Harvest is prohibited statewide November 1-30.

Longspine porgy is not listed with a species-specific size or bag limit in Alabama. It falls under the reef fish aggregate creel limit: a 20-fish aggregate daily bag limit applies to reef fish species (e.g., grunts, porgies, gray triggerfish, lane snapper) that have no other specific bag limit. No minimum size limit is specified for porgies.

All sturgeon species (including Gulf sturgeon, Atlantic sturgeon, Alabama sturgeon, and Lake sturgeon) have a closed season in all Alabama public waters, including saltwater/state waters. Any sturgeon caught must be immediately returned to the water with the least possible harm — no harvest or possession is legal at any time. Gulf sturgeon is additionally federally listed as threatened under the ESA.

Jolthead porgy is covered under Alabama's 20-fish aggregate creel limit for 'reef fish species' (which explicitly includes porgies, along with grunts, gray triggerfish, lane snapper, etc.) for which there is no other specific bag limit. No separate minimum size limit is published for this species in Alabama state waters.
Minimum 24 in fork length.
Minimum 10 in total length.

Lemon shark falls under Alabama's 'All Other Shark Species' recreational category (54 inches fork length minimum, 1 shark per person per day) — it is not on Alabama's prohibited-species list for recreational harvest. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when using natural bait, and chumming/bloodbaiting for sharks is prohibited within 300 feet of shoreline or on/near piers. Note: Lemon shark IS listed as a prohibited species for COMMERCIAL harvest in Alabama's Large Coastal Shark complex (non-ridgeback group) — this restriction applies to commercial, not recreational, fishing. Alabama state waters also close to shark harvest automatically if adjacent federal Gulf waters close for that species.

Lesser Amberjack must be 14"-22" fork length (slot limit) in Alabama state waters. There is no species-specific bag limit; lesser amberjack falls under Alabama's 20-fish 'Reef Fish Aggregate' daily creel limit that covers reef fish species without an individually assigned bag limit (e.g., grunts, porgies, banded rudderfish). Unlike greater amberjack, lesser amberjack is not flagged on the state chart as opening/closing with federal season dates, so it is treated as open year-round subject to the size slot and aggregate bag.

Longbill spearfish is an Atlantic HMS billfish. Under NOAA Fisheries Atlantic HMS regulations, retention/landing of longbill spearfish is prohibited for both recreational and commercial anglers year-round — it is catch-and-release only. These federal HMS rules apply in Alabama state waters as well as federal waters since Alabama's Marine Resources Division defers to federal Gulf Fisheries regulations for HMS-managed species. No minimum size or bag limit applies because possession is not allowed at all.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species — no open season, retention never allowed)
rows.notes: Longfin Mako Shark (Isurus paucus) is a federally prohibited HMS shark species under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations (prohibited since 2000) and is explicitly listed as prohibited for both recreational and commercial harvest under Alabama Admin. Code r. 220-3-.30. Must be released immediately with minimal harm without removing from the water; cannot be retained, possessed, or landed in Alabama state waters under any circumstance.
Minimum 12 in total length (gray snapper).

rows.season: Closed year-round (Prohibited species — no open season)
rows.notes: Narrowtooth shark (Carcharhinus brachyurus) is on Alabama's prohibited species list — recreational and commercial harvest/possession is not allowed in Alabama state waters. No size or bag limit applies because retention is banned outright.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species - no open season)
rows.notes: Night Shark is listed as a prohibited species under Alabama Admin. Code r. 220-3-.30 and on the Outdoor Alabama Saltwater Recreational Size & Creel Limits chart. Recreational and commercial harvest is prohibited in Alabama state waters - it must be released immediately if caught, consistent with its status as a federally prohibited HMS shark species under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations.

Nurse shark is not on Alabama's prohibited species list; it falls under the 'All Other Shark Species' category (54" minimum fork length, 1 per person per day). Recreational shark fishing is open year-round in AL state waters (only commercial harvest follows a weekday-only federal-linked season), but anglers must use non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks with natural bait, cannot chum/bloodbait within 300 ft of shore or from piers, and a valid NOAA HMS Angling permit with shark endorsement is required per federal HMS rules that apply alongside state limits.

Oceanic whitetip shark is a NOAA HMS prohibited species; it is listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. Federal HMS regulations apply in all U.S. Atlantic waters, including the Gulf of Mexico, and supersede state limits for this species — no retention or possession is allowed by commercial or recreational fishermen. Sharks must be released in the water with minimal harm. Alabama's own state size/creel limit list (outdooralabama.com) does not separately enumerate oceanic whitetip among its named prohibited sharks, but the species is unambiguously covered by the federal prohibited shark species group that governs Alabama state waters for this HMS species.

Pigfish are classified as a grunt species, which falls under Alabama's reef fish aggregate bag limit. The official Outdoor Alabama size/creel limit chart states there is a twenty (20) fish aggregate creel limit for reef fish species (for example, grunts, porgies, gray triggerfish, lane snapper, etc.) for which there is no other bag limit. No separate minimum size limit is published for pigfish/grunts specifically.

Porbeagle is not individually listed or prohibited in Alabama state regulations, so it falls under the catch-all 'All Other Shark Species' category: 54 in. minimum fork length (30 in. dressed), 1 shark per person per day. No closed season is specified for this category in AL state waters; commercial shark seasons close in state waters when federal waters close. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when using natural bait for sharks. Note: porbeagle is a cold-water pelagic species rarely encountered in Alabama/Gulf waters, but the state size/bag rule applies if one is caught. This is a state-water rule; federal Atlantic HMS shark rules (NOAA) apply concurrently and also list porbeagle as a retainable pelagic shark at 54" FL, one per vessel per trip, with a requirement to release it if a tuna/swordfish/billfish is aboard.
Slot limit: 16–26 inches total length. One fish over 26 inches (one 'bull red') may be retained per day. Verify current rules directly with Alabama DCNR as regulations change annually.
Slot 16-26 in total length. No red drum may be possessed in federal waters by anyone under Alabama jurisdiction.
Vessels holding a federal reef-fish for-hire permit fish the federal season, which closed at 12:01 a.m. on October 26, 2026. Separate from the private and state-charter season.

rows.season: Closed — the 2026 private angler season closed Nov 16, 2026 when the quota was met.
rows.notes: Private boats, shore and pier anglers, and state-licensed charters without a federal reef fish permit. Alabama closed the season at 12:01 a.m. on November 16, 2026 to stay within its 664,552 lb allocation. 2027 dates are announced in the spring.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season; NOAA HMS Angling/Charterboat permit required)
rows.notes: Alabama does not publish a separate state size/bag limit for Atlantic sailfish. Per Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-3-.30, species regulated federally (like HMS billfish) must follow the applicable federal limits in Alabama waters. NOAA's Atlantic HMS rule sets a 63-inch lower-jaw-fork-length (LJFL) minimum size for sailfish and a 1-fish-per-harvester-per-day bag limit that is aggregated across billfish species (sailfish, blue marlin, white marlin, roundscale spearfish). A valid HMS Angling or Charterboat/Headboat permit is required to target/retain sailfish. No specific vessel cap for sailfish alone was found in current sources, so boatLimit is left null rather than guessed.

rows.season: Closed year-round — no open season (prohibited species)
rows.notes: Sand Tiger Shark is listed as a prohibited species under Alabama regulations — recreational and commercial harvest, possession, and landing are unlawful in Alabama state waters, matching NOAA HMS prohibited species status federally. Catch-and-release only; sharks may not be removed from the water if caught incidentally, per Alabama's careful catch-and-release guidance for prohibited species.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season / harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Sandbar shark is a prohibited species in Alabama state waters for both recreational and commercial harvest, with a narrow exception only for anglers possessing a NOAA Fisheries sandbar shark research permit. This mirrors NOAA HMS federal prohibited species status for sandbar shark. No retention, size, or bag limits apply since harvest is not permitted for the general public — must be released if caught.

Alabama state waters recreational limit for Scalloped Hammerhead: 78 inches minimum fork length, 1 shark per person per day (combined with Smooth Hammerhead category). Scalloped hammerhead is NOT on Alabama's prohibited-shark list. Alabama shark seasons close in state waters when the corresponding federal (NOAA HMS Gulf) season closes, so anglers should verify no active federal closure before retaining. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks required when using natural bait for sharks.

rows.season: Open April 1 - December 31, 2026 (closed January 1 - March 31, 2026); Alabama state waters open/close with the federal Gulf season for scamp grouper
rows.notes: Scamp is part of Alabama's mixed-species grouper aggregate: 4 fish per person total, with no more than 2 red grouper and 2 gag grouper counted within that aggregate (scamp, black, and yellowfin grouper are not individually sub-capped but share the 4-fish aggregate). Minimum size is 16 inches total length. Alabama state-water season for scamp tracks the Gulf federal season, which for 2026 remains closed Jan 1-Mar 31 and open the rest of the year; NOAA's new fixed Jan1-June30 closure for the 'Other Shallow-Water Grouper' complex (scamp, yellowmouth, black, yellowfin) does not take effect until January 1, 2027.

Sevengill shark (Heptranchias perlo) is on Alabama's prohibited species list — recreational AND commercial harvest is banned in Alabama state waters year-round; no possession, size, or bag limit applies because retention is illegal. Must be released immediately. This aligns with its status as a NOAA Atlantic HMS-managed/prohibited shark species, so federal and state rules agree here.
Minimum 12 in fork length.

Shortfin mako sharks are a prohibited species in Alabama state waters - must be released immediately with minimal injury. This aligns with the federal NOAA Atlantic HMS zero retention limit in place since July 2022. Alabama's 2025 regulation update explicitly added shortfin mako to the prohibited species list to mirror adjacent federal waters rules.

Silky shark is an Atlantic HMS prohibited species; retention limit is zero for both recreational and commercial fisheries. Must be released immediately with minimal injury, without removing from the water. Federal NOAA HMS rules apply regardless of state (Alabama) jurisdiction.

rows.season: Closed / No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus griseus) is listed as a prohibited species under Alabama's saltwater fishing regulations. Recreational and commercial harvest is banned in Alabama state waters; any caught must be released without removal from the water.

Alabama state waters: 12-inch minimum total length, 15 fish per angler per day bag limit. No maximum size or boat limit confirmed. Regulations should be verified directly with Alabama DCNR as they are subject to annual change.

Smooth hammerhead is a federally-managed HMS shark; NOAA HMS rules apply in AL state waters (ADCNR explicitly defers shark regs to federal rules). Minimum size is 78 in. measured as fork length. Limit is 1 hammerhead (great/smooth/scalloped combined) PER VESSEL per trip, not per angler. Cannot be retained if a swordfish, tuna, or billfish is aboard. A valid HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement is required. Smooth hammerhead retention is prohibited only in the U.S. Caribbean, not in the Gulf/Atlantic, so AL Gulf waters remain open.

Snowy grouper has no recreational minimum size limit and falls under Alabama's Mixed Species Grouper Aggregate Creel Limit of 4 grouper per person per day (no more than 2 red grouper and no more than 2 gag grouper may be included within that 4-fish aggregate; snowy, black, scamp, yellowmouth, yellowfin, warsaw, yellowedge, and speckled hind count toward the same 4-fish total). Snowy grouper is part of the Gulf 'deep-water grouper complex,' which is NOT subject to the Feb 1-Mar 31 seaward-of-20-fathom closure that applies to shallow-water grouper species (scamp, black, yellowmouth, yellowfin) and red grouper, so Alabama state-water harvest of snowy grouper remains open year-round under current regulations.

rows.season: Closed Nov 1 - Nov 30; open the rest of the year
rows.notes: Minimum 14 in total length. Harvest is prohibited statewide November 1-30.
Daily limit 15.

Speckled Hind is managed under the Gulf 'Deepwater Grouper' complex (with Warsaw, snowy, and yellowedge grouper) and has been closed to all recreational and commercial harvest in Gulf federal waters for years due to severely overfished stock status. Alabama Admin. Code r. 220-3-.46 requires Alabama state waters to mirror federal open/closed status for all Gulf Reef Fish species — when federal waters are closed to a species' harvest, Alabama state waters close to that species as well. Since federal Gulf harvest of speckled hind remains prohibited (zero bag limit), Alabama state waters harvest is likewise prohibited. No minimum/maximum size applies because retention is not allowed at all.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational); state shark season closes automatically if/when corresponding federal Gulf shark season closes
rows.notes: Spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) is not individually listed or prohibited in Alabama's saltwater regulations; it falls under the catch-all 'All Other Shark Species' category. That category requires a 54-inch minimum fork length (or 30 inches dressed/carcass length) and a 1-shark-per-person daily bag limit. Alabama's Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-3-.30 confirms 'All other shark species' bag limit = 1, and does not include spiny dogfish on the prohibited species list. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when using natural bait for sharks. No AL-specific closed season was found for recreational shark fishing in state waters, but state waters close to shark harvest concurrently with any federal Gulf shark season closure.

Spotted Eagle Ray is listed as a prohibited species in Alabama state waters — recreational and commercial harvest and possession are unlawful year-round. This is a statewide prohibition (Alabama Admin. Code r. 220-3-.30) and does not vary by season.
Slot 15-22 in total length; one of the six may exceed 22 in.

Alabama Marine Resources Division (MRD) sets a general daily bag limit of 2 Striped Bass for fish caught within MRD jurisdiction (Rule 220-3-.30), with no closed season. Note: a separate, more restrictive rule applies specifically in the Dog, East Fowl, Fish, Fowl, Perdido, and West Fowl Rivers (Mobile/Baldwin Counties), where a 16-inch minimum size and 2-fish bag limit apply. No boat limit is specified — limits are per angler.

Alabama DCNR regulates 'Flounder' as a single category covering all flounder species encountered in state waters (primarily southern and Gulf flounder; summer flounder would fall under this same generic rule if encountered). Recreational limit is 14-inch minimum total length, 5 fish per person per day, with harvest prohibited the entire month of November. Commercial limits differ (40/person or vessel, 80 for gillnet) and do not apply to recreational anglers.

Swordfish is a federally-managed Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) — NOAA rules apply in ALL waters, including Alabama state waters; Alabama DCNR does not set separate limits for this species. Minimum size is 47 inches lower-jaw fork length (LJFL), OR 25 inches cleithrum-to-caudal-keel length if the fish was damaged by a shark bite and the head/tail section is retained instead. Bag limit is 1 fish per person. Vessel limit varies by permit/vessel type: 4 per trip for private recreational (HMS Angling permit) vessels, 6 per trip for charter vessels, and 15 per trip for headboats — captain and crew do not count toward the limit on for-hire vessels and have a zero bag/possession limit themselves. Swordfish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded from the vessel. A federal HMS Angling or HMS Charterboat/Headboat permit is required to fish for swordfish in federal waters, but per FWC guidance this permit is NOT required when fishing for swordfish in state waters (though the federal size/bag rules still apply). All swordfish landings must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours.

Alabama's saltwater regulation code (Rule 220-3-.30) lists a single generic 'Snook' size/bag limit that applies to the genus Centropomus (which includes swordspine snook, Centropomus ensiferus) in Alabama state waters — there is no species-specific carve-out for swordspine snook separate from common snook. This is a newly created rule (first regulated in 2025) with no closed season specified; it is a size/bag-limited, open year-round fishery. Commercial limit is also 1 fish.

Tiger shark is not on Alabama's list of prohibited shark species, so it falls under the 'All Other Shark Species' category: 54 inch minimum fork length (30" dressed), 1 shark per person per day. No closed recreational season is specified for this category on the current size/creel chart; commercial shark seasons close in state waters when federal Gulf shark seasons close, but this closure language is listed under the commercial license page, not the recreational creel limit chart. Anglers should also note it is unlawful to target/chum for sharks from piers/beaches in a manner unsafe to swimmers.
Daily limit 3.

Vermilion snapper in Alabama state waters are subject to federal Gulf reef fish regulations that are incorporated by reference. The bag limit for vermilion snapper in the Gulf is managed under NOAA/GULF COUNCIL rules — state-specific per-angler limits should be verified directly at the Alabama DCNR source URL. A 10-inch minimum size limit is commonly cited but confirm current value.

Wahoo does not appear as a separately listed line-item with its own size/bag limit on Alabama's official saltwater creel/size limit chart or in Admin Code 220-3-.30, unlike heavily-regulated species (red snapper, grouper, amberjack, red drum, etc.). Alabama's rule text notes a general 20-fish aggregate creel limit applies only to 'reef fish species... for which there is no other bag limit' (Gulf Reef Fish Table, 50 CFR 622 App. A) — wahoo is a coastal migratory pelagic, not a reef fish, so that aggregate limit does not clearly apply to it either. No closed season for wahoo is referenced anywhere in AL DCNR materials, consistent with neighboring states (FL: no closed season) so 'Year-round' is used for season, but numeric bag/size limits could not be confirmed from Alabama's own chart and are left null rather than guessed.

Wahoo is not a Highly Migratory Species under NOAA HMS federal management. Alabama DCNR does not appear to publish a specific bag limit, minimum size, or closed season for wahoo in state waters based on available training data. Verify directly with the Alabama DCNR saltwater fishing regulations page.

White marlin is a federally-managed Atlantic HMS species; NOAA HMS rules apply in Alabama state waters (Alabama has no separate state size/bag limit for billfish and Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-3-.30 requires species without a state limit to follow federal rules). Minimum size is 66" lower-jaw fork length (LJFL). There is no per-angler daily bag limit for white marlin, but retention is capped by a combined annual U.S. landing limit of 250 fish for blue marlin, white marlin, and roundscale spearfish combined. Billfish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded, and a valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit is required.

Yellowtail snapper in Alabama state waters subject to a 10-inch minimum total length and a 10-fish per angler aggregate bag limit. Verify current regulations at the Alabama DCNR source URL as rules may have changed.

Yellowtail snapper in Alabama state waters subject to a 10-inch minimum total length and a 10-fish per angler aggregate bag limit. Verify current regulations at the Alabama DCNR source URL as rules may have changed.

African pompano is not a federally-managed 'reef fish' species under the Gulf of Mexico Reef Fish FMP (unlike red snapper, grouper, amberjack, or triggerfish) — NOAA/GMFMC has no distinct ACL, season, or size/bag rule for it in Gulf federal waters. Florida's FWC minimum size (24" fork length), bag limit (2 per harvester), and vessel cap (2 per vessel) explicitly extend into adjacent federal Gulf waters for vessels operating from/landing in Florida, with hook-and-line and spearing allowed offshore. No closed season is published, so it is treated as open year-round. Anglers landing in other Gulf states (AL, MS, LA, TX) should confirm that state's own African pompano rule, as it is not uniformly codified at the federal level.

Albacore Tuna is an HMS species managed federally by NOAA HMS. No minimum size or bag limit is currently specified for recreational anglers in federal Gulf waters under NOAA HMS regulations, but HMS Angling permit or HMS Charter/Headboat permit may be required depending on vessel type. Verify current HMS regulations as they are updated frequently.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season for Almaco Jack in Gulf federal waters)
rows.notes: Almaco jack has no species-specific size or season limit in Gulf federal waters (unlike greater amberjack, which has a 34-inch minimum size and seasonal closures, or lesser amberjack/banded rudderfish, which have a slot limit). Almaco jack falls under the 'Gulf reef fish, combined' aggregate bag limit of 20 fish per person per day (50 CFR 622.38(b)(5)) for reef fish species without an individual bag limit — this is a shared cap across all such unspecified reef fish, not a species-specific allowance. A dehooking tool, non-stainless steel circle hooks with natural bait, and a venting tool/descending device are required when fishing for Gulf reef fish.

rows.season: No open season — retention prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Atlantic angel shark (Squatina dumeril) is listed as a Prohibited Species under NOAA's Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) shark management program, which governs all U.S. federal Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico waters. It must be released immediately without removing it from the water, using gear that minimizes injury. This applies to both commercial and recreational fishermen.

Atlantic sharpnose shark (a small coastal shark) has no minimum fork length and a recreational bag limit of 1 per person per trip, with no closed season under current NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations (applies coastwide, including Gulf federal waters). A vessel must have a valid HMS Angling or Charterboat/Headboat permit with shark endorsement. Note: NOAA proposed a rule (Jan 5, 2026, comment period extended to May 29, 2026) that would change this to 1 per VESSEL per trip instead of 1 per person, but as of the most recent official update this has NOT been finalized — the per-person limit remains in effect. Check back for a final rule.

rows.season: Year-round (no federal seasonal closure currently in effect for Gulf banded rudderfish/lesser amberjack)
rows.notes: Banded rudderfish is managed jointly with lesser amberjack in the Gulf 'Jacks Complex' under the Gulf Reef Fish FMP. Federal rule (50 CFR 622.37) sets a 14 to 22 inch fork length slot limit, and the two species share a 5-fish aggregate daily bag limit (50 CFR 622.38), separate from the general reef fish aggregate bag limit. NOAA's current Gulf seasonal closures page does not list banded rudderfish/lesser amberjack among species with an active seasonal closure, indicating the fishery remains open year-round unless an in-season closure notice is issued if the annual catch limit is projected to be met.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species - no retention permitted)
rows.notes: Basking sharks are federally classified as a prohibited shark species under NOAA's Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) regulations, which govern Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean waters. They must be released immediately with minimal injury, without removing them from the water. This is not a GMFMC reef fish/migratory species regulation but an HMS rule that overrides state and regional fishing seasons — retention is never legal regardless of season.

rows.season: Year-round closure (prohibited species - no open season)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sand Tiger Shark (Odontaspis noronhai) is designated a 'prohibited species' under NOAA Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) regulations (50 CFR part 635), which govern shark fishing in the U.S. Atlantic, Gulf of America (formerly Gulf of Mexico), and Caribbean. It may not be retained, possessed, sold, or purchased in commercial or recreational fisheries and must be released immediately with minimal injury, without removing it from the water. This is a federal rule, not a Gulf-specific GMFMC reef fish season.

rows.season: Year-round closed (prohibited species - no retention allowed)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus nakamurai) is classified by NOAA as a prohibited Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) shark. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water; it may not be retained, possessed, sold, or purchased in any form, in commercial or recreational fisheries, in any Atlantic HMS jurisdiction including the Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico) federal waters.

rows.season: Year-round closure (no open season) — prohibited species
rows.notes: Bigeye Thresher Shark is a NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited species in all U.S. Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America), and Caribbean waters. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and cannot be boated, possessed, or landed by recreational anglers under any HMS permit.

Bigeye tuna is managed under NOAA Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) rules, which apply uniformly across the Atlantic, Gulf of America, and Caribbean federal waters — there is no separate Gulf-specific rule. Minimum size is 27 inches curved fork length, and there is no recreational daily bag/possession limit for bigeye tuna. A valid HMS Angling or HMS Charterboat/Headboat permit is required, and bigeye tuna cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard.

rows.season: Closed year-round — Bignose Shark is a prohibited species; no open season
rows.notes: Bignose Shark is federally listed as a PROHIBITED species under NOAA Atlantic HMS shark regulations. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and cannot be retained by recreational or commercial anglers in any US Atlantic, Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico), or Caribbean waters. This is a ridgeback shark species on the prohibited list.

rows.season: Year-round, except closed Feb 1, 2027 – Mar 31, 2027 seaward of the ~20-fathom contour; closed Jan 1, 2027 – Jun 30, 2027 and every year after.
rows.notes: From Jan 1, 2027 harvest of the other shallow-water groupers (black, yellowmouth, scamp, yellowfin) is prohibited Jan 1 – Jun 30 each year.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational Atlantic HMS shark fishery, Gulf of America federal waters) — 2026
rows.notes: Blacknose shark is managed as an Atlantic HMS 'small coastal shark' species. Minimum size is 54 inches fork length. The retention limit is an AGGREGATE of 1 shark per vessel per trip drawn from a shared list of species (including blacktip, bull, hammerheads, lemon, nurse, spinner, tiger, blue, thresher, porbeagle, sharpnose, finetooth, blacknose, and bonnethead) — not 1 blacknose specifically plus others. Vessel must have a valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit with shark endorsement, and use non-offset/non-stainless circle hooks. A proposed rule (published Jan 5, 2026, comment period closed May 29, 2026) would revise blacknose minimum size and retention limits and remove the Atlantic/Gulf management boundary, but as of Aug 3, 2026 no final rule has been published, so current regulations remain in effect. Three areas are closed seasonally to recreational blacknose shark fishing (see HMS Compliance Guide for coordinates/dates).

rows.season: Year-round — no targeted fishing for Atlantic Bluefin Tuna allowed in Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico) federal waters (2026)
rows.notes: NOAA Fisheries prohibits targeted/directed fishing for Atlantic Bluefin Tuna in the Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico). Retention is only allowed for incidentally caught trophy-sized bluefin (73 inches curved fork length or greater) while fishing for other HMS, limited to 1 per vessel per day, subject to the small Gulf incidental 'trophy' subquota which can close the fishery early. All bluefin under 73 inches CFL caught in the Gulf must be released immediately, handled to maximize survival and without removing from the water. This is a standing federal regulation (50 CFR part 635), not a seasonal opening.

Bonefish is not a species managed under a Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council (GMFMC) Fishery Management Plan, so NOAA Fisheries' Gulf federal-waters reef fish/pelagic regulations page does not list a bonefish season. Florida's state regulation (Fla. Admin. Code R. 68B-34.004) prohibits all harvest and possession of bonefish and explicitly extends this catch-and-release-only rule into federal waters off Florida. A recreational angler may only temporarily possess one bonefish at a time, solely for photographing/measuring/weighing at the catch site, then must release it alive immediately in the same area. No commercial harvest is allowed at all.

Atlantic bonito is not managed under any federal fishery management plan in Gulf waters. It was not included in the Coastal Migratory Pelagics FMP (jointly managed by GMFMC/SAFMC) alongside similar species like little tunny and king mackerel, and it is not regulated as an HMS species (tunas/sharks/swordfish/billfish) by NOAA HMS — confirmed by state references explicitly excluding 'Atlantic bonito, little tunny (false albacore), and blackfin tuna' from HMS permit requirements. No federal season, size limit, or bag/boat limit currently exists for this species in Gulf federal waters; anglers may retain it year-round subject to any applicable state regulations in state waters.

Federal HMS management (NOAA/GMFMC & SAFMC jointly via HMS division) — bonnethead shark is managed as part of the small coastal shark complex with no closed season currently in effect and no minimum size limit. Anglers must have a valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit with a shark endorsement, and must use non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks (except with flies/artificial lures). Bag limit is 1 bonnethead per person per trip (not per vessel).

rows.season: Year-round (open), subject to in-season closure by NOAA Fisheries if landings approach quota, 2026
rows.notes: Bull shark is managed under NOAA's 'Aggregated Large Coastal Shark' recreational group (with blacktip, lemon, nurse, spinner, tiger). Federal recreational retention limit is 1 shark per vessel per trip (not per angler) from this group, with minimum 54-inch fork length. Applies to Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico) federal waters as NOAA HMS manages sharks Atlantic-wide, including the Gulf. A Jan 2026 Federal Register proposed rule (Amendment 14) may revise these limits later in 2026, but as of Aug 25, 2026 the status-quo 54-inch/1-per-vessel rule remains in effect.

Caribbean Reef Shark is a federally designated PROHIBITED SPECIES under the Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) FMP (50 CFR 635), applicable in all federal Gulf of America/Gulf of Mexico waters. Recreational and commercial retention is prohibited year-round. Anglers must release any Caribbean Reef Shark immediately with minimal injury, keeping the fish in the water. No minimum size, slot, or bag/boat limit applies because retention is not permitted at all. HMS rules (NOAA) govern this species uniformly across all Gulf federal waters regardless of state.

rows.season: Year-round — Caribbean Sharpnose Shark retention prohibited
rows.notes: Caribbean sharpnose shark is a NOAA Atlantic HMS 'prohibited species.' It must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water — no retention is allowed in any U.S. Atlantic, Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico), or Caribbean federal waters, for recreational or commercial fisheries. This applies regardless of season.

rows.season: Year-round (Gulf of Mexico/Gulf of America Zone, federal waters)
rows.notes: Applies to the Gulf of Mexico Zone (west of the Florida East Coast Zone) under the Gulf Council. Minimum fork length is 36 inches. Vessel limit of 2 fish per trip may not exceed the per-person daily bag limit, so a max of 2 anglers' worth of cobia per boat regardless of passenger count over 2. No closed season is currently in effect for the Gulf Zone (unlike the Florida East Coast/Atlantic zones, which do have seasonal closures under separate ASMFC/SAFMC rules). The 2-fish-per-day allowance for multi-day for-hire trips does not apply to cobia.

In Gulf of America federal waters, cubera snapper have a 12-inch TL minimum size and NO closed season. Cubera count fully within the 10-fish per person Gulf snapper aggregate bag limit (which excludes only red, vermilion, and lane snapper) regardless of size — the additional 'up to 2 fish over 30 inches not counted in the aggregate' allowance is a South Atlantic-off-Florida provision (50 CFR 622.187/622.44) and does NOT apply in Gulf federal waters. There is no separate vessel/boat limit for cubera in the Gulf.

rows.season: Year-round (open, subject to in-season NOAA quota closures)
rows.notes: Finetooth sharks are managed under the Consolidated Atlantic HMS FMP and apply identically in Gulf federal waters. They fall into the 'all other sharks' recreational retention category (grouped with blacktip, bull, hammerheads, spinner, tiger, etc.); permitted vessels may land only ONE shark total from that category per trip (a per-vessel, not per-angler, limit). Minimum fork length is 54 inches. Shark must be landed with fins naturally attached. Requires HMS Angling/Charter-Headboat permit with shark endorsement, non-offset non-stainless circle hooks. Some areas/times are closed to recreational finetooth shark fishing — check the HMS Recreational Compliance Guide for coordinates. A pending 2026 rulemaking (comment period closed May 29, 2026) proposes lowering the minimum size for the finetooth/blacknose group, but as of this check that change is NOT yet finalized/in effect.
Closed annually Jan 1 – Aug 31. The 2026 season opened Sept 1 and closed Oct 1, 2026.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species, no open season)
rows.notes: Galapagos shark is on NOAA's federal Atlantic HMS prohibited shark species list. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and may not be retained, landed, or possessed in Gulf of Mexico federal waters at any time of year. This prohibition applies to all HMS-permitted vessels regardless of state or federal waters.

rows.season: Harvest prohibited in federal Gulf waters.
rows.notes: Goliath grouper harvest has been prohibited in Gulf federal waters by the GMFMC since March 1990. NOAA's official species page confirms the fishery 'is still closed to harvest by the South Atlantic, Gulf, and Caribbean fishery management councils.' All goliath grouper caught in federal Gulf waters must be released immediately; there is no recreational retention allowed. Note: Florida operates a separate limited lottery harvest tag program (e.g., Mar 1–May 31, 2026) but that applies ONLY in Florida STATE waters, not federal Gulf waters — do not conflate the two.

rows.season: Open — closed Jan 1, 2027 – Feb 28, 2027 and Jun 1, 2027 – Jul 31, 2027.
rows.notes: Sub-cap of 1 within the 20-fish reef-fish aggregate. An in-season closure can come earlier.

Great hammerhead is managed as part of NOAA's Large Coastal Shark 'Hammerhead' group (great, scalloped, smooth). Recreational minimum size is 78 inches fork length. The vessel limit is 1 hammerhead OR other authorized large/small coastal shark per vessel per trip (not per angler) - it is an aggregate 'one shark' vessel limit, not a per-person bag limit. Hammerheads cannot be retained if any tuna, swordfish, or billfish is on board. Vessel must hold a valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit with a shark endorsement. This rule is uniform across the Atlantic HMS program for Atlantic, Gulf of America, and Caribbean recreational fisheries; the only regional difference is that great/smooth/scalloped hammerheads are fully prohibited (no retention at all) specifically in the U.S. Caribbean EEZ - that prohibition does NOT apply to Gulf of Mexico federal waters, where retention remains open under the above size/limit rules.

rows.season: Closed — the 2026 season closed Oct 14, 2026 when the quota was met.
rows.notes: Closed Nov 1 – Jul 31 and Aug 1 – Aug 31, so the season runs Sept 1 – Oct 31; the 2026 season closed early on Oct 14.

rows.season: Closed - No open season (year-round harvest prohibition)
rows.notes: Gulf sturgeon (Acipenser oxyrinchus desotoi) and Atlantic sturgeon (Acipenser oxyrinchus oxyrinchus) are both ESA-listed (Gulf sturgeon threatened since 1991; Atlantic sturgeon endangered/threatened by DPS since 2012) and are federally protected prohibited species in all U.S. waters, including Gulf of Mexico federal waters managed under GMFMC. NOAA Fisheries states it is illegal to fish for, catch, or keep sturgeon, including Atlantic, Shortnose, and Gulf. Any accidental hooking must be released immediately with minimal handling, kept in the water; removal from water (including for photos) is prohibited. No recreational harvest, possession, or retention is permitted under any circumstance.
Gulf federal waters north of Cape Sable. 14 in fork length, five per harvester.

rows.season: Year-round — no federal recreational seasonal closure.
rows.notes: Gulf migratory group. The Southern Zone gillnet closure is commercial only.

rows.season: Open year-round (recreational retention authorized, no closed season)
rows.notes: Lemon shark is managed as a Large Coastal Shark (non-ridgeback LCS) under NOAA's Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) program, which applies uniformly across Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean federal waters (GMFMC does not set separate shark rules; NOAA HMS governs). Minimum size is 54 inches fork length; retention limit is 1 shark per vessel per trip (not per angler), combined with other 'all other sharks' species in that trip limit. Requires HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement and non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks. Note: a 2026 NOAA proposed rule (Federal Register, published Jan 5, 2026) may eventually revise lemon shark size/retention limits, but as of Oct 24, 2026 the current regulations remain in effect.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season for lesser amberjack in Gulf federal waters)
rows.notes: Lesser amberjack is managed jointly with banded rudderfish under a slot limit (14"-22" fork length) and a 5-fish daily aggregate bag limit for the two species combined (not 5 lesser amberjack individually). This aggregate limit is excluded from the 20-fish Gulf reef fish aggregate. Unlike greater amberjack, there is currently no seasonal closure specific to lesser amberjack/banded rudderfish in Gulf federal waters.

Longbill spearfish is a federally managed Atlantic HMS billfish. Harvest, retention, and landing of longbill spearfish is prohibited in all U.S. Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico waters (state and federal) — anglers must release any longbill spearfish caught. This differs from other spearfish/marlin species (e.g., roundscale spearfish, white/blue marlin) which have minimum sizes and a combined 250-fish annual U.S. landings limit.

Longfin mako shark (Isurus paucus) is listed on NOAA's Atlantic HMS prohibited shark species list. It must be released with minimal injury and cannot be retained in any U.S. Atlantic HMS fishery, including the Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America) federal waters managed under this framework. This is a NOAA HMS-wide rule, not a GMFMC-specific season, and applies regardless of state or region.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season for gray/mangrove snapper in Gulf federal waters), 2026
rows.notes: Gray (mangrove) snapper in Gulf of Mexico federal waters is managed under a 12-inch total length minimum size limit (50 CFR 622.185(a)(3), covering cubera, gray, and yellowtail snappers) and falls within the 10-fish aggregate Gulf reef fish snapper bag limit rather than having its own standalone daily bag number. There is no federal seasonal closure specific to gray snapper in the Gulf. Note this differs from Florida STATE waters, where FWC sets a separate 10-inch minimum and 5-fish species-specific bag limit within the 10-fish aggregate — this record is for FEDERAL Gulf waters only.

Mutton snapper in Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico) federal waters has no closed season and may be harvested year-round. The 5-fish daily bag limit is counted within (not in addition to) the 10-snapper aggregate bag limit for Gulf reef fish. Minimum size is 18 inches total length for both recreational and commercial harvest. These measures were set by a 2018 NOAA final rule (effective July 23, 2018) and remain the current federal Gulf regulation as of this check; no more recent rule change was found. Anglers fishing Gulf federal reef fish waters must also carry a venting tool or descending device per the DESCEND Act.

rows.season: No open season — prohibited species, no retention allowed year-round
rows.notes: Narrowtooth shark (Carcharhinus brachyurus) is classified as a prohibited HMS shark species in the U.S. Atlantic, Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico), and Caribbean. It must be released immediately with minimal harm and cannot be retained, possessed, or landed under any circumstances by recreational or commercial fishermen.

Night shark (Carcharhinus signatus) is designated a Prohibited Species under NOAA's Atlantic HMS regulations (50 CFR 635), applicable in all U.S. Atlantic waters including the Gulf of Mexico/Gulf of America. Retention is never allowed; if caught, it must be released immediately with minimal injury, kept in the water, and not removed from the water at any time.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational Atlantic shark fishery is open; no closed season for Large Coastal Sharks in Gulf federal waters as of Aug 2026)
rows.notes: Nurse shark is managed as a non-ridgeback Large Coastal 'Other Shark' under NOAA Atlantic HMS rules, which apply uniformly to Gulf federal waters. Recreational minimum size is 54 inches fork length. The retention limit is 1 shark per vessel per trip, chosen from an approved list that includes nurse, blacktip, bull, lemon, spinner, tiger, and other species combined (not 1-per-angler). A valid HMS Angling/Charter permit with shark endorsement and non-offset circle hooks are required. NOAA has an open rulemaking (proposed rule, Jan 2026) that could revise size/bag limits for nurse and other LCS species later in 2026 — recheck before publishing long-term.

Oceanic whitetip sharks are a prohibited HMS species. Commercial and recreational retention/possession is banned in all U.S. federal Atlantic/Gulf of Mexico/Caribbean waters. The species is also listed as threatened under the ESA (since 2018). Any oceanic whitetip caught must be released immediately without removing it from the water, using gear/methods that maximize survival. There is no open season, size limit, or bag limit since retention is never allowed.

Permit is not managed under a Gulf Council federal FMP; Florida FWC regulations (which explicitly extend to adjacent federal waters) govern harvest in Gulf federal waters off Florida. General statewide/Gulf rule: 11-inch fork length minimum, 6-fish daily bag limit, open year-round. A separate 'Special Permit Zone' (state and adjacent federal waters off SE Florida/Keys, roughly Biscayne Bay south through waters off Cape Sable) instead uses an 11–22 inch fork-length slot limit, with 1 fish over 22 inches allowed within the per-person bag. If your vessel is fishing in that southeast Florida/Keys zone, the slot limit applies instead of the straight 11-inch minimum.

rows.season: Year-round (Atlantic HMS recreational shark fishery, includes Gulf of America/Gulf of Mexico federal waters), 2026
rows.notes: Porbeagle is managed under NOAA's Atlantic HMS 'Pelagic Sharks' group and is an authorized (retainable) species for recreational anglers with an HMS Angling/Charterboat permit + shark endorsement. Minimum size is 54 inches fork length, measured straight-line snout to tail fork. Bag limit is 1 shark per vessel per trip (aggregated across the authorized shark group, not per angler). Porbeagle sharks alive at haulback must be released unharmed if a tuna, swordfish, or billfish is aboard. These HMS rules apply uniformly in federal Gulf of Mexico/Gulf of America waters as they are managed coastwide by NOAA, not the GMFMC.

Queen snapper is managed under the Gulf of America Reef Fish FMP as part of the 'other snapper' group within the 10-fish aggregate snapper bag limit; it does not have a species-specific bag limit or minimum size limit. No closed season currently applies to queen snapper in Gulf federal waters (unlike red snapper, which has separate season restrictions). Anglers must use non-offset circle hooks with natural bait and have venting/descending gear ready per Gulf reef fish gear rules.

Sailfish is a NOAA-managed Atlantic HMS billfish; federal rules apply in Gulf federal waters regardless of state. Minimum size is 63" measured lower-jaw to fork length. Bag limit is 1 fish per person, not to exceed 4 per recreational (non-for-hire) vessel per day/trip (for-hire/charter vessels may retain up to 15 per vessel, 6 for charter boats per some state summaries — recreational cap of 4/vessel used here as the standard private-vessel limit). Billfish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded. Vessel must have a valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit; all landed sailfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours (800-894-5528 or hmspermits.noaa.gov). Released sailfish may not be removed from the water in federal waters.

Sand tiger shark (Carcharias taurus) is a NOAA HMS-managed 'prohibited species' in all U.S. Atlantic Ocean waters, including the Gulf of Mexico, under the Consolidated Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan. It has been illegal to land this species recreationally or commercially since 1997/2000. Anglers must release sand tiger sharks immediately with minimal injury and without removing them from the water — no possession, landing, or sale is permitted anywhere in federal Gulf waters.

Sandbar shark is designated a Prohibited Species under the Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan (applies to Gulf of America/Gulf of Mexico, Atlantic, and Caribbean federal waters). No recreational or general commercial retention is allowed; any sandbar shark caught must be released immediately with minimal injury without removing it from the water. Only permitted Shark Research Fishery participants with an observer aboard may land sandbar sharks for scientific data collection — this is not open to recreational anglers.

rows.season: Year-round (open access, subject to NOAA HMS shark season/quota status)
rows.notes: Scalloped hammerhead is an AUTHORIZED (not prohibited) recreational shark species in federal Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America) waters under Atlantic HMS regulations — the retention ban only applies in the U.S. Caribbean (effective Feb 2, 2024). In the Gulf, it is grouped with great and smooth hammerhead: 78-inch fork-length minimum, and the bag limit is 1 hammerhead shark OR any other authorized shark per vessel per trip (not per angler) — retaining any hammerhead also means no other 'other' shark may be kept. Hammerhead sharks cannot be retained if tuna, swordfish, or billfish is aboard. Requires HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement, non-offset non-stainless circle hooks.

rows.season: Year-round, except closed Feb 1, 2027 – Mar 31, 2027 seaward of the ~20-fathom contour; closed Jan 1, 2027 – Jun 30, 2027 and every year after.
rows.notes: From Jan 1, 2027 harvest of the other shallow-water groupers (black, yellowmouth, scamp, yellowfin) is prohibited Jan 1 – Jun 30 each year.

rows.season: Year-round closed to retention (no open season — prohibited species)
rows.notes: Sharpnose sevengill shark is classified as a Prohibited Species under NOAA Atlantic HMS shark regulations (50 CFR 635), which govern all U.S. Atlantic waters including the Gulf of America/Gulf of Mexico EEZ. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water; no recreational or commercial retention is permitted at any time. This applies regardless of state or federal jurisdiction within Gulf federal waters.

Shortfin mako shark is a prohibited species in all U.S. Atlantic HMS fisheries, which includes federal Gulf of Mexico waters. The retention limit has been zero since July 5, 2022, and remains in effect in 2026 per NOAA's current shark regulations page and 2026 landings update. Any shortfin mako caught (dead or alive) must be released immediately with minimal harm; no minimum size or bag/boat limit applies because retention is prohibited entirely.

Silky shark is a federally designated PROHIBITED species under the Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan. Recreational retention, possession, or landing is banned in all U.S. Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico federal waters, regardless of state. Any silky shark caught must be released immediately with minimal injury, without removing it from the water. This is an HMS species so federal NOAA rules apply uniformly and are not overridden by Gulf state regulations.

rows.season: Closed year-round (Prohibited species - no open season)
rows.notes: Bluntnose Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus griseus) is classified as a Prohibited Species under NOAA Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) regulations, which govern shark fishing in federal Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico) waters. It cannot be retained, possessed, purchased, or sold under any circumstances and must be released immediately if caught incidentally.

Smalltooth sawfish (U.S. DPS) is listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 2003. It is illegal to catch, harm, harass, possess, or kill this species in any U.S. waters, including Gulf of Mexico federal waters. If accidentally hooked, anglers must keep the fish in the water and cut the line as close to the hook as possible without removing it from the water; report catches to 844-4-SAWFISH or sawfish@myfwc.com. This is not a managed 'season' or bag-limit fishery — it is a full take prohibition.

Federal HMS rules apply in Gulf of America federal waters (NOAA overrides state regs here). Smooth hammerhead is managed together with great and scalloped hammerhead in NOAA's 'Hammerhead Sharks' recreational management group. Minimum size is 78 inches fork length (raised from the old 54" LCS default). The 1-shark limit is PER VESSEL PER TRIP, shared across the broader group of allowed large coastal/pelagic sharks (tiger, blacktip, bull, lemon, nurse, spinner, blue, porbeagle, common thresher, and all hammerheads) — it is not an additional 1-per-angler bag on top of that. Hammerheads cannot be retained if a tuna, swordfish, or billfish is already on board or has been offloaded. Retention of all hammerhead species is fully prohibited in the U.S. Caribbean EEZ (not applicable to Gulf). Recreational shark management groups are managed by retention limit, not quota-based season closures, so the fishery is open year-round absent a specific rule change.

Snowy Grouper in Gulf federal waters has no recreational minimum size limit and no closed season (it is a deep-water grouper species, not subject to the Feb 1–Mar 31 shallow-water grouper closure). It counts toward the 4-fish Gulf grouper aggregate daily bag limit (combined total of all grouper/tilefish species per person per day) rather than having its own individual bag limit. Bag limit for captain and crew on for-hire (charter/headboat) vessels is zero.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season currently in effect; fishing year runs Apr 1, 2025 - Mar 31, 2026)
rows.notes: Gulf migratory group Spanish mackerel recreational fishery in federal (EEZ) waters is open year-round with no scheduled closure and no trip limit; an in-season accountability measure can trigger an early federal closure if the ACL is projected to be met, but no such closure is in effect as of Aug 16, 2026. A proposed rule (Framework Amendment 14, comment period through Aug 21, 2026) would lower the annual catch limit and shift to a post-season accountability measure but does NOT change the 12-inch minimum size or 15-fish bag limit. This is the GMFMC (Gulf) regulation only — do not apply to Atlantic migratory group Spanish mackerel, which has a different bag limit (2-3 fish depending on state) under SAFMC.

Spotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari) is a federally and state-designated prohibited species in the Gulf of Mexico. No retention, landing, or possession is allowed under any circumstances; must be released immediately with minimal harm (gills kept submerged).

rows.season: Year-round (open season; subject to in-season NOAA quota closures) - 2026
rows.notes: Tiger shark is managed as part of NOAA's Atlantic HMS 'non-hammerhead Large Coastal Shark' recreational group, which applies uniformly across the Atlantic, Gulf of America, and Caribbean federal waters. Minimum size is 54 inches fork length. Retention limit is 1 shark per vessel per trip drawn from the authorized shark list (which includes tiger, blacktip, bull, lemon, nurse, spinner, blue, common thresher, porbeagle, etc.) - not 1 per angler. Vessel must have a valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit with a shark endorsement, and non-offset, non-stainless circle hooks are required. NOAA can close the season early if annual quotas are met, so anglers should check current status before each trip. A 2026 proposed rule (NOAA-NMFS-2024-0039) could revise these size/bag limits later in the year, but as of this check it had not been finalized.

No minimum size limit for Warsaw grouper in Gulf federal waters. Warsaw grouper counts within the 4-grouper-per-person aggregate bag limit, but harvest is capped at 1 warsaw grouper per VESSEL per day (shared with speckled hind, which also has its own separate 1-per-vessel cap). No recreational seasonal closure applies to Warsaw grouper specifically (unlike shallow-water grouper species such as gag/red grouper).

rows.season: Year-round (open recreational fishery, subject to change if annual landing cap is reached)
rows.notes: Minimum size is 66 inches lower-jaw fork length, and the daily bag limit is 1 fish per harvester, aggregated with roundscale spearfish. This is an Atlantic HMS-managed species — NOAA HMS regulations apply uniformly in federal Atlantic and Gulf of America waters (not managed separately by GMFMC). U.S. total recreational + commercial landings of blue marlin, white marlin, and roundscale spearfish combined are capped at 250 fish annually nationwide; NOAA can close the fishery inseason if that cap is projected to be met. Billfish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is already aboard or has been offloaded. An HMS Angling or HMS Charter/Headboat permit is required for the vessel.

Yellowfin tuna are managed federally as an Atlantic HMS species (not under the Gulf Council's reef fish/pelagic FMP), so the same NOAA HMS recreational rules apply in Gulf of America (Mexico) federal waters as elsewhere. Minimum size is 27 inches curved fork length (CFL); retention limit is 3 fish per person per day/trip. A valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit is required, and the fishery is open year-round unless NOAA issues an in-season closure notice.

rows.season: Year-round, except closed Feb 1, 2027 – Mar 31, 2027 seaward of the ~20-fathom contour; closed Jan 1, 2027 – Jun 30, 2027 and every year after.
rows.notes: From Jan 1, 2027 harvest of the other shallow-water groupers (black, yellowmouth, scamp, yellowfin) is prohibited Jan 1 – Jun 30 each year.

rows.season: Year-round in South Atlantic federal waters (open as of Aug 24, 2026); subject to in-season closure if the recreational Other Jacks Complex annual catch limit is met
rows.notes: Almaco jack is managed as part of the South Atlantic 'Other Jacks Complex' (with banded rudderfish and lesser amberjack) under the Snapper-Grouper FMP. It falls within the 20-fish aggregate South Atlantic snapper-grouper bag limit, but no more than 10 fish of any single species (including almaco jack) may be kept per person per day. No recreational minimum size limit is currently specified for almaco jack (commercial minimum is 20 inches fork length, not applicable to recreational anglers). A descending device is required on board. NOAA can close the recreational season in-season via accountability measure once the complex ACL is projected to be met (has occurred in past years, e.g., 2018, 2019, 2021); no such 2026 closure notice was found as of this check.

Atlantic Angel Shark (Squatina dumeril) is classified as a NOAA Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) prohibited shark species. It was added to the prohibited species list and must be released immediately with minimal injury without removing it from the water; commercial and recreational retention is banned in all U.S. Atlantic waters, including South Atlantic federal waters. This is a national HMS rule, not a SAFMC-specific regulation.

Atlantic mackerel (Scomber scombrus) is managed coastwide in federal waters (including the South Atlantic EEZ) under the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council's Mackerel, Squid, and Butterfish FMP, not by SAFMC. There is no recreational season closure or minimum size limit; the limit is a 20-fish-per-person possession limit for private and for-hire anglers (not a traditional 'daily bag limit,' but functions as such). No vessel/boat limit is specified for the recreational sector. This is distinct from Atlantic king/Spanish mackerel, which ARE managed by SAFMC with different size/bag rules.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed recreational season for Atlantic sharpnose shark in federal Atlantic HMS waters)
rows.notes: Atlantic sharpnose shark is managed under NOAA's Consolidated Atlantic HMS FMP, which applies uniformly to all Atlantic federal waters (including South Atlantic/SAFMC region) — it is not managed separately by SAFMC. There is no minimum size limit for Atlantic sharpnose shark. The recreational bag limit is 1 shark per person per trip/day (this is on top of, and separate from, the 1-shark-per-vessel limit for other authorized 'Large Coastal/Pelagic/Hammerhead' shark species requiring a 54" or 78" fork length).
