Anglers must hold an HMS Angling/Charter-Headboat permit with a shark endorsement and use non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks when fishing with bait.

No recreational minimum size limit in South Atlantic federal waters. Banded rudderfish has no species-specific bag limit; it is one of the species included in the 20-fish-per-person/day aggregate bag limit for 'species without an individual bag limit' (which also includes almaco jack, lesser amberjack, porgies, grunts, etc., with no more than 10 of any one species within that aggregate). It must be landed with head and fins intact. As part of the 'Other Jacks Complex' (with almaco jack and lesser amberjack), the recreational sector can be closed mid-year via NOAA accountability measure if the complex's ACL is reached (has happened in past years, e.g., 2016, 2018, 2019, 2021), reopening automatically Jan 1 of the following year. No such 2026 closure notice was found as of this check.

Basking shark is a federally designated Prohibited Species under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations. It cannot be retained, possessed, sold, or purchased in commercial or recreational fisheries anywhere in U.S. Atlantic waters (including South Atlantic EEZ). Any basking shark caught must be released immediately with minimal injury, kept in the water if possible, without removing it from the water. This applies to all HMS-permitted vessels; SAFMC federal waters regs are also subject to NOAA HMS rules under 50 CFR 635.

rows.season: Closed year-round — Prohibited Species (no open season)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sand Tiger Shark (Odontaspis noronhai) is a federally designated PROHIBITED shark species under the NOAA Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and cannot be retained, possessed, sold, or purchased by commercial or recreational fishermen in any U.S. Atlantic waters, including South Atlantic federal waters managed under SAFMC/NOAA HMS jurisdiction. This applies coastwide with no size or bag limit since retention is never legal.

rows.season: Closed year-round (Prohibited species — no possession/retention allowed)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus nakamurai) is classified as a 'Sixgill' prohibited species complex under the NOAA Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan, applicable in all U.S. Atlantic federal waters including the South Atlantic region. Recreational and commercial harvest is prohibited — any bigeye sixgill shark caught must be released immediately without removing it from the water, in a manner maximizing survival. Note: taxonomic work has split some Western Atlantic populations into Hexanchus vitulus (Atlantic Sixgill Shark), but NOAA's federal shark FMP has not been updated to reflect this and continues to manage/prohibit under the 'Sixgill' complex designation.

rows.season: Year-round closed to retention — Prohibited Species (2026)
rows.notes: Bigeye thresher shark (Alopias superciliosus) is designated a prohibited species under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water — no retention is permitted in recreational or commercial fisheries in any Atlantic HMS management area, including South Atlantic federal waters (SAFMC region). This is a nationwide federal HMS rule, not a SAFMC-specific season.

Bigeye tuna is managed under NOAA HMS Atlantic Tunas regulations (BAYS group), which apply uniformly in all Atlantic federal waters, including the South Atlantic. There is no recreational bag/possession limit for bigeye tuna, but a 27-inch curved fork length minimum size applies, and the fishery is open year-round (Jan 1 - Dec 31) unless later restricted. Retention is prohibited if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded. Vessel must hold a valid HMS Angling or HMS Charter/Headboat permit.

Bignose shark is a NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited species and must be released immediately with minimal injury, without removing it from the water. This applies year-round in all U.S. Atlantic HMS-managed waters, including South Atlantic federal waters. No retention is allowed under any recreational or commercial permit.

rows.season: Open year-round except for the annual shallow-water grouper spawning closure of January 1 – April 30 (currently OPEN as of Aug 17, 2026; next closure Jan 1, 2027 – Apr 30, 2027)
rows.notes: Black grouper is managed as part of the South Atlantic shallow-water grouper complex (with gag, red grouper, scamp, red/rock hind, coney, graysby, yellowfin/yellowmouth grouper), closed Jan 1–Apr 30 each year for spawning. Bag limit is 1 fish/person/day within the overall 3-fish grouper/tilefish aggregate, and no more than 1 of that aggregate may be gag or black grouper combined. Private recreational vessel limit is 2 fish/vessel/day (for-hire vessel limit is 2/trip); for-hire captain and crew have a zero bag limit for gag/black grouper. Minimum size is 24 inches total length, and fish must be landed with head and fins intact. A descending device is required onboard.

rows.season: Year-round / currently open (no closed season for blackfin snapper in South Atlantic federal waters as of 2026)
rows.notes: Blackfin snapper has no recreational minimum size limit in South Atlantic federal waters (removed effective March 30, 2020, under Regulatory Amendment 26). It is managed within the Deepwater Complex and counts toward the 10-fish aggregate snapper bag limit shared with silk snapper and queen snapper (per person per day). Must be landed with head and fins intact; descending device required onboard.

Species referred to as 'Blackline Tilefish (Caulolatilus cyanops)' corresponds to NOAA's managed species 'Blueline Tilefish' in South Atlantic federal waters. Season opened May 1, 2026 and is set to close September 1, 2026 (recreational catch limit not projected to be reached before the fixed closure). No minimum size limit applies. Bag limit is 2 fish per person per day during the open season; captain and crew of charter/headboat vessels may not retain blueline tilefish. During the closed period (Sept 1 - Apr 30), bag and possession limit is zero. A descending device is required onboard for all vessels fishing for South Atlantic snapper-grouper species.

rows.season: Year-round (subject to in-season closure if quota is reached)
rows.notes: NOAA manages blacknose shark under the Atlantic HMS FMP; the recreational limit is 1 blacknose shark per vessel per trip (not per angler), with a 54-inch fork length minimum, same across all HMS permit types (Angling, Charter/Headboat). Fins must remain naturally attached. This rule applies to all Atlantic federal waters, including the South Atlantic. A proposed rule (Amendment/Jan 5, 2026 Fed. Reg.) could revise blacknose minimum sizes and bag limits, but as of Aug 5, 2026 it remains in the comment/review stage and has NOT taken effect — current published limits (1/vessel/trip, 54" FL) are still in force. Season can close early if the linked small-coastal-shark quota is projected to be reached.

rows.season: Year-round (open access; no closed recreational season currently in effect)
rows.notes: Blacktip shark falls under NOAA's Atlantic HMS recreational 'Other Sharks' group (with bull, lemon, nurse, spinner, tiger, blue, porbeagle, common thresher). Minimum size is 54 inches fork length, and the limit is 1 shark of this entire group per VESSEL per trip (not per angler) — i.e., keeping one blacktip uses up the vessel's entire 'other sharks' allowance for that trip. This is separate from the 1-per-person allowances for Atlantic sharpnose/bonnethead. A valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit with shark endorsement is required, and non-offset non-stainless circle hooks must be used. Note: a NOAA proposed rule (comment period closed May 29, 2026) would revise shark species groupings and minimum sizes, but as of retrieval the 54-inch/1-per-vessel rule remains in effect and unchanged.

rows.season: Open year-round for school/large school/small medium Atlantic bluefin tuna (27" to <73" curved fork length); adjusted retention limits in effect June 1, 2026 – December 31, 2026. Trophy-sized bluefin (≥73" CFL) fishery is CLOSED in all Atlantic trophy areas (including Gulf of Maine, Southern New England, and southern areas) through December 31, 2026 due to subquota closures.
rows.notes: Limits are per VESSEL per day/trip, not per angler, and vary by permit type: HMS Angling (private vessels) = 2 bluefin tuna (27"-<73" CFL), of which only 1 may be a large school/small medium (47"-<73"); HMS Charter/Headboat when fishing recreationally = 3 fish (same size restriction); headboats = 6 fish (same size restriction) per a NOAA-provided table dated May 27, 2026. No more than one day's limit may be landed regardless of trip length. Trophy (≥73" CFL) retention is prohibited in all regions for the rest of 2026 (Southern New England closed July 3, 2026; Gulf of Maine closed Aug 4, 2026 — the last open trophy area). Bluefin cannot be retained if a hammerhead shark is aboard or has been offloaded. These NOAA HMS rules apply uniformly to South Atlantic federal waters (all Atlantic management areas except Gulf of America, where targeted bluefin fishing is prohibited).

Bluefish are managed coastwide (Maine to Florida) as a single stock by the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council in conjunction with ASMFC, with NOAA Fisheries as the implementing federal body — there is no separate South Atlantic Council rule for this species. There is no closed season and no federal minimum size limit. The federal bag limit is 5 fish/person/day on private recreational vessels; for-hire (party/charter) vessels have a higher 7 fish/person/day limit. Anglers should also check state-specific bluefish rules, which can be more restrictive in South Atlantic state waters.

Bonefish has no federal Fishery Management Plan under NOAA/SAFMC and is not listed among species with seasonal closures on NOAA's South Atlantic pages. Management is set by Florida FWC, which made bonefish catch-and-release only statewide effective Sept. 1, 2013, and this prohibition on harvest explicitly extends into federal waters off Florida. No possession, harvest, or landing is allowed anywhere off the Florida coast (state or federal EEZ waters); multiple hooks with live/dead natural bait are also prohibited when targeting bonefish. Fish over 27 in. may be documented (not kept) for FWC's Reel Big Fish program.

No minimum size limit for bonnethead shark in Atlantic federal waters. Bag limit is 1 bonnethead shark per person per trip (not per vessel). Managed under the Consolidated Atlantic HMS FMP as part of the 'small coastal shark' complex; NOAA does not open/close this fishery by season/quota, it is managed via retention limits year-round. Anglers must have HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit with shark endorsement, and use non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks. NOTE: A NOAA proposed rule (Fed. Reg. Jan 5, 2026) that could change the bonnethead bag limit to 1 per VESSEL per trip was still in public comment/review as of this check (comment period closed May 29, 2026) and had NOT yet been finalized/implemented — current in-force limit remains 1 per person.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational season open; subject to in-season quota closures) - 2026
rows.notes: Bull shark is managed under NOAA HMS as part of the 'Other sharks' recreational category (Large Coastal Shark complex). Requires HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement. Minimum size is 54 inches fork length (snout to fork of tail). Bag limit is 1 shark per VESSEL per trip (not per angler) - this may be filled by a bull shark or any other 'other shark' species, and does not stack with the separate Atlantic sharpnose/bonnethead per-angler allowances. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks required (except flies/artificial lures) south of 41°43'N. Federal HMS rules apply uniformly along the whole Atlantic coast (no separate SAFMC council rule for sharks - NOAA HMS Management Division sets these federally).

Caribbean Reef Shark is designated a prohibited species under the Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) Fishery Management Plan, applicable in all U.S. Atlantic, Gulf, and Caribbean waters, including South Atlantic federal waters under SAFMC/NOAA jurisdiction. It may not be retained, possessed, or landed by commercial or recreational fishermen and must be released with minimal injury without removing it from the water; this is a nationwide HMS rule, not state-specific.

Caribbean sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon porosus) is a federally PROHIBITED shark species under the Consolidated Atlantic HMS Management Plan. It must be released immediately with minimal injury, without removing it from the water, in both recreational and commercial fisheries in federal South Atlantic waters (and all other Atlantic HMS jurisdictions). Do not confuse with the similarly named but retainable 'Atlantic sharpnose shark' (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae), which has a 1-per-person bag limit with no minimum size.

Applies to the Florida East Coast Zone (federal South Atlantic waters off Florida), where cobia are managed jointly by the Gulf of Mexico and South Atlantic Fishery Management Councils as part of the Gulf migratory group. Per Amendment 32 (effective Nov 21, 2022), the recreational bag limit is 1 fish per person per day regardless of trip duration/number, with a vessel limit of 2 fish per trip not to exceed the per-person limit, and a 36-inch fork length minimum size. Note: this is DIFFERENT from the Atlantic migratory group cobia (Georgia through New York), which was removed from the federal Coastal Migratory Pelagics FMP and is now managed by states/ASMFC under the Atlantic Coastal Fisheries Cooperative Management Act, with state-specific seasons (e.g., NC has seasonal closures Jan 1-Apr 30).

Federal South Atlantic waters: Cubera snapper under 30" TL count toward the 10-fish aggregate snapper bag limit. Cubera snapper 30" TL or larger are NOT part of that aggregate and are limited to 2 fish per person per day, not to exceed 2 per vessel per day — this larger-fish rule applies specifically off the Atlantic coast of Florida (50 CFR 622.187/622.39). Fish must be landed with head and fins intact, and a descending device is required aboard.

rows.season: Year-round (federal Atlantic waters, recreational shark fishery is open year-round unless NOAA announces an in-season closure)
rows.notes: Finetooth shark is a small coastal shark managed under NOAA's Atlantic HMS Consolidated FMP, not by SAFMC directly. It is grouped in the 'all other sharks' recreational category. Permitted vessels may land a total of 1 shark from that category per vessel per trip (not per angler), with a 54-inch minimum fork length, non-offset/non-stainless circle hooks required, and fins must remain naturally attached. A NOAA proposed rule (Amendment 16, published Jan 5, 2026, comment period closed May 29, 2026) could revise recreational shark minimum sizes and retention limits, but as of Sep 14, 2026 no final rule has been issued, so current limits still apply.

rows.season: CLOSED as of Aug 2, 2026 - The 2026 recreational season ran May 1, 2026 - Aug 2, 2026 (93 days); season closed early via accountability measure and remains closed through Dec 31, 2026. Next opens May 1, 2027.
rows.notes: When open, the standard recreational limit is 1 gag (or black grouper) per person per day within a 3-grouper aggregate bag limit, min. size 24in TL; for-hire vessel limit is 2 gag/black per vessel per trip (not to exceed the per-person bag limit), and captain/crew on federally permitted for-hire vessels have a zero bag limit. NOAA closed the 2026 season early (effective 12:01am Aug 2, 2026) because 2025 recreational landings exceeded the ACL, per the accountability measure under Amendment 53. As of today (Aug 31, 2026) gag grouper harvest/possession in South Atlantic federal waters is prohibited (bag limit = 0) until the season reopens May 1, 2027.

rows.season: Closed year-round — prohibited species, no open season
rows.notes: Galapagos shark (Carcharhinus galapagensis) is classified as a PROHIBITED Atlantic HMS shark species under 50 CFR Part 635. It may not be retained, possessed, or landed in federal Atlantic waters (or any US Atlantic state waters) — it must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water. This applies regardless of the SAFMC/South Atlantic region since HMS sharks are managed by NOAA's Atlantic HMS Division, not SAFMC.

rows.season: Closed for 2026: recreational season opened January 1, 2026, closed at 12:01 a.m. March 27, 2026, and remains closed through December 31, 2026. Reopens January 1, 2027.
rows.notes: South Atlantic federal recreational golden tilefish season for 2026 closed early on March 27, 2026 after NOAA projected the 2,741-fish recreational ACL would be reached; bag/possession limit is 0 during the closure (through Dec 31, 2026). No minimum size limit applies when the season is open (per SAFMC species page). This is distinct from the Mid-Atlantic Council's separate golden tilefish fishery (Maine–Virginia), which is open year-round with an 8-fish/person/trip limit under a different management area.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season) — harvest prohibited
rows.notes: Goliath grouper harvest has been prohibited in South Atlantic federal waters since 1990. Catch-and-release only in federal waters. Note: Florida operates a separate limited-entry lottery harvest season (Mar 1–May 31) in STATE waters only (24-36 in. slot, 1 fish/permit), which does NOT apply to federal waters.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season currently in effect for federal South Atlantic waters)
rows.notes: Gray triggerfish in South Atlantic federal waters has a 12-inch fork length minimum size limit. It falls within the 20-fish aggregate 'other snapper-grouper' bag limit, but harvest of any single species within that aggregate (including gray triggerfish) is capped at 10 fish per person per day. A descending device is required onboard when fishing for snapper-grouper species. No seasonal closure is currently in effect for this species (unlike red snapper, gag, or golden tilefish, which do have active 2026 closures/seasons).

rows.season: Year-round (recreational retention permitted, subject to species-group bag limit)
rows.notes: Great hammerhead is an authorized recreational shark species (non-ridgeback Large Coastal Shark) in Atlantic HMS federal waters, INCLUDING South Atlantic — it is NOT prohibited here (prohibition on hammerhead retention applies only in the U.S. Caribbean EEZ). Minimum size is 78 inches fork length. Bag limit is 1 hammerhead OR any other single authorized 'large' shark species per vessel per trip (shared limit across the authorized-species list, not 1 per person). Hammerhead sharks cannot be retained if a swordfish, tuna, or billfish is aboard. Requires HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement; non-offset, non-stainless circle hooks required. A 2026 proposed rule (Draft Amendment 16) may later change size/retention structure but has not been finalized as of this check.

rows.season: Open year-round in South Atlantic federal waters, except closed April 1-30 each year for spawning; currently OPEN as of Aug 5, 2026
rows.notes: South Atlantic (SAFMC) greater amberjack recreational fishery is open year-round except for a mandatory April 1–30 spawning closure in the South Atlantic EEZ, during which harvest and possession are prohibited (limit zero). This is separate and less restrictive than the Gulf of America stock, which is under a rebuilding closure. Minimum size is 28 inches fork length; bag limit is 1 fish per person per day (not per vessel).

Jolthead porgy has no individual minimum size limit and no individual bag limit. It is one of 14 species in the South Atlantic snapper-grouper aggregate bag limit (20 fish/person/day total), with harvest of any single one of these species capped at 10 fish within that 20-fish aggregate, per Regulatory Amendment 26 (effective Mar 30, 2020). A NOAA-approved descending device must be aboard any vessel fishing for/possessing snapper-grouper species. Season may close in-season via Accountability Measure if the aggregate ACL is met.

rows.season: Year-round (all federal South Atlantic waters currently open to recreational harvest)
rows.notes: Applies to the Atlantic migratory group of king mackerel (Miami-Dade/Monroe County line, FL north through the NC/VA area and beyond). Amendment 34 (effective June 8, 2023) raised the recreational bag limit off the east coast of Florida from 2 to 3 fish/person, aligning it with the 3-fish limit already in place from Georgia through New York, so the entire Atlantic migratory group is now 3 fish/person/day. Minimum size is 24 inches fork length. Anglers on trips longer than 24 hours aboard a permitted charter/headboat with two licensed operators may possess up to two daily bag limits. State and federal bag limits cannot be combined.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational retention open year-round under federal HMS regulations; no recreational closed season for lemon shark)
rows.notes: Lemon shark is an AUTHORIZED (not prohibited) species under NOAA Atlantic HMS recreational shark regulations, classified as a non-ridgeback large coastal shark. Current federal rule (50 CFR 635, Amendment 2, still in effect as of Oct 2026) sets a 54-inch fork-length minimum and a combined retention limit of ONE shark per vessel per trip, shared across the whole 'all other sharks' group (blacktip, bull, lemon, nurse, spinner, tiger, and hammerheads) — not per angler. Anglers need an HMS Angling Permit with shark endorsement, must use non-offset non-stainless circle hooks, and all sharks must be landed with head/tail/fins naturally attached. NOTE: NOAA proposed changes to shark recreational retention limits and minimum sizes (Federal Register, Jan 5, 2026, Docket 2025-24264), including a possible size range up to 115 in and 1-3 fish per vessel for the lemon/bull/nurse/tiger group, but as of Oct 24, 2026 this remains a PROPOSED rule, not yet final/effective — current in-force limits are the ones reported here.

rows.season: Open year-round (Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2026), subject to in-season NOAA closure if the recreational catch limit for the 'Other Jacks Complex' is reached; confirmed open as of Aug 24, 2026
rows.notes: Lesser amberjack is managed together with almaco jack and banded rudderfish as the South Atlantic 'Other Jacks Complex' under the Snapper-Grouper FMP. These species fall within a 20-fish per person per day aggregate bag limit shared with several other snapper-grouper species (porgies, gray triggerfish, bar jack, white grunt, margate, sailor's choice, Atlantic spadefish), but harvest of any single species within that aggregate — including lesser amberjack — is capped at 10 fish per person per day. There is no recreational minimum size limit for lesser amberjack (unlike greater amberjack's 28-inch FL minimum); a 20-inch fork length minimum applies only to the commercial sector. NOAA has closed this complex mid-year in past seasons (e.g., 2018, 2019, 2021) when the recreational catch limit was met, so anglers should watch for NOAA Fishery Bulletins announcing any 2026 closure.

Longbill spearfish is a federally prohibited billfish species under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations. It may be caught but must be released; no minimum size or bag limit applies because retention is not permitted at all. Applies to all Atlantic HMS-permitted vessels, including South Atlantic federal waters. Do not confuse with roundscale spearfish, blue marlin, white marlin, or sailfish, which do have retention allowances.

rows.season: No open season — retention prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Longfin mako shark (Isurus paucus) is classified as a Prohibited Species under the Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water in all U.S. Atlantic HMS fisheries, including South Atlantic federal waters under SAFMC/NOAA jurisdiction. This has been in effect since 1999-2000 and is not tied to an annual season.

20-inch fork length minimum size applies only in federal waters off the east coast of Florida through South Carolina (not north of SC per Amendment 10); no minimum size off Georgia is separately called out and none applies north of SC. Bag limit is 10 dolphin per person per day; vessel limit is 54 per vessel per day (reduced from 60 by Dolphin Wahoo Amendment 10, effective 2022). No closed season currently in effect for dolphin/mahi-mahi in South Atlantic federal waters.

Federal South Atlantic waters (NC, SC, GA, FL EEZ): 12-inch total length minimum; 10-fish bag limit, which is itself the overall 10-fish snapper aggregate bag limit (gray/mangrove snapper can fill the entire aggregate). A descending device is required aboard all vessels fishing for or possessing snapper-grouper species in South Atlantic federal waters. This is distinct from Florida state-water rules (10-inch minimum, 5-fish bag) — do not substitute state limits for federal EEZ waters.

18-inch total length minimum applies in South Atlantic federal waters. The 5-fish recreational bag limit for mutton snapper is nested within the broader 10-snapper aggregate bag limit (which itself falls under the 20-fish snapper-grouper aggregate). No closed season currently applies to mutton snapper in South Atlantic federal waters (unlike the Gulf's Riley's Hump spawning closure).

rows.season: Closed year-round — Prohibited Species (no open season, no retention permitted)
rows.notes: Narrowtooth shark (Carcharhinus brachyurus) is classified by NOAA Fisheries as a 'prohibited species' under the Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) regulations (50 CFR 635), which apply uniformly in all federal Atlantic waters including the South Atlantic. Prohibited sharks may not be retained, possessed, or removed from the water and must be released immediately with minimal harm, regardless of coast or region.

rows.season: Closed year-round — prohibited species, no open season
rows.notes: Night shark (Carcharhinus signatus) is a federally prohibited Atlantic HMS shark species. Retention is banned in all U.S. Atlantic waters, including South Atlantic federal waters managed under NOAA/SAFMC. Any night shark caught must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water, per NOAA HMS regulations (50 CFR 635).

Nurse shark is a non-ridgeback 'Aggregated Large Coastal Shark' species that recreational anglers may retain in Atlantic federal waters (including South Atlantic). Only one shark total (not one per species) from the aggregated LCS list — which includes blacktip, bull, hammerheads, lemon, nurse, spinner, and tiger — may be retained PER VESSEL PER TRIP, at a 54-inch fork-length minimum. This is a group limit, not a per-angler bag limit or a nurse-shark-specific allowance. No closed season currently applies to this group.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season) — retention prohibited
rows.notes: Oceanic whitetip shark is a NOAA HMS-designated prohibited species in all U.S. Atlantic waters (including South Atlantic federal waters), effective since Feb 2, 2024 (89 FR 278, Jan 3, 2024). Also listed as threatened under the ESA. Recreational and commercial retention/possession is banned; sharks must be released in the water with minimal injury. Applies uniformly under NOAA HMS rules regardless of South Atlantic vs Gulf jurisdiction — this is a federal Atlantic-wide (not state-specific) prohibition, listed on NOAA's official prohibited species list.

Porbeagle is an Atlantic HMS 'Pelagic Shark' authorized for recreational retention with a 54-inch fork-length minimum size. The 1-shark limit is per vessel per trip and is shared across the entire authorized shark list (not 1 porbeagle in addition to other species) — anglers may keep only ONE shark total from the authorized list (e.g., blacktip, bull, hammerhead, lemon, nurse, spinner, tiger, blue, common thresher, porbeagle, Atlantic sharpnose, finetooth, blacknose, bonnethead) per vessel per trip. Porbeagle sharks alive at haulback must be released unharmed if a swordfish, tuna, or billfish is also on board. Requires a valid HMS Angling or Charterboat/Headboat permit with shark endorsement. This is a federal NOAA HMS rule applied uniformly in South Atlantic federal waters (not a SAFMC council-specific measure).

rows.season: Year-round (open unless closed by annual catch limit) - 2026
rows.notes: Queen snapper is part of the South Atlantic Deepwater Complex. The 12-inch TL minimum size limit was removed for queen, silk, and blackfin snapper by Regulatory Amendment 26 (effective March 30, 2020) to reduce regulatory discards. Queen snapper falls within the 10-fish aggregate 'snapper' bag limit, which itself is part of the larger 20-fish snapper-grouper aggregate bag limit in South Atlantic federal waters. The recreational season stays open year-round unless NOAA closes it early if the Deepwater Complex commercial/recreational annual catch limit is projected to be met.

rows.season: Open May 1 - June 30 annually (currently CLOSED July 1 - December 31, 2026)
rows.notes: Red porgy recreational harvest in South Atlantic federal waters is open only May 1 through June 30 each year; closed January 1-April 30 and July 1-December 31. As of today (Aug 6, 2026) the season is CLOSED - bag/possession limit is 0. When open, limit is 1 fish per person per day or per trip, whichever is more restrictive, and fish must be landed with head and fins intact. Regulation set under Amendment 50 (effective Jan 19, 2023) and confirmed to continue for 2026 and subsequent years.

Atlantic sailfish is managed as an Atlantic HMS billfish under federal rules applicable in all South Atlantic federal waters (and consistent state waters). Minimum size is 63 inches lower-jaw fork length. The 1-per-harvester bag limit is an aggregate limit shared across all billfish species (sailfish, blue marlin, white marlin, roundscale spearfish) â€” not 1 sailfish plus 1 of each other species. Vessel cap of 4 per trip applies to private recreational vessels (15 for for-hire vessels) for the combined billfish bag, per FWC guidance mirroring federal HMS rules. HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit required to fish for or possess billfish in federal waters, and all landed billfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours (800-894-5528 or hmspermits.noaa.gov). No closed season currently in effect for sailfish.

Sand tiger shark (Carcharias taurus) is federally listed as a Prohibited Species under the Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) Fishery Management Plan, applicable to all US Atlantic waters including the South Atlantic. Sand tigers must be released immediately with minimal injury and cannot be removed from the water, boated, gaffed, or landed. No possession, harvest, or retention is legal for commercial or recreational fishermen at any time. Take has been prohibited in federal waters since 1997 and in all East Coast state waters since 2008 (ASMFC).

Sandbar shark is a prohibited species under the Atlantic HMS Consolidated Fishery Management Plan. Recreational harvest is prohibited in all federal Atlantic waters (and Gulf/Caribbean); if caught, it must be released immediately with minimal harm. Only a small number of permitted commercial vessels in the NOAA Shark Research Fishery (with observers aboard) may land sandbar sharks. This applies to South Atlantic federal waters under NOAA/SAFMC jurisdiction.

rows.season: Year-round (open recreationally, subject to NOAA quota-based closures) — 2026
rows.notes: Scalloped hammerhead is NOT a prohibited species in South Atlantic federal waters (the Caribbean-only retention ban does not apply here). It is managed as part of the 'hammerhead' group (great, scalloped, smooth) under Atlantic HMS shark rules: 78 in fork length minimum, and the recreational retention limit is ONE shark total per vessel per trip drawn from the whole authorized large-coastal/pelagic shark list (not a per-angler bag limit). Hammerheads cannot be retained if a tuna, swordfish, or billfish is aboard. Fishery is subject to in-season NOAA closures once regional/sub-regional quotas are projected to be met.

rows.season: Open year-round except for seasonal closure January 1 - April 30 each year (closed Jan 1 - Apr 30, 2026; currently open as of Aug 5, 2026)
rows.notes: Effective July 6, 2026 (Amendment 55 final rule, published June 4, 2026), scamp and yellowmouth grouper were combined into a new 'Scamp and Yellowmouth Grouper Complex' with a rebuilding plan. The recreational bag limit was reduced from 3 fish to an aggregate complex bag limit of 1 fish (either scamp or yellowmouth grouper, combined) per person per day, counted within the overall 3-fish grouper/tilefish aggregate bag limit. Minimum size remains 20 in Total Length; fish must be landed with head and fins intact. Scamp is part of the shallow-water grouper spawning closure (Jan 1 - Apr 30 annually) in South Atlantic federal waters. A descending device is required on board all vessels fishing for/possessing snapper-grouper species.

In federal South Atlantic waters (south of Cape Hatteras, NC, 35°15.0321' N), scup is managed under the SAFMC Snapper-Grouper FMP as part of the 'Other Porgies Complex' (jolthead, knobbed, whitebone, saucereye porgy, and scup). No minimum size limit applies to this complex south of Cape Hatteras (a 9-inch TL minimum applies only NORTH of Cape Hatteras, which is outside this South Atlantic jurisdiction). Up to 10 fish from this porgy complex may be retained per person per day, nested within the broader 20-fish aggregate recreational bag limit for South Atlantic snapper-grouper species not otherwise under an individual bag limit. The recreational season for this complex is currently open with no specific closed dates identified; closure could occur if/when the commercial or recreational ACL is met. Always verify current open/closed status via NOAA/SAFMC alerts before landing fish.

rows.season: Year-round — species prohibited (no open season for retention)
rows.notes: Sevengill shark (Heptranchias perlo / Notorynchus cepedianus complex, listed as 'Sevengill' by NOAA) is classified as a Prohibited Species under NOAA Atlantic HMS shark regulations, applicable in all U.S. Atlantic federal waters including the South Atlantic. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water; retention, possession, or landing is unlawful under any circumstance. This is a single nationwide Atlantic HMS rule (not split by SAFMC/GMFMC region) — confirmed listed on NOAA's official recreational and commercial Atlantic shark statuses pages as well as corroborating state guides (NJ, MA, GA, NC) that reference the same federal prohibited list.

Short bigeye (Pristigenys alta) is an unmanaged member of the South Atlantic Snapper-Grouper Complex with no species-specific size limit or closed season. It falls under the federal 'South Atlantic snapper-grouper, combined' aggregate bag limit of 20 fish per person per day (50 CFR 622.187(b)(8)), with no more than 10 fish of any single species within that 20-fish aggregate. No individual minimum size limit applies to short bigeye under current federal regulations.

rows.season: Closed to retention year-round (zero retention limit in effect since July 5, 2022)
rows.notes: Shortfin mako shark retention (commercial and recreational) is prohibited in all U.S. Atlantic HMS fisheries, including South Atlantic federal waters, per NOAA final rule effective July 5, 2022, implementing ICCAT Recommendation. All shortfin makos caught must be released regardless of condition at haulback. Pre-2022 minimum sizes (71 in males / 83 in females FL) no longer apply since retention itself is banned. This is a federal HMS rule applying coastwide, not specific to South Atlantic vs Gulf.

Silky shark is a NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited species — it cannot be retained, possessed, sold, or purchased in any Atlantic HMS fishery (recreational or commercial), including South Atlantic federal waters. Any silky shark caught must be released immediately with minimal harm, without removing it from the water. This is a nationwide Atlantic HMS rule, not a SAFMC-specific regional measure.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species - no retention permitted)
rows.notes: Bluntnose Sixgill Shark is listed as a federally Prohibited Species under the Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan (50 CFR 635). It must be released immediately with minimal injury and cannot be retained by recreational or commercial anglers in South Atlantic federal waters (SAFMC jurisdiction). This is an HMS species managed exclusively by NOAA Fisheries nationwide, not by the SAFMC council process.

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round (federally protected endangered species)
rows.notes: Smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) is listed as endangered under the U.S. Endangered Species Act (effective April 1, 2003), making it the first marine fish federally protected. It is illegal to catch, harm, harass, kill, or possess this species in any U.S. waters, including South Atlantic federal waters; it is also unlawful to possess, sell, carry, or transport sawfish or their parts (e.g., rostrum). There is no recreational harvest season, bag limit, or size limit — any incidental hook-and-line capture must be released immediately using NOAA's safe handling/release protocols and reported to NOAA Fisheries.

rows.season: Year-round (federal recreational Atlantic shark fishery; open unless NOAA announces a quota-based closure)
rows.notes: Smooth hammerhead is grouped with great and scalloped hammerhead sharks under NOAA's Atlantic HMS recreational shark rules. Bag limit is 1 hammerhead OR 1 other authorized large coastal/pelagic shark per vessel per trip (not per person), with a 78-inch fork length minimum. Hammerhead sharks cannot be retained if a swordfish, tuna, or billfish is aboard. Note: retention of great, smooth, and scalloped hammerhead sharks is PROHIBITED in the U.S. Caribbean EEZ only (effective Feb 2, 2024) — this prohibition does NOT apply to South Atlantic federal waters, where retention remains allowed under the above limits.

Recreational harvest of Atlantic Spanish mackerel in South Atlantic federal waters (NC/SC border to Miami-Dade/Monroe Co., FL line) is open year-round with no recreational closed season; only the commercial sector is subject to periodic closures (e.g., southern zone commercial closure Feb 7 - Feb 28, 2026, reopening March 1, 2026 for the 2026/2027 fishing year). Minimum size is 12 inches fork length. Recreational bag/possession limit is 15 fish per person per day; state and federal bag limits cannot be combined. Charter/headboat trips over 24 hours may possess up to two daily bag limits under specific conditions. No federal 'per vessel' boat limit is specified separately from the per-person bag limit.

Speckled hind harvest and possession is prohibited in all South Atlantic federal waters, both recreationally and commercially. SAFMC established an ACL of zero for this species (Amendment 17B) and the Council confirms all areas remain closed to both recreational and commercial fishing; this has been in effect since 2011 with no scheduled reopening. If caught incidentally, fish must be released using a descending device (required on board all vessels fishing for/possessing snapper-grouper species) to reduce barotrauma mortality.

rows.season: Closed year-round — harvest prohibited (no open season)
rows.notes: Spotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari) is a federally prohibited species in South Atlantic (and Gulf) EEZ waters, as well as in Florida and other adjacent state waters. No retention, harvest, or possession is allowed under any circumstances; any ray caught must be released immediately with minimal harm (handling/release rules similar to other prohibited elasmobranchs apply).

rows.season: Closed year-round — no open season (federal moratorium since 1990)
rows.notes: Atlantic striped bass fishing (targeting, catch-and-release, and possession) is prohibited in the federal EEZ (generally 3-200 nautical miles offshore) under 50 CFR 697.7, per the Atlantic Striped Bass Conservation Act moratorium in place since 1990. This is a permanent 'no-target closure' - even catch-and-release is not allowed. This applies coastwide including South Atlantic federal waters. Anglers may transit federal waters with striped bass legally caught in state waters, but cannot target or retain any striped bass while in the EEZ. State-water regulations (0-3 nm) differ by state and are not covered by this federal EEZ rule.

rows.season: Year-round (fishery open, subject to retention limits)
rows.notes: Tiger shark is managed under the Atlantic HMS large coastal shark 'aggregated' recreational bag limit: anglers may keep only 1 shark per vessel per trip chosen from a list of allowed species (Atlantic blacktip, bull, hammerheads, lemon, nurse, spinner, tiger, blue, common thresher, porbeagle, etc.) — it is not an additional 1 tiger shark on top of other species. Minimum size is 54 inches fork length. Vessel must hold a valid HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement, and non-offset/non-stainless circle hooks are required south of 41°43'N.

No minimum size limit for wahoo in South Atlantic federal waters. Must be landed with head and fins intact. Regulated under the Dolphin Wahoo Fishery Management Plan (SAFMC/NOAA) for federal Atlantic waters from Maine to the Florida Keys — distinct from separate Puerto Rico/USVI Caribbean rules (32-inch FL minimum, 2/10 bag/vessel limits) which do not apply here.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season) — harvest and possession prohibited in South Atlantic federal waters
rows.notes: Warsaw grouper (and speckled hind) have an Annual Catch Limit of zero in South Atlantic federal waters under Amendment 17B to the Snapper-Grouper FMP. All fishing for, possession, and retention of these species is prohibited; fish caught incidentally must be released immediately with minimum harm using required descending devices. This is a permanent federal closure, not a seasonal one — it applies regardless of year.

White marlin is managed under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations (applies to all federal Atlantic waters, including South Atlantic — not SAFMC). No closed season and no per-angler/per-vessel daily bag limit, but minimum size is 66 inches lower-jaw fork length (LJFL). Retention is capped nationally: U.S. total landings of blue marlin, white marlin, and roundscale spearfish combined are limited to 250 fish annually, and NOAA can close the fishery early if that cap is reached. Billfish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is already on board or has been offloaded. A valid HMS Angling or Charterboat/Headboat permit is required, and all landings must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours.

Yellowfin tuna is managed under NOAA HMS Atlantic Tunas rules (applies uniformly to Atlantic South, Mid-Atlantic, Gulf, and Caribbean federal waters - no separate SAFMC season). Minimum size is 27 inches curved fork length (CFL); recreational retention limit is 3 fish per angler per day/trip (not a per-vessel limit). Vessel must hold a valid HMS Angling or HMS Charter/Headboat permit. Tunas cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded. No closed season or quota-based closure currently in effect for yellowfin (unlike bluefin tuna, which has separate, frequently adjusted limits).

rows.season: Year-round except closed January 1 - April 30, 2026 (shallow-water grouper spawning closure); currently OPEN as of August 5, 2026
rows.notes: Yellowmouth grouper is managed as part of the South Atlantic shallow-water grouper spawning closure (Jan 1–Apr 30 annually) and is currently open. Under Amendment 55 (final rule published June 4, 2026, effective July 6, 2026), yellowmouth grouper was removed from the 'other shallow-water grouper' complex and combined with scamp into a new 'Scamp and Yellowmouth Grouper Complex.' The aggregate bag limit for this new complex is now 1 fish (scamp OR yellowmouth grouper, combined) per person per day, nested within the overall 3-fish grouper/tilefish aggregate bag limit — down from the prior 3-fish species-specific limit. No separate vessel/boat limit was established. Minimum size remains 20 inches total length. This is a South Atlantic-specific (SAFMC) regulation; do not apply Gulf of America rules, which differ.

Minimum size is 24 inches FORK LENGTH (not total length). Bag limit is 2 per harvester OR 2 per vessel, whichever is less (not additive). This is a single statewide FWC rule (Ch. 68B-35, F.A.C.) applying to both the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of Florida — no separate Atlantic-only regulation exists for African pompano. State waters: hook and line only. Federal waters: hook and line and spearing permitted (state recreational limits extended into federal waters).

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round without a special FWC permit
rows.notes: Alligator gar cannot be legally taken or possessed anywhere in Florida (Atlantic or Gulf, salt or fresh water) without a special FWC scientific/management permit; any incidentally caught fish must be released immediately. This is a single statewide FWC rule — there is no separate Atlantic-coast allowance. The species itself is found only in Panhandle rivers, with limited occurrence outside that freshwater range.

Almaco jack is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' in Florida Atlantic state waters recreational fishery — no recreational minimum size limit and no closed season. Default recreational bag limit is 2 fish OR 100 pounds per person per day, whichever is greater. A 20-inch fork-length minimum size limit applies only to COMMERCIAL harvest in Atlantic state waters (not recreational). Note: federal South Atlantic waters manage almaco jack jointly with banded rudderfish and lesser amberjack as the 'Other Jacks Complex' and can have separate closures — this entry covers STATE waters only.

rows.season: Year-round closed to harvest — prohibited species, no open season
rows.notes: Atlantic Angel Shark (Squatina dumeril) is designated a prohibited shark species in all Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic coasts alike — FWC applies this rule statewide, not coast-specific). It may not be harvested, possessed, landed, purchased, sold, or exchanged. If caught, it must be released immediately without removing it from the water, with gills kept submerged (per Fla. Admin. Code 68B-44 and FWC prohibited species rules). This state rule aligns with the federal NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited shark species list, under which Atlantic angel shark has been prohibited since 1999 (expanded prohibited group rule).

Applies to Atlantic coast of Florida (Nassau through Miami-Dade counties, excluding Monroe County). No minimum size limit. Bag limit is 50 fish per person per day, per species (shared aggregate limit with Spot). This differs from the Gulf coast (and Monroe County), where the limit is 100 lbs per person per day instead of a fish-count limit — do not apply the Gulf rule here.

Atlantic sharpnose shark has no minimum size limit and is one of FWC's 'Group 1' harvestable sharks. This is a statewide FWC regulation applying to both Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters (no coast-specific split for this species). Sharks must be landed in whole condition (no finning/filleting at sea), hook-and-line gear only, and a Shore-based Shark Fishing permit + Shark-Smart course is required if fishing from shore. Bag limit of 1 shark/person or 2/vessel (whichever is less) applies across the combined 'harvestable sharks' group, not per species.

Atlantic thread herring (threadfin herring/greenback) has no species-specific recreational size or bag limit published by FWC. It is treated as an 'unregulated' species, so the default statutory recreational limit applies: 2 fish OR 100 pounds per person per day, whichever is greater (amounts beyond that are considered commercial quantities and require a saltwater products license). This rule applies statewide (both Atlantic and Gulf state waters) — FWC does not publish a separate Atlantic-specific rule for this species.

FWC regulates Banded Rudderfish together with Lesser Amberjack under one combined rule for both Atlantic and Gulf state and federal waters. Slot limit is 14-22 inches fork length, with a 5 fish per person aggregate bag limit shared between the two species (not species-specific). No closed season applies to this pairing (only Greater Amberjack has a separate seasonal closure).

Basking Shark is a federally and state-designated PROHIBITED species. It cannot be harvested, possessed, or landed in Florida state waters (Atlantic or Gulf) at any time. If caught, it must be released immediately with minimal injury, kept in the water with gills submerged (if fishing from a vessel), or the line cut without removing it from the water (if fishing from shore). This prohibition applies under both FWC state rules and NOAA Atlantic HMS federal regulations.

rows.season: Closed year-round - Prohibited species (no open season)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sand Tiger Shark (Odontaspis noronhai) is classified as a prohibited species in all Florida state waters (both Atlantic and Gulf coasts - this is a single statewide rule, not coast-specific). Harvest, landing, and possession are illegal at all times. If caught, it must be released immediately with gills kept submerged in the water; delaying release beyond hook removal is prohibited.

rows.season: Year-round closed to harvest (catch-and-release only, statewide)
rows.notes: Bigeye sixgill shark (Hexanchus nakamurai) is on FWC's Prohibited Species list for sharks — harvest, possession, landing, purchase, and sale are prohibited year-round in all Florida state waters (this rule is statewide, not split by Gulf/Atlantic coast). If caught, the shark must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay (immediately if fishing from shore); non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hooks are required with natural bait, and anglers must carry a device to quickly cut the leader/hook.

rows.season: Closed year-round (harvest prohibited) - no open season, 2026
rows.notes: Bigeye Thresher (Alopias superciliosus) is on FWC's Prohibited Species list for sharks in Florida state waters (applies statewide, both Gulf and Atlantic coasts). Harvest, landing, and possession are illegal; if caught it must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay. Do not confuse with the 'common thresher' shark, which IS harvestable (54" fork length min, 1 bag/2 vessel limit) - these are different species.

Bigeye tuna is a federally managed Atlantic HMS species; NOAA HMS regulations apply in Florida state and federal waters alike (FWC state waters do not set separate rules). Minimum size is 27 inches curved fork length (CFL), measured along the body curve from tip of jaw to fork of tail; no recreational bag limit is currently set for bigeye tuna. A federal HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit is required to target/retain bigeye tuna even in FL state waters, and tuna cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard. Landed bigeye tuna must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours.

rows.season: Closed year-round (harvest prohibited) - Florida state waters
rows.notes: Bignose shark (Carcharhinus altimus) is on FWC's Prohibited Species list for state waters (both Gulf and Atlantic coasts - one statewide rule, per FWC's Sharks prohibited species page, governed by F.A.C. Chapter 68B-44). It must be released immediately with gills kept submerged; delaying release or removing it from the water is illegal. This is also consistent with NOAA HMS federal Atlantic rules, where bignose shark retention is likewise prohibited (listed on CITES Appendix II with retention barred in the U.S.).

rows.season: May 1 - December 31, 2026 (closed January 1 - April 30, 2026 for shallow-water grouper spawning closure)
rows.notes: Black grouper in Florida Atlantic state waters (including all state waters off Monroe County) is managed jointly with gag grouper under a combined 1-fish-per-person daily bag limit (gag or black, whichever combination) within the broader 3-fish grouper/tilefish aggregate bag limit. Vessel limit is 2 black grouper per vessel per day, not to exceed the bag limit, whichever is more restrictive. Annual closure Jan 1-Apr 30 applies to the shallow-water grouper complex (including black grouper) in Atlantic state and adjacent federal waters. State Reef Fish Angler Designation required for private recreational vessel anglers 16+.

Blackfin Snapper has no minimum size limit and is grouped with Black, Wenchman, Queen, and Silk snapper. Bag limit is 10 per person, but this counts within (not in addition to) Florida's 10-fish snapper aggregate bag limit that applies to all snapper species combined in both Atlantic and Gulf state waters. No closed season currently in effect.

No minimum size limit. Bag limit is 2 fish per harvester OR 10 fish per vessel, whichever is greater (not additive) — e.g., a boat with 2 or more anglers may keep up to 10 total, but a single angler is limited to 2. This FWC rule applies in Florida state waters AND has been extended into adjacent federal waters, superseding the federal default. No federal HMS Angling Permit is required to target/retain blackfin tuna in FL state or federal waters. Applies statewide (Atlantic and Gulf) per FWC.

Blackline tilefish (Caulolatilus cyanops), along with anchor, goldface, and sand tilefish, are tracked as separate restricted-species codes by FWC but are NOT among the tilefish species given their own published size/bag/season rules on the FWC Tilefish regulations page — that page only sets specific bag limits and seasons for golden tilefish and blueline (gray) tilefish, and the Atlantic grouper/tilefish 3-fish aggregate bag limit explicitly names only 'golden and blueline tilefish.' Per FWC's own convention for its 'Other Reef Fish' category, species without published season info are open year-round, which is why seasonText is set to Year-round. No minimum size, maximum size, or numeric bag/vessel limit could be confirmed specifically for blackline/unicorn tilefish, so those fields are left null rather than guessed.

Blacknose shark is a Group 1 harvestable shark species in Florida with no minimum size limit. This rule is statewide (applies equally to Atlantic and Gulf state waters, not coast-specific). Overall shark bag limit is 1 shark per person per day, with a vessel-wide cap of 2 sharks per day regardless of number of anglers aboard. All sharks must be landed in whole condition (head, tail, fins naturally attached); non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks required with natural bait. Shore-based anglers need the free Shark-Smart course/permit. Federal HMS rules (54" fork length min, 1 fish/vessel/trip) apply separately in federal waters and to HMS permit holders.

Blacktip shark is a Group 1 shark under FWC's state-waters shark management rules, meaning it has no minimum size limit. Bag limit is 1 shark per harvester per day, with a maximum of 2 sharks per vessel per day (whichever is less), regardless of number of anglers aboard. Sharks must be landed in whole condition (heads, tails, fins attached). This is a single statewide rule applying to both Florida Gulf and Atlantic state waters — FWC does not differentiate blacktip shark regs by coast. Shore-based anglers additionally need the free Shore-based Shark Fishing Permit and completion of the Shark-Smart course. Confirm before harvest since blacktip can be easily confused with the 54-inch-minimum spinner shark.

rows.season: Year-round (subject to in-season closure to catch-and-release only if the 250-fish combined annual landings limit for blue marlin/white marlin/roundscale spearfish is reached, per 50 CFR 635.27)
rows.notes: Blue marlin is a NOAA Atlantic HMS-managed billfish, so federal rules apply in FL state waters too (state does not set separate limits). Minimum retention size is 99 inches, measured lower-jaw-to-fork (multiple sources confirm this figure for both Florida and Gulf states). There is no per-angler/per-vessel daily bag limit specifically for blue marlin, but U.S. recreational landings of blue marlin, white marlin, and roundscale spearfish combined are capped at 250 fish annually; NOAA has previously restricted the fishery to catch-and-release only for the remainder of a year once that cap is hit. Billfish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded, and all landed billfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours (800-894-5528 or hmspermits.noaa.gov). An HMS Angling or Charterboat/Headboat permit is required to fish for Atlantic billfish, though FWC notes this federal permit is not required specifically when fishing for billfish in Florida state waters.

Blue runner (hardtail) has no minimum size limit and a statewide recreational bag limit of 100 fish per harvester per day, established under FWC Rule 68B-61.004, F.A.C. This rule applies uniformly to both Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters (no coast-specific split published by FWC) and extends into adjacent federal waters where no federal management plan exists (Gulf), and in the Atlantic since blue runner was removed from the SAFMC snapper-grouper FMP with FWC assuming management authority. There is no closed season.

rows.season: Year-round with in-season federal retention limits; current recreational retention limits (private HMS Angling permits) in effect June 1, 2026 – December 31, 2026
rows.notes: Atlantic bluefin tuna is a federal HMS species — NOAA Fisheries regulations apply uniformly in Florida Atlantic state waters (FWC does not set separate state limits). As of June 1, 2026, private vessels with HMS Angling permits may retain 2 bluefin tuna per vessel per day/trip measuring 27 in. to <73 in. curved fork length (CFL), of which only 1 may be a large school/small medium fish (47–<73 in.). Charter/headboats have higher vessel limits (3 fish; headboats 6 fish) under the same size rules. Fish <27 in. must be released. Retention of 'trophy' bluefin (≥73 in. CFL) is currently closed in ALL trophy areas nationwide for the remainder of 2026 (Gulf of Maine area closed Aug 4, 2026, following earlier closures elsewhere), so no giant/trophy bluefin may be kept anywhere, including off Florida's Atlantic coast, at this time. Limits are per vessel, not per angler, and apply regardless of trip length. NOAA may adjust or close the fishery further later in 2026.

Applies to Florida Atlantic state waters (Nassau through Miami-Dade counties). Minimum size is 12" fork length. Daily bag limit is 3 fish per person for anglers on private recreational vessels; anglers on for-hire (charter/guide) vessels have a 5 fish per person bag limit. This is a separate, more restrictive rule than the Gulf coast, where the bag limit is 10 per harvester with no minimum size. FWC regulations do not extend into federal Atlantic waters. No closed season currently in effect for recreational harvest.

Bonefish is a statewide catch-and-release only fishery in Florida (both Atlantic and Gulf state waters) — no size limit, no harvest allowed. Rule in effect since Sept 1, 2013. Anglers may temporarily possess a bonefish at the site of capture only to photograph, measure, or weigh for record documentation (e.g., Catch a Florida Memory program) before release; hook-and-line only, multiple-hook rigs with natural bait prohibited.

Atlantic Bonito has no species-specific size or bag limit in Florida. FWC classifies it as an 'unregulated species,' subject to the statewide default recreational bag limit of two fish or 100 pounds per person per day, whichever is greater. This applies to Florida state waters on both the Atlantic and Gulf coasts (bonito are noted as rarely found in the Gulf, but the same statewide 'unregulated species' rule applies).

Bonnethead is a 'no minimum size limit' harvestable shark under FWC's shark rules. Retainable sharks are managed as a single group: 1 shark per person per day, with a maximum of 2 sharks per vessel regardless of angler count. Hook-and-line gear only; sharks must be landed in whole condition (head, tail, fins naturally attached). A Shore-based Shark Fishing permit + free online course is required if fishing for/harvesting sharks from shore, piers, or bridges. FWC does not publish a separate Atlantic-only shark rule for bonnethead — this regulation applies statewide in Florida state waters (Atlantic and Gulf).

Bull shark is a Group 2 harvestable shark in Florida with a 54-inch minimum fork length (measured tip of snout to fork of tail, not total length). Bag limit is 1 shark per person per day, with an overall vessel limit of 2 sharks per day regardless of number of anglers aboard (whichever is less). Shark must remain in whole condition (head, tail, fins attached) until landed. Regulation applies statewide in FL state waters — FWC does not publish a separate Atlantic-only shark rule; this is one unified state rule for both coasts. Shore-based anglers additionally need the free Shore-based Shark Fishing Permit and Shark-Smart course. Recreational anglers fishing state waters only (not on an HMS-permitted vessel) are not required to hold the federal HMS shark endorsement, though federal HMS rules apply separately in federal waters.

Caribbean Reef Shark (Carcharhinus perezii) is on FWC's Prohibited Species list for sharks — harvest, possession, and landing are prohibited in all Florida state waters (this is a statewide rule, applying equally to Gulf and Atlantic coasts, not just the Atlantic side). If caught, the shark must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay; if fishing from shore, release without delay is required and the hook/leader must be cut if removal would cause delay. This rule aligns with NOAA HMS federal regulations, which also list Caribbean Reef Shark among prohibited ridgeback sharks in Atlantic HMS waters.

Caribbean sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon porosus) is on FWC's Prohibited Species list for state waters — it may not be harvested or possessed. If caught, it must be released immediately with gills kept submerged (do not remove from the water), and released without delay per FWC handling rules for prohibited sharks. This rule applies statewide, with no distinction between Florida's Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Note: this species is distinct from the commonly harvested Atlantic sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae), which IS legal to keep with no minimum size.

Cero mackerel is officially listed by FWC as an 'unregulated' species (no size limit, no closed season). The default statewide recreational bag limit for unregulated species applies: 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is greater (not a strict 2-fish cap if weight exceeds 100 lbs with fewer fish). This applies to both Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters — FWC does not publish a coast-specific rule for cero mackerel.

No closed season for cobia in Florida state waters. Minimum size is 36 inches fork length. Daily bag limit is 1 fish per person or 2 per vessel, whichever is less — this is a statewide rule applying identically to both Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters. This state-waters rule matches current federal Gulf and Atlantic cobia regulations as well.

Florida Atlantic state waters: 12" TL minimum size. Cubera snapper 30" TL or larger: bag limit of 2 per harvester OR 2 per vessel, whichever is less, and these large fish do NOT count toward the 10-fish snapper aggregate bag limit. Cubera snapper under 30" TL are counted within the standard 10-fish-per-day snapper aggregate bag limit. No closed season currently in effect.

Finetooth shark has no minimum size limit in Florida state waters (Atlantic and Gulf) and is managed within FWC's aggregate shark bag limit, not as a species-specific limit. Daily bag limit is 1 shark per person per day OR 2 sharks per vessel, whichever is less, across all retainable shark species combined (only one of which may be finetooth). Hook-and-line gear only; shore-based shark anglers must complete FWC's free online shark ID course. This rule is statewide and applies identically to both Florida's Atlantic and Gulf coasts.

rows.season: Closed for 2026 (season ran May 1 - August 2, 2026; harvest closed via FWC Executive Order effective 12:01 a.m. Aug 2, 2026, matching the South Atlantic federal season; expected to reopen ~May 1, 2027 pending future FWC/NOAA action)
rows.notes: Applies to Florida ATLANTIC state waters only (including Monroe County waters, which follow Atlantic rules), NOT the Gulf. Gag grouper falls within the Atlantic Grouper/Tilefish aggregate bag limit of 3 fish per harvester per day, but only 1 of those 3 may be gag OR black grouper combined. A 2-gag-per-vessel-per-day cap also applies (whichever limit is more restrictive controls). For-hire captain and crew have a zero bag limit for gag. Season is closed as of today (Sept 4, 2026); it closed early via FWC executive order to align with the reduced South Atlantic federal season (May 1 - Aug 2, 2026) and prevent quota overage.

Galapagos shark is listed by FWC as a Prohibited Species in Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic, no coast-specific split for this species). Harvest, possession, or landing is illegal year-round. Sharks caught must not be removed from the water; gills must remain submerged, and the shark must be released without delay per F.A.C. Chapter 68B-44. Applies to both Atlantic and Gulf state waters identically.

rows.season: Closed - Atlantic State Waters closed March 27, 2026 through December 31, 2026 (reopens January 1, 2027)
rows.notes: Golden tilefish has no minimum size limit. Bag limit is 1 golden tilefish per harvester per day, and golden tilefish counts within the 3-fish aggregate bag limit for grouper and tilefish (golden + blueline) species combined in Atlantic state waters. Florida state Atlantic season mirrors the federal South Atlantic recreational closure (closed March 27, 2026 announced by NOAA Fisheries after reaching the 2026 recreational ACL). This is Atlantic-specific; Gulf golden tilefish rules differ (100 lbs/person or 2 fish over 100 lbs, no closed season).

rows.season: March 1 - May 31, 2026 (permit-only limited harvest; harvest prohibited outside this window and year-round in closed areas)
rows.notes: Goliath grouper harvest is closed statewide EXCEPT for a highly restricted lottery-permit program. Only permit holders (drawn via random lottery, applications Oct 1-15 annually) may harvest ONE goliath grouper per permit during the Mar 1-May 31 open season, within a 24-36in total length slot. Statewide quota capped at 200 fish/year (50 max from Everglades NP). On the ATLANTIC coast specifically, harvest is PROHIBITED in state waters of Martin County south through the Atlantic coast of the Keys and all of the St. Lucie River/tributaries - so much of the southeast Atlantic coast remains closed to harvest even for permit holders. Harvest remains prohibited in all federal waters. Anglers without a permit must practice catch-and-release only, everywhere, year-round.

Applies to Florida Atlantic state waters only (distinct from Gulf coast, which has a closed season and different size/bag limits). Minimum size is 12 inches fork length. Bag limit is 10 per person per day. Anglers fishing from a private vessel must have the State Reef Fish Angler designation. Special regulations apply in Biscayne National Park.

Great hammerhead shark is on Florida's Prohibited Species List (effective Jan. 1, 2012) and may not be harvested, possessed, landed, purchased, sold, or exchanged in Florida state waters (Atlantic or Gulf — FWC applies this rule statewide). It must be released immediately with gills kept submerged in the water; it cannot be brought aboard a vessel or onto shore/dry land. This is a catch-and-release-only species in FL state waters.

rows.season: Open year-round except closed April 1-30, 2026 (Jan 1 - Mar 31, 2026 and May 1 - Dec 31, 2026)
rows.notes: Applies to Florida Atlantic state waters only (different from Gulf coast, which has 34-inch minimum and a Sept 1-Oct 31 season). Recreational spawning closure each April, consistent with federal Atlantic commercial closure. Special reduced bag limits (1 fish per person per day for all amberjack species combined) apply in Monroe County/Biscayne National Park waters.

Currently in the annual harvest closure (Oct 15-Nov 30) to protect pre-spawning aggregations; all flounder caught must be released. When open (Dec 1-Oct 14), min size 14in TL, bag 5/person/day. FWC applies one statewide rule covering both Gulf and Atlantic state waters (and federal waters) for Gulf flounder, Southern flounder, summer flounder, and fringed flounder - no separate Atlantic-only regulation exists. For-hire captain/crew bag limit is 0.

rows.season: Closed year-round — no open harvest season; sturgeon are a prohibited species in all Florida state waters
rows.notes: Atlantic sturgeon (Acipenser oxyrinchus) is listed as a prohibited species under Florida saltwater regulations (and also protected federally under the Endangered Species Act / ASMFC moratorium). It is unlawful to harvest, possess, land, purchase, sell, or exchange sturgeon in Florida state waters, Atlantic or Gulf coast alike — this is a single statewide prohibition, not a coast-specific rule. Any sturgeon caught incidentally must be released immediately without removing it from the water.

Atlantic state waters, which FWC defines as all state and federal waters south of Cape Sable, the Florida Keys included. Open May 1 – Oct 31 each year. 16 in fork length, one per harvester. State Reef Fish Angler designation required from a private vessel.

Crevalle jack is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' statewide (same rule applies on both the Atlantic and Gulf coasts) — no closed season and no minimum size limit. The default recreational harvest limit for unregulated marine species in Florida is 100 pounds OR 2 fish, whichever is greater (exceeding this threshold is considered a commercial quantity requiring a commercial license). Bag limit listed here (2) reflects the 'or 2 fish' floor of that rule; anglers may keep up to 100 lbs combined weight if greater than 2 fish.

rows.season: Year-round (open all of 2026, no closed season)
rows.notes: Applies to Florida Atlantic state waters (excluding Monroe County). Minimum size is 24 inches fork length, hook-and-line/spearing only. Note this differs from the Gulf state waters rule (including Monroe County), which allows 3 per harvester — do not apply the Gulf limit here. Bag limit may be reduced to 1 in some state waters if adjacent federal Atlantic waters close to recreational harvest.

Ladyfish is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' — no specific size, season, or bag limit exists. Default Florida Statute limit applies: 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is greater (not a strict 2-fish cap if weight is used). This applies statewide; FWC does not differentiate Atlantic vs. Gulf coast for this species.

FWC's new 10-inch minimum size and 20-fish bag limit for lane snapper (approved Nov 2025, effective Apr 1, 2026) apply ONLY to Gulf state waters, not the Atlantic. Florida Atlantic state waters retain the original 8-inch minimum size limit and no species-specific bag limit beyond the standard 10-fish-per-harvester aggregate snapper bag limit (all snapper species combined, unless stated otherwise). Season is open year-round with no closure.

Lemon sharks are on FWC's Prohibited Species list for all Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic) — no recreational or commercial harvest, possession, landing, purchase, sale, or exchange is allowed. Any lemon shark caught must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released immediately without delay. This rule applies statewide (same on Atlantic and Gulf coasts) and has been in effect since March 23, 2010. Harvest remains legal only in adjacent federal waters, which are outside this Atlantic state-waters jurisdiction.

Bag limit of 5 per person is an aggregate limit combining Lesser Amberjack and Banded Rudderfish (not 5 of each species separately). Size limit is a slot limit: fish must be at least 14" but no more than 22" fork length. No closed season applies to Lesser Amberjack (unlike Greater Amberjack, which has separate seasonal closures). Private-boat anglers 16+ must register as a Florida State Reef Fish Angler to harvest this species. This regulation applies to both State and Federal waters off Florida's Atlantic coast.

Little tunny (bonito) is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated' tuna species in Florida state waters, not subject to federal HMS regulation. No minimum size limit applies. The default statewide bag limit for unregulated species is 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is greater — for little tunny this typically means the 100 lb threshold governs. No federal HMS Angling Permit is required to target little tunny (that permit requirement applies only to bluefin, bigeye, albacore, yellowfin, and skipjack tuna). This rule applies to Florida state waters on both the Atlantic and Gulf coasts (FWC does not differentiate little tunny by coast).

Longbill spearfish retention is prohibited in Florida state waters (FWC Rule 68B-33, FAC) and this prohibition is corroborated by NOAA Atlantic HMS federal regulations, which also list longbill spearfish as prohibited from recreational/commercial retention. Catch-and-release only; must be released immediately if caught. Applies to Florida Atlantic state waters.

Longfin mako (Isurus paucus) is on FWC's Prohibited Species list for sharks — no recreational or commercial harvest, possession, landing, purchase, sale, or exchange is allowed in Florida state waters (Atlantic or Gulf). If caught, the shark must be released immediately without removing it from the water; gills must remain submerged and total length must stay in the water while removing hooks/tackle.

20-inch fork length minimum applies. Private recreational: 5 fish/person or 30/vessel, whichever is less. For-hire vessels: 5 fish/person, no separate vessel cap (limited to customers x bag limit). Captain and crew may not retain a bag limit (statewide). No closed season for this species in FL Atlantic state waters.

Mangrove (gray) snapper have no closed season in Florida state waters. Minimum size is 10 inches total length in both Atlantic and Gulf state waters. Daily bag limit is 5 per harvester, and this limit counts toward Florida's overall 10-fish snapper aggregate bag limit (combined total of all snapper species, excluding lane/vermilion which have separate limits). Federal waters have a different 12-inch minimum and different bag structure — this record applies to FL Atlantic STATE waters only.

Mutton snapper is open year-round for recreational harvest in Florida Atlantic state waters. The 5-fish bag limit counts within the overall 10-fish snapper aggregate bag limit per harvester per day. Total length is the measurement standard. Regulations are identical for Florida's Atlantic and Gulf state waters (FWC publishes one statewide rule for this species).

Narrowtooth shark (Carcharhinus brachyurus) is on Florida's Prohibited Shark Species list — no minimum size, no harvest, no possession, and no landing is permitted in Florida state waters (Gulf or Atlantic). Anglers must keep gills submerged and release without delay; if hook removal would delay release, cut the line/hook as close as possible. This rule applies statewide (same regulation for both FL coasts) and is separate from FWC's Group 1/Group 2 harvestable shark categories.

Night shark (Carcharhinus signatus) is a Prohibited Species in Florida state waters (both Atlantic and Gulf coasts) — no harvest, possession, landing, purchase, or sale is allowed. This mirrors the federal NOAA HMS prohibition (in effect since 2000) on this species. If caught, it must be released immediately with gills kept submerged; do not remove from the water.

Nurse shark is in FWC's harvestable 'large coastal/other' shark group, requiring a 54-inch minimum FORK length (not total length) to retain. Bag limit is 1 shark per harvester per day OR 2 per vessel per day, whichever is less (not additive). This is a single statewide FWC rule applying equally to Florida's Atlantic and Gulf state waters — no separate Atlantic-only regulation exists for sharks. Harvest requires a free Shore-based Shark Fishing permit (for land-based anglers) and completion of the Shark-Smart course; non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hooks are mandatory with natural bait. Retained sharks must be landed whole (head, tail, fins attached).

rows.season: Closed year-round — no open season (harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Oceanic Whitetip Shark is classified by FWC as a prohibited species in all Florida state waters (Atlantic and Gulf coasts alike — this is a single statewide rule, not coast-specific). Harvest, possession, and landing are illegal at any time. If caught, the shark must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay when fishing from shore or a vessel; this rule aligns Florida state waters with the federal NOAA HMS prohibition on retention in all U.S. Atlantic, Gulf, and Caribbean waters (effective Jan 3, 2024).

Opah (moonfish) is not individually listed in FWC's recreational regulations and is treated as an 'unregulated' species in Florida state waters. Default recreational bag limit applies: 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is MORE (e.g., a single large opah well over 100 lbs still counts as meeting the daily limit). No minimum/maximum size and no closed season apply. This rule is the same for both Atlantic and Gulf Florida state waters — FWC does not publish a coast-specific rule for opah.

rows.season: Year-round in Atlantic state waters, except the Special Permit Zone (waters south of Cape Florida including Biscayne Bay south of Rickenbacker Causeway), which is closed April 1 - July 31, 2026
rows.notes: General Atlantic state waters: slot limit not less than 11" or more than 22" fork length; daily bag limit of 2 per harvester, which may include 1 fish over 22", with a vessel limit of 2 fish over 22" per day. In the Special Permit Zone (south Florida, south of Cape Florida on the Atlantic side), the rule differs: 22" minimum fork length only (no upper slot), bag limit of 1 per harvester (max 2 per vessel), and the zone is closed to permit harvest April 1 - July 31. Hook-and-line only in state waters; multiple hooks with live/dead bait and snatch hooks prohibited.

Pigfish (a grunt species) is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated' species with no size limit or closed season. The default recreational bag limit for unregulated species applies: 2 fish or 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is more (100 lbs governs for small-bodied fish like pigfish since 2 fish would rarely reach that weight). This rule applies statewide in Florida, including Atlantic state waters.

Pinfish are classified as an 'unregulated species' by FWC statewide (applies equally to Atlantic and Gulf state waters — no coast-specific rule). No minimum/maximum size limit and no closed season. Default recreational harvest limit under Florida Statute is 2 fish OR 100 pounds per person per day, whichever is greater; exceeding this requires a Saltwater Products License as it is deemed a commercial quantity.
