Standard gear rules still apply (e.g., pinfish traps must be ≤2ft x 2ft x 2ft / 8 cubic ft with proper mesh/escape rings).

Porbeagle shark is a state-managed 'harvestable' shark statewide in Florida (same rule applies to both Gulf and Atlantic state waters — FWC does not differentiate porbeagle by coast). It falls in FWC's 54-inch fork length minimum size group. Bag limit is 1 shark per harvester per day OR 2 per vessel, whichever is less, and retainable sharks are managed as one combined group (not species-specific stacking). Shore-based anglers need the free Shore-based Shark Fishing permit/course; non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks required with natural bait. Federally, HMS anglers must release porbeagles alive at haulback if tuna/swordfish/billfish are aboard.

Queen snapper is grouped with Wenchman, Blackfin, and Silk snapper under FWC's 'Other Snapper' category. There is no minimum size limit for this species (minimum size limits were removed in South Atlantic federal waters in 2020, and Florida state waters mirror this — no size limit is listed). The 10-fish bag limit for this group counts within, not in addition to, the overall 10-fish snapper aggregate bag limit per angler per day. Species is open year-round with no closed season specified.

rows.season: Open Year-round (state waters closed Jan 1 - Apr 30 annual spawning closure); 2026 season: May 1 - Dec 31, 2026 open, next closure begins Jan 1, 2027
rows.notes: Red grouper is included in Florida's Atlantic Grouper/Tilefish 3-fish aggregate bag limit (not a species-specific bag on top of other groupers). Atlantic state waters (including all Monroe County state waters, both Gulf and Atlantic sides) are closed to harvest of red grouper Jan 1 - Apr 30 each year for spawning protection; season reopens May 1. As of today (Aug 5, 2026) the fishery is open. This is separate from Gulf state waters, which have different (year-round, 2-fish, 4-fish aggregate) rules — this record applies to Atlantic state waters only.

Applies to Florida Atlantic state waters only (Gulf red porgy rules differ — no min size, year-round season, 100 lb bag limit in Gulf). FWC set a standing recreational season of May 1–June 30 with a 14-inch TL minimum size and 1 fish/person/day bag limit for Atlantic red porgy in 2023 to align with South Atlantic federal regulations; this recurring seasonal closure (opening May 1, closing July 1) has been reaffirmed annually by FWC press releases through 2025, with no announced changes for 2026.

Minimum size is 63 inches measured from tip of lower jaw to fork. Bag limit is 1 per person, applied as an aggregate limit across all Atlantic billfish species (sailfish, blue marlin, white marlin, roundscale spearfish) combined — not per species. Vessel limit is 4 per private recreational vessel (15 per for-hire vessel; charter for-hire captain/crew have zero bag). Sailfish caught in state waters may be kept aboard, but if released and you are in federal waters (or hold a federal HMS permit while in state waters) it may not be removed from the water. All harvested billfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours. HMS permit required only in federal waters, not state waters.

Sand seatrout is not individually regulated by FWC (only spotted seatrout has species-specific slot limits/seasons). Sand seatrout falls under FWC's default 'unregulated species' rule: no size limit, no closed season, and a recreational harvest limit of 2 fish OR 100 pounds per person per day, whichever is greater. This applies statewide, including Florida Atlantic state waters — FWC does not publish a separate Atlantic-specific rule for sand seatrout.

rows.season: No open season - harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Sand Tiger Shark is a prohibited species in Florida state waters (both harvest and possession banned) and is also listed as a prohibited species under NOAA's federal Atlantic HMS shark management program, which applies in all US Atlantic waters. If caught, it must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released immediately without delay; a non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hook and a device to cut the leader/hook are required when shark fishing.

Sandbar Shark is a Prohibited Species in Florida state waters (both Gulf and Atlantic coasts — this is a single statewide rule, not coast-specific). No recreational or commercial harvest, possession, or landing is allowed. If caught, the shark must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released immediately without delay; non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hooks and a line/leader-cutting device are required when shark fishing. Limited harvest is only permitted for a few vessels under the federal NMFS-observed research fishery program, which does not apply to recreational anglers.

rows.season: Year-round closure — no open season (harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Scalloped hammerhead (along with great and smooth hammerhead) has been a prohibited species in all Florida state waters since Jan 1, 2012. No recreational or commercial harvest, possession, or landing is allowed on either the Atlantic or Gulf coast — this is a single statewide rule, not coast-specific. If hooked, the shark must remain in the water and be released immediately (non-offset, non-stainless circle hooks required with natural bait). Federal HMS rules differ in federal waters (3-200 nm), where scalloped hammerhead retention is also prohibited for recreational anglers per NOAA HMS regulations.

rows.season: Open May 1 - Dec 31, 2026 (Atlantic state waters; closed annually Jan 1 - Apr 30 for spawning)
rows.notes: Scamp is part of the Atlantic 'shallow water grouper' complex (with black, gag, yellowfin, yellowmouth, red, coney, graysby, red/rock hind) that closes annually Jan 1-Apr 30 in all Atlantic state and federal waters, including Monroe County waters on both the Atlantic and Gulf sides. The 3-fish bag limit is an AGGREGATE limit shared among all Atlantic grouper species plus golden/blueline tilefish, not 3 scamp specifically. This is the Atlantic-side rule only; Gulf scamp regulations (16in min, 4-fish aggregate, year-round) differ and do not apply here.

10" total length minimum applies to both Atlantic and Gulf state waters. Schoolmaster is included within Florida's 10-fish-per-harvester-per-day snapper aggregate bag limit (not a separate species-specific limit) — if you keep any other 'aggregate' snapper species (e.g., gray/mangrove, mutton, dog, mahogany, cubera <30in), those count toward the same 10-fish total. Lane and vermilion snapper are exceptions with their own separate limits. No closed season is published for schoolmaster, so it is open year-round in Florida Atlantic state waters. Special reduced size/possession rules apply if fishing inside Biscayne National Park.

Sharpnose Sevengill Shark (Heptranchias perlo) is on FWC's statewide Prohibited Shark Species list — no harvest, possession, or landing allowed in Florida state waters (Gulf or Atlantic). Must be released immediately with gills submerged; do not remove from water. This is a single statewide FWC rule, not Atlantic-specific.

Statewide rule — same regulations apply to both Florida Gulf and Atlantic state waters (FWC does not split sheepshead rules by coast). Vessel/boat limit of 50 fish per trip applies only during March and April; outside those months there is no separate boat limit beyond the 8-per-person bag limit. Regulations extend into adjacent federal waters. Legal gear: hook-and-line, cast net, seine, or spear.

rows.season: Year-round harvest prohibition — no open season for retention
rows.notes: Shortfin mako shark retention is prohibited year-round in Florida Atlantic state waters. FWC set the state waters recreational bag limit to zero (Nov 30–Dec 1, 2022 Commission meeting) to align with federal HMS rules. NOAA Fisheries has maintained a zero retention limit in all Atlantic HMS commercial and recreational fisheries since July 5, 2022, with no changes as of Aug 2026. Any shortfin mako caught must be released immediately without removing from the water. Commercial harvest has been prohibited since Jan 2020. This applies to both Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters — FWC publishes one statewide rule for this species.

Silky shark (Carcharhinus falciformis) is on Florida's statewide Prohibited Shark Species list (FAC Ch. 68B-44, effective Jan 19, 2010). Harvest, possession, or landing is illegal in all Florida state waters (this is a statewide rule, applying equally to Atlantic and Gulf coasts — not coast-specific). Sharks must be released without delay, kept in the water with gills submerged; do not remove from water or bring aboard/onto shore. This is a state-waters rule; federal HMS rules (NOAA) also apply for offshore/EEZ waters and largely mirror this prohibition for silky shark under Atlantic HMS regulations.

Silver seatrout has no species-specific FWC regulations (FWC's species profile page lists no size/bag/season rule). It falls under Florida's default 'unregulated species' rule, which applies statewide (both Gulf and Atlantic coasts) with no distinction by region: no minimum size limit, and a recreational harvest limit of 100 lbs or 2 fish per person per day, whichever is greater. This is consistent with FWC's listing for the closely related Sand Seatrout, which also has no size limit and a 100 lb bag limit.

rows.season: No open season - harvest prohibited year-round, 2026
rows.notes: Bluntnose Sixgill Shark (listed by FWC as 'Sixgill Shark') is on Florida's Prohibited Shark Species list. All harvest, possession, landing, purchase, sale, or exchange is illegal in Florida state waters. If caught, the shark must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay (cut hook/leader if needed to avoid delay). This is a single statewide FWC rule that applies identically to both the Atlantic and Gulf coasts - there is no separate Atlantic-specific harvest allowance for this species.

Smalltooth sawfish is a prohibited species in all Florida waters (Gulf and Atlantic) and federally endangered under the ESA since 2003. It has been protected from harvest in Florida since 1992. If accidentally hooked, it must be released immediately without removing from the water; do not lift, land, or remove the rostrum. Targeting sawfish is illegal.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season — harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Smooth hammerhead sharks are a prohibited species in Florida state waters (statewide rule, applies equally to Gulf and Atlantic coasts). No recreational or commercial harvest, possession, or landing is allowed at any time. If caught, the shark must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released immediately without delay; non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hooks are required with natural bait, and a device to cut the hook/leader must be carried.

FWC issued Executive Order 26-18 closing recreational harvest of snowy grouper in Atlantic state waters (including all state waters off Monroe County) effective 12:01 a.m. June 7, 2026, matching the federal South Atlantic closure. Harvest is currently prohibited (bag/vessel limit = 0) and will not reopen until May 1, 2027 per the 2026-27 South Atlantic Snapper-Grouper FMP schedule. When open, the in-season limits are: no minimum size limit, 1 snowy grouper per vessel per day, counted within the 3-fish grouper/tilefish aggregate bag limit per person/day.

rows.season: Open Dec 1, 2025 - Oct 14, 2026; Closed Oct 15 - Nov 30, 2026 (annual recreational closure)
rows.notes: FWC regulates flounder statewide with one unified rule covering Gulf flounder, Southern flounder, summer flounder, and fringed flounder together; Atlantic and Gulf state waters share identical size/bag/season limits per FWC's official flounder page. Rules apply in both state and federal waters off Florida. As of today (Oct 18, 2026), the fishery is in its annual closed season (Oct 15-Nov 30); it reopens Dec 1, 2026.

FWC publishes a single statewide recreational regulation for Spanish Mackerel that applies to both Gulf and Atlantic state waters — no Atlantic-specific split for this species. Minimum size is 12 inches fork length; season is open year-round with no closure.

Spanish sardine is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' (a baitfish primarily targeted by commercial harvesters) with no minimum size, no closed season, and no specific bag limit. Florida law sets a default recreational harvest limit of two fish OR 100 pounds per harvester per day, whichever is greater, before a commercial license is required. This rule applies statewide (both Gulf and Atlantic state waters) — FWC does not publish a coast-specific rule for this species.

Spiny dogfish is on FWC's prohibited species list for Florida waters (both Atlantic and Gulf). No harvest, possession, or landing is allowed; any caught while fishing from shore or a vessel must be released immediately with minimal harm, per 68B-44 F.A.C. This is a statewide FWC rule, not coast-specific.

Applies to Atlantic coast counties (Nassau through Miami-Dade, excluding Monroe County). No minimum size limit. Bag limit of 50 per person per species (Spot and Atlantic croaker combined) has been in effect since Dec. 1, 2021. Gulf coast and Monroe County have a different bag limit (100 lbs per person) — not applicable to this Atlantic query.

Spotted eagle ray is designated a prohibited/protected species in Florida. Harvest, possession, landing, purchase, sale, or exchange is banned in both state and federal waters (applies statewide, both Atlantic and Gulf coasts). If caught incidentally, it must be released immediately without unnecessary harm; gills must stay submerged and it may not be removed from the water.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational harvest permitted; no closed season) - 2026
rows.notes: Recreational striped (black) & silver mullet have NO minimum size limit (the 11-inch fork-length minimum applies only to commercial harvest). Recreational daily bag is 50 fish aggregate (striped+silver combined) per harvester, with a seasonal aggregate VESSEL limit: 100 fish/vessel Feb 1–Aug 31, dropping to 50 fish/vessel Sept 1–Jan 31. As of today (Aug 21, 2026) the 100/vessel period is in effect. This rule is statewide and applies equally to Florida's Atlantic and Gulf state waters (FWC does not publish a separate Atlantic-only mullet rule). A commercial-only weekend closure (Sat morning–12:01am Mon) exists but does not restrict recreational harvest.

rows.season: Closed Oct 15 - Nov 30, 2026 (reopens Dec 1, 2026); open Dec 1 - Oct 14 otherwise
rows.notes: FWC regulates Gulf flounder, Southern flounder, Summer flounder, and Fringed flounder together under one statewide 'Flounder' rule that applies identically to both Atlantic and Gulf state waters and adjacent federal waters. As of today (Oct 22, 2026) recreational harvest is CLOSED under the annual Oct 15-Nov 30 closure; season reopens Dec 1, 2026. No vessel limit for private anglers; for-hire captain/crew have a 0 bag limit.

rows.season: Open now. Closed Dec 15, 2026 – Jan 31, 2027 and Jun 1, 2027 – Aug 31, 2027.
rows.notes: Managed under the same FWC snook rule as common snook. Swordspine snook reaches about 15 inches, so it never meets the 28-inch slot - in practice it is catch and release.

Tarpon is a catch-and-release-only fishery statewide in Florida (Atlantic and Gulf state waters, extending into federal waters) with no minimum size limit. Harvest/possession of a single tarpon is allowed only when pursuing a Florida state or world record while holding an annual Tarpon Tag ($51.50). Vessel, transport, and shipment limited to one tagged fish. Any tarpon over 40 inches (fork length) MUST remain in the water at all times, including for photos/measurement, unless being harvested under a record-pursuit tag. Hook-and-line only; snagging, snatch hooking, spearing, and multiple hooks with live/dead natural bait are prohibited. Special gear restrictions (no weighted jigs below the hook) apply year-round in Boca Grande Pass.

rows.season: Year-round harvest prohibition — no open season (catch-and-release only, statewide)
rows.notes: Tiger Shark is on FWC's Prohibited Species list and cannot be harvested, possessed, or landed in Florida state waters (Atlantic or Gulf). This is a statewide rule, not coast-specific. Must be released immediately with gills kept submerged; use non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks; shore anglers need the free Shark-Smart permit even for catch-and-release targeting. Federal (NOAA HMS) waters allow limited harvest under separate quota, but this does not apply in FL state waters.

Statewide FWC regulation (applies to both Atlantic and Gulf coasts, and extends into federal waters). Hook-and-line gear only; no nets or spearing; harvest prohibited with multiple hooks used with live/dead natural bait; snatch hooking prohibited. Special rules apply in Biscayne National Park.

Applies to Florida Atlantic state waters only (0-3 nm). Atlantic minimum size is 12 inches total length. The 5-fish daily bag limit is per harvester and is NOT included within the separate 10-fish snapper aggregate bag limit. Gulf state waters have a different rule (10" minimum, 10-fish bag) - not applicable here. Note: a temporary 10-fish 'snapper grouper aggregate' bag limit applies only to anglers participating in the 2026 Atlantic Red Snapper EFP program/for-hire red snapper season declarations, not to standard recreational vermilion snapper harvest in state waters.

FWC publishes one statewide recreational regulation for wahoo (not split by Gulf/Atlantic coast). No minimum size limit; open year-round. No recreational vessel limit specified on the FWC recreational page (a commercial vessel trip limit exists separately but does not apply to recreational anglers).

FWC applies one statewide weakfish rule with a special zone: in the Weakfish Management Area (WMA) covering part of Nassau County (Atlantic side, FL-GA line south to the tip of Amelia Island plus inland Nassau waters), minimum size is 12 inches and the bag limit is 1 fish per harvester per day. In all other Florida state waters (including the rest of the Atlantic coast), there is no minimum size limit and the bag limit is 100 pounds per harvester per day (not a fish-count limit). No closed season is published. Regulations also apply to weakfish-like fish (sand seatrout and hybrids).

White marlin is a federally-managed Atlantic HMS billfish. Florida FWC applies the same regulation statewide (both Atlantic and Gulf state waters) and defers to NOAA HMS rules, which apply in state waters as well as federal waters. Minimum size is 66 inches measured tip of lower jaw to fork of tail; daily bag limit is 1 fish per harvester (aggregate with other billfish per FWC quick-reference chart). All landed billfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours (800-894-5528 or hmspermits.noaa.gov). No federal HMS Angling Permit is required to target billfish in Florida state waters, but is required in federal waters.

Menhaden (including yellowfin menhaden) is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' for recreational purposes — no specific season, size limit, or gear-specific bag limit exists. Florida's statutory default recreational harvest limit for any unregulated marine species applies: 100 lbs OR 2 fish per harvester per day, whichever is greater (i.e., you may keep more than 2 fish as long as total weight is under 100 lbs, or up to 2 fish if their combined weight exceeds 100 lbs). This rule applies statewide, with no separate Atlantic-coast distinction published by FWC for this species.

Yellowmouth grouper is part of Florida's Atlantic shallow-water grouper complex, closed annually Jan 1-Apr 30 for spawning; open May 1-Dec 31. No individual sub-limit for yellowmouth — it counts within the 3-fish Atlantic grouper/tilefish aggregate bag limit per person per day (only 1 of which may be gag or black grouper). This is the Atlantic-specific rule; the Gulf coast has a different (4-fish, year-round) regulation and should not be used for Atlantic state waters.

No closed season for yellowtail snapper. 12-inch total length minimum. Counts within the 10-fish per person snapper aggregate bag limit (combined with other snapper species). Special reduced regulations apply if fishing within Biscayne National Park.

Minimum size is 24" fork length. Daily bag limit is 2 per harvester per day, not to exceed 2 per vessel (boat limit caps at 2 regardless of number of anglers aboard). Allowable gear: hook and line only in state waters (spearing allowed in federal waters, not applicable here). No slot/max size limit applies to African Pompano (that applies to Florida Pompano/Permit, not African Pompano).

Albacore tuna is a federally-managed Atlantic HMS species; NOAA rules apply in both state and federal Gulf waters (state jurisdiction does not set separate limits). NOAA Fisheries confirms there are no minimum size or bag/catch limits for albacore (or skipjack) tuna in the Atlantic/Gulf HMS fishery, unlike bigeye/yellowfin which have a 27" CFL minimum. Anglers targeting albacore in FL state or federal waters must hold a Federal HMS Angling Permit (issued per vessel in federal waters, per angler in state waters). Species falls under FWC's 'Billfish, Tuna, and Swordfish' regulatory page, which lists the group season as open year-round.

rows.season: Closed to harvest year-round (no open recreational season) - 2026
rows.notes: FWC prohibits take or possession of alligator gar in Florida waters without a special Scientific Collector's Permit; any alligator gar caught must be released immediately. This is a statewide FWC freshwater/nongame fish rule (alligator gar occur only in panhandle rivers, i.e. Gulf-side drainages), not a Gulf-vs-Atlantic saltwater season split.

Almaco Jack is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' in Florida Gulf state waters (recreational). Default statutory bag limit is 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is greater — no recreational minimum size limit and no closed season apply. (Florida's only almaco jack size limit, 20in fork length, applies solely to COMMERCIAL harvest in Atlantic state waters, per Fla. Admin. Code 68B-14.0035 — not applicable to Gulf recreational anglers.)

Atlantic angel shark (Squatina dumeril) is a Prohibited Species in Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic). It is illegal to harvest, possess, land, or unnecessarily harm this species. If caught, it must be released immediately without removing it from the water; gills must remain submerged and the fish must not be brought aboard a vessel, pier, or onto dry land.

Atlantic Sharpnose Shark is a Group 1 harvestable shark in Florida state waters with no minimum size limit. Bag limit is 1 shark per person per day, capped at 2 sharks per vessel regardless of number of anglers aboard (whichever is less), and sharks are managed as a group for bag-limit purposes (only one retainable shark of any harvestable species per angler per day). Shark must be landed in whole condition; shore anglers need the free Shark-Smart Fishing permit/course. This rule applies statewide in FL state waters (Gulf and Atlantic) — FWC does not differentiate Atlantic Sharpnose regs by coast.

Size limits are fork length. Bag limit of 5 per person is an aggregate combined with Lesser Amberjack (not 5 banded rudderfish alone). This applies in both Atlantic and Gulf state waters; no separate closed season applies to banded rudderfish/lesser amberjack (unlike Greater Amberjack, which is currently closed Sept 27, 2025 - Aug 31, 2026).

Basking Shark is a federally and state-listed prohibited shark species. It may not be harvested, possessed, or landed in Florida Gulf state waters at any time; must be released immediately with minimal injury, keeping gills submerged if possible. This prohibition applies statewide (both Gulf and Atlantic coasts) and matches NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited species rules that govern all U.S. Atlantic/Gulf waters.

Bigeye Sixgill Shark is a Prohibited Species in Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic). No harvest, possession, landing, purchase, or sale is allowed at any time. Must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released immediately without delay, cutting the hook/leader if necessary rather than removing it. This is a state-water rule under FAC Chapter 68B-44; NOAA Atlantic HMS federal rules also list this species as prohibited from retention in the Atlantic shark fishery.

Bigeye thresher shark is on FWC's prohibited species list for Florida state waters and is also a NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited species. It must be released immediately without removing from the water (kept in water, gills submerged) and cannot be harvested, boated, or landed under any circumstances. This applies in both state and adjacent federal Gulf waters.

Bigeye tuna is a federally managed Atlantic HMS (Highly Migratory Species). FWC's own saltwater regs page states that tuna managed federally as HMS require a federal HMS Angling Permit in both state AND federal waters and are subject to federal, not state, regulations — so Florida Gulf state-water limits mirror the NOAA HMS rule rather than a separate FWC limit. Under longstanding NOAA Atlantic HMS rules, bigeye tuna has a 27-inch curved-fork-length (CFL) minimum size and NO recreational daily bag limit (unlike yellowfin, which has a 3-fish/angler limit). Retention also requires a valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit, and tunas cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard.

Bignose Shark (Carcharhinus altimus) is on Florida's list of prohibited shark species. Harvest, possession, landing, purchase, or sale is unlawful in Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic). Catch-and-release only — must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay per FWC shark handling rules.
Slot 14-24 in; the five may include one fish over 24 in.

rows.season: Year-round in Gulf state waters shoreward of the 20-fathom break; closed February 1 - March 31, 2026 seaward of the 20-fathom break
rows.notes: <cite index="16-6">Several species of Gulf grouper (red, black, scamp, yellowfin and yellowmouth) are closed Feb. 1-March 31 seaward of the 20-fathom break.</cite> Outside that seasonal deep-water closure, Gulf black grouper harvest is open year-round in state waters. <cite index="13-6">Gulf Grouper Aggregate Bag Limit – all species of grouper in the Gulf are included in a 4 fish per harvester per day aggregate bag limit in any combination of grouper species.</cite> Black grouper has no separate sub-limit within that 4-fish aggregate in the Gulf (unlike gag, which is capped at 2). <cite index="13-7">Zero bag limit for captain and crew of for-hire vessels applies to Gulf gag, black, and red grouper only.</cite> No distinct per-vessel limit applies to Gulf black grouper (the 2-fish vessel limit for black grouper applies only in Atlantic state waters/Monroe County). Minimum size is 24 inches total length, consistent with the Gulf gag/black grouper size standard.

No minimum size limit for Blackfin Snapper in Florida Gulf state waters. Counts toward the 10-fish-per-person snapper aggregate bag limit (grouped with Black, Wenchman, Queen, and Silk snapper on FWC's site, which lists no closed season for this group, unlike Red Snapper which has federally/state-set seasonal dates). Reef fish gear requirements (non-stainless steel circle hooks with natural bait, dehooking device, venting tool) apply.

No minimum size limit. Daily bag limit is 2 fish per person OR 10 fish per vessel, whichever is greater (i.e., the 10-per-vessel cap can be reached collectively even if fewer than 5 anglers are aboard). This species-specific limit was adopted by FWC (effective Jan 1, 2025) and explicitly extends into federal Gulf/Atlantic waters as well as state waters — no HMS Angling Permit is required for blackfin tuna.

Blacknose shark is a Group 1 harvestable shark in FL state waters with no minimum size limit. Bag limit is per person per day, with sharks managed as a single group (all harvestable shark species combined count toward the 1/person, 2/vessel limit). Must be landed in whole condition (head, tail, fins attached); hook-and-line gear only; non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hooks required with live/dead natural bait. Shore-based anglers need free Shore-based Shark Fishing permit + Shark-Smart course.

Blacktip shark is a Florida 'Group 1' shark species with no minimum size limit. Bag limit is 1 shark per harvester per day OR 2 sharks per vessel, whichever is less (not additive). Sharks must be landed in whole condition (head, tail, fins attached). Shore-based anglers need the free Shore-Based Shark Fishing permit and non-offset/non-stainless circle hooks with natural bait are required. No closed season identified for this species in FL state waters.

Blue marlin is a federally-managed Atlantic HMS (billfish); federal NOAA HMS rules apply in both Florida state and federal Gulf waters, overriding any state-specific limit. Minimum size is 99 inches lower-jaw fork length, and bag limit is 1 fish per person per day. There is no fixed open/closed season, but total U.S. recreational landings of blue marlin, white marlin, and roundscale spearfish combined are capped at 250 fish annually, and a valid HMS Angling or Charterboat/Headboat permit is required in federal waters (not required in FL state waters). All harvested billfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours. No separate per-vessel bag limit for blue marlin was found (the commonly cited '1 per person, max 4 per vessel/15 for-hire' figure applies to swordfish, not blue marlin).

No minimum or maximum size limit for blue runner (hardtail) in Florida. Recreational bag limit is 100 fish per harvester per day, with no closed season, per FWC rule 68B-61. This limit also extends into adjacent federal Gulf waters off Florida. Commercial harvesters are not subject to this bag/possession limit but require a Saltwater Products License.

rows.season: Closed to targeted recreational fishing (Gulf of America/Gulf of Mexico) — no open season for retention except incidental catch
rows.notes: NOAA Fisheries HMS regulations (federal, apply uniformly in Florida Gulf state waters) prohibit targeted recreational fishing for Atlantic bluefin tuna in the Gulf of Mexico/Gulf of America. Only incidentally caught trophy-sized bluefin (≥73 inches curved fork length) may be retained while fishing for other HMS, limited to 1 per vessel per year under the Angling/Charter-Headboat trophy category, subject to trophy sub-quota availability. All bluefin under 73 inches CFL must be released. This is a federal HMS rule, not an FWC-specific regulation — FWC saltwater fishing pages defer to NOAA HMS rules for this species.

Gulf Region (includes Monroe County) recreational bluefish: 12" fork length minimum, 10 fish per harvester per day, no closed season. This differs from the Atlantic Region (Nassau-Miami-Dade), which has a 3-fish bag limit. Per F.A.C. 68B-43, must remain in whole condition (head & tail intact) until landed.

Bonnethead shark is managed under Florida's small coastal shark regulations. A landing permit is required. Verify current rules directly with FWC as shark regulations have been subject to change. Federal HMS rules may apply in federal waters — this record covers FL Gulf state waters only.

Bonefish is a catch-and-release only fishery statewide in Florida (Gulf and Atlantic state waters) since Sept 1, 2013 — no possession or harvest allowed, hook-and-line only. No minimum/maximum size limit applies since fish must be released; anglers may temporarily photograph/measure fish over 27" for the Angler Recognition Program before release.

Atlantic bonito (Sarda sarda) is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated' tuna species in Florida state waters (Atlantic and Gulf). No minimum size limit applies. Default bag limit is 2 fish per harvester per day OR 100 lbs per day, whichever is greater/more — no specific boat limit is set for this species.

Bonnethead shark is managed under Florida's small coastal shark regulations. A landing permit is required. Verify current rules directly with FWC as shark regulations have been subject to change. Federal HMS rules may apply in federal waters — this record covers FL Gulf state waters only.

Bull shark falls in FWC's 'Group 2' shark management group, requiring a 54-inch minimum fork length to harvest. Bag limit is 1 shark per harvester per day, or 2 sharks per vessel per day, whichever is less. Sharks must be landed in whole condition (head, tail, fins attached). Shore-based anglers need a free Shore-based Shark Fishing Permit plus completion of the Shark-Smart educational course. This regulation is set statewide by FWC and applies equally to Gulf and Atlantic state waters — there is no separate Gulf-only bull shark rule.

Caribbean Reef Shark (Carcharhinus perezii) is on FWC's Prohibited Species list for sharks — no harvest, possession, or landing allowed in Florida state waters (Gulf or Atlantic). Fish must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay; if hook removal would delay release, cut the hook/leader as close to the hook as possible. This applies to recreational and commercial fishing alike.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species - no open season)
rows.notes: Caribbean sharpnose shark is a prohibited species in Florida state waters (added to prohibited list effective Jan 19, 2010). No harvest, possession, or landing is allowed. Must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay if caught. This differs from the similarly-named but harvestable 'Atlantic sharpnose shark,' which has no minimum size limit — anglers must distinguish the two species carefully.

Cero mackerel is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' — no minimum size, no specific bag limit, no closed season, and no gear-specific size/slot rules. Standard gear rules still apply. Default statewide harvest allowance for unregulated species is 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day (whichever is greater); this is a weight/count alternative, not a simple per-day fish bag limit, so bagLimit is left null to avoid misrepresenting it as a standard per-fish cap. Because there's no closed season, 'Year-round' open status is accurate.

Minimum size is 36 inches fork length (not total length). Bag limit is 1 fish per person per day OR 2 per vessel per day, whichever is less. No closed season. This rule applies statewide to both Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters (identical limits on both coasts). Fish must remain in whole condition until landed ashore.

12" TL minimum size limit applies in both Atlantic and Gulf FL state waters. Cubera under 30" count within the 10-fish snapper aggregate daily bag limit per harvester. Anglers may ADDITIONALLY keep up to 2 cubera 30" or larger per harvester OR per vessel (whichever is less) per day, and those 2 large fish do NOT count against the 10-fish snapper aggregate. No closed season is currently in effect for Gulf state waters.

Finetooth shark has no minimum size limit in Florida state waters. Bag limit is 1 shark per harvester or 2 sharks per vessel, whichever is less. Sharks must be landed in whole condition (heads, tails, fins attached). Hook-and-line gear only; non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hooks required with natural bait. This regulation applies statewide (both Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters) as FWC does not differentiate finetooth shark rules by coast.

Gafftopsail catfish is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' in Florida state waters (applies to both Gulf and Atlantic coasts) — no minimum size, no closed season, and no species-specific bag limit. The default statutory recreational harvest limit for unregulated species applies: two fish OR 100 pounds per person per day, whichever is greater. Bag limit shown here (100 lbs) reflects that default; standard gear rules still apply.

rows.season: September 1 - September 30, 2026 (closes 12:01 a.m. Oct. 1); regional exception applies for Franklin, Wakulla, Jefferson, and Taylor counties (Apr 1-Jun 30 and Sep 1-Dec 31)
rows.notes: Bag limit of 2 gag grouper per person counts within the 4-grouper aggregate bag limit (combined total of grouper species). Season excludes all Gulf state waters off Monroe County. Set via FWC executive order to align with the 2026 NOAA federal Gulf season. State Reef Fish Angler Designation required for private recreational anglers targeting gag grouper. Charter captain/crew have a 0 fish bag limit in state waters.

Galapagos shark is a designated Prohibited Species under FWC rules (Ch. 68B-44, F.A.C.). It may not be harvested, possessed, or landed in Florida state waters (Gulf or Atlantic). If caught, it must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released immediately without delay; this rule applies statewide, not just Gulf coast.

Goldface tilefish is not managed with an individual bag limit in Florida Gulf state waters; it is counted within the 20 reef-fish aggregate bag limit (shared with species such as almaco jack, blueline tilefish, vermilion snapper, gray triggerfish, etc.). No recreational minimum size limit applies. Season is open year-round in the Gulf (unlike the Atlantic, which has closures for related tilefish species).

rows.season: Open March 1 - May 31 and Aug 1 - Dec 31, 2026 (currently open)
rows.notes: Gray Triggerfish in Florida Gulf State Waters has a split annual season (spring and fall segments) with a June 1-July 31 closed spawning period and a Jan 1-Feb 28 closed period. The 1-fish bag limit counts within the 20 reef fish aggregate bag limit. Anglers fishing from a private vessel must have the State Reef Fish Angler Designation. Note: this differs from Florida Atlantic State Waters, which has a 12" FL minimum size, 10-fish bag limit, and is open year-round.

Great hammerhead sharks are on FWC's Prohibited Species List for all Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic alike — this is one statewide rule, not coast-specific). No harvest, possession, or landing is allowed year-round; the shark must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay when fishing from shore, per FWC's shark regulations.

White (great white) shark is classified as a Prohibited Species in Florida state waters. It may not be harvested, possessed, or landed at any time. If caught incidentally, it must be released immediately without removing it from the water, with gills kept submerged; delaying release beyond hook removal is prohibited.

rows.season: Closed — 2026 Gulf state waters season (Sept 1 – Oct 13, 2026) has ended; harvest closed as of 12:01 a.m. Oct 14, 2026 and remains closed until the next scheduled opening, Sept 1, 2027
rows.notes: Greater Amberjack is currently CLOSED to recreational harvest in Florida Gulf state waters (bag/possession limit = 0) because FWC's executive order aligning with the federal season ended the 2026 season on Oct 13, 2026 (closes 12:01 a.m. Oct 14). When open, the Gulf regulation is: 34" fork length minimum, 1 fish per person per day. Season will not reopen until Sept 1, 2027 per NOAA's regularly scheduled 2027 season, unless FWC issues another executive order. This is the Gulf-specific rule — Florida's Atlantic coast amberjack season/limits differ (28" FL min, open Jan–Mar & May–Dec).

FWC's generic 'Tilefish' regulation for Gulf state waters applies to all tilefish species not separately named (anchor, blackline, goldface, sand, etc.), since only golden and blueline tilefish have their own species-specific rule pages. Gulf State rule: no minimum size, daily bag limit is 100 lbs per person OR 2 fish per person, whichever is greater (i.e., anglers may keep 2 fish even if under 100 lbs, or more fish if total weight is at least 100 lbs). Season is open year-round in Gulf state waters.

rows.season: Closed Oct 15 - Nov 30; open the rest of the year
rows.notes: Minimum 14 in total length. The closure covers gulf, southern, summer and fringed flounder.

FWC classifies menhaden (pogies/bunkers) as an 'unregulated species' with no specific size, season, or gear restrictions. Default recreational harvest limit for unregulated species is 100 pounds OR two fish/organisms per person per day, whichever amount is GREATER (not a traditional 'bag limit' of a fixed fish count — recorded here as 100 lbs since that governs most menhaden catches). This applies statewide, including Florida Gulf state waters.

Longspine porgy has no species-specific FWC regulation and falls under Florida's default 'Unregulated Species' rule, which applies statewide in both Gulf and Atlantic state waters. The default limit is 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is greater — so the 100 lb threshold typically governs actual harvest since longspine porgy are small panfish-sized reef fish. No minimum/maximum size limit or closed season applies.

rows.season: Closed year-round — no open season (harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Gulf sturgeon (Acipenser oxyrinchus desotoi) and Atlantic sturgeon are fully protected under Florida law and the federal Endangered Species Act. No take, possession, or sale is permitted. Any sturgeon caught incidentally must be released immediately without removing it from the water. This applies in both Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters.
Gulf state waters. 14 in fork length, five per harvester. State Reef Fish Angler designation required from a private vessel.

Crevalle jack is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' (no specific size, season, or gear rules beyond standard recreational gear). The default statutory bag limit for unregulated species applies: 2 fish OR 100 pounds per person per day, whichever is greater (i.e., you may keep either up to 100 lbs of fish, or exactly 2 fish if their combined weight exceeds 100 lbs). This rule is the same for both Florida Gulf and Atlantic state waters — FWC does not publish a coast-specific rule for this species.

King mackerel (Scomberomorus cavalla) recreational harvest in Florida Gulf state waters (including Monroe County) is open year-round with no closed season. Minimum size is 24 inches fork length (not total length). Daily bag limit is 3 fish per harvester in Gulf state waters (differs from the 2-fish limit in Atlantic state waters). Legal gear is hook-and-line or spearing only; fish must be landed whole (head & tail intact). This is a state-managed recreational limit set by FWC Rule 68B-12; federal HMS rules do not apply to king mackerel (it is managed under the Gulf/South Atlantic Coastal Migratory Pelagics FMP, not NOAA HMS).

Ladyfish is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' — no minimum/maximum size, no closed season, and no species-specific bag limit. The statewide default recreational harvest limit for unregulated species applies: 2 fish OR 100 pounds per person per day, whichever is more (this is a single combined threshold, not a strict 2-fish cap — anglers may keep more than 2 fish as long as total weight stays under 100 lbs). This rule is identical for both Florida Gulf and Atlantic state waters (FWC does not differentiate by coast for this species).

FWC increased the Gulf state-waters minimum size for lane snapper from 8 in to 10 in total length and established a species-specific 20-fish-per-person recreational bag limit, effective April 1, 2026. This 20-fish limit is separate from (not part of) the general 10-fish snapper aggregate bag limit that applies to other snapper species. No closed season/quota closure has been announced for Gulf lane snapper; regulation pages list it as open year-round.

Lemon shark is on FWC's Prohibited Species list — no recreational or commercial harvest is allowed in Florida state waters. This applies statewide (both Gulf and Atlantic coasts); FWC does not differentiate by coast for this species. Catch-and-release is permitted, but the shark must remain in the water at all times with gills submerged and cannot be removed from the water.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season for Lesser Amberjack)
rows.notes: Slot limit: fork length must be no less than 14" and no more than 22". Bag limit of 5 per person is an AGGREGATE combining Lesser Amberjack and Banded Rudderfish together (not 5 of each). This applies in both Gulf and Atlantic state/federal waters. Do not confuse with Greater Amberjack, which has separate, more restrictive size/season rules on the same FWC page.

Little tunny (listed by FWC as 'Atlantic bonito, little tunny (bonito)') is an 'unregulated' tuna species in Florida state waters (not managed by NOAA HMS quotas). Default recreational limit applies: 2 fish OR 100 lbs per day, whichever is greater — no minimum size, no closed season, and no federal HMS Angling Permit required in state or federal waters.

rows.season: Closed year-round — harvest prohibited (no open season) in Florida state waters
rows.notes: Longbill Spearfish is on FWC's prohibited species list; it is unlawful to harvest, possess, land, purchase, sell, or exchange this species in Florida state (Gulf or Atlantic) waters. This differs from Roundscale Spearfish, which has an open aggregate billfish bag limit (66" LJFL, 1 per harvester) — Longbill Spearfish is not part of that allowance and may not be retained at all.

rows.season: Closed year-round – harvest prohibited (no open season), effective ongoing as of 2026
rows.notes: Longfin mako shark (Isurus paucus) is on Florida's Prohibited Species List for both recreational and commercial harvest in ALL Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic — one statewide rule, no coast-specific variance). Anglers must release immediately without removing the shark from the water; gills must remain submerged and the fish may not be brought aboard a vessel, onto a pier/bridge, or onto dry land. This is a Florida-specific prohibition (separate from and stricter than the federal NOAA HMS shortfin mako 'zero retention' rule, which applies to a different mako species). Non-offset, non-stainless circle hooks and a line/leader-cutting device are required when targeting sharks.

Gulf of Mexico state waters: no minimum size limit for dolphin/mahi-mahi. Daily bag limit is 10 fish per person, or 60 per vessel, whichever is less (vessel limit does not apply to for-hire vessels; captain/crew bag and possession limit is zero). Note: Atlantic state waters have different rules (20" min, 5/person, 30/vessel) — do not confuse with Gulf.

Mangrove (gray) snapper have no closed season in Florida Gulf state waters. The 5-fish per person bag limit falls within the overall 10-fish snapper aggregate bag limit (all snapper species combined) for Gulf state waters. Minimum size is 10 inches total length, measured tip of snout to tip of tail with tail pinched.

Nassau Grouper is completely closed to harvest in Florida state waters. The species is federally listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act, and FWC prohibits all recreational and commercial harvest. Possession is also prohibited.

rows.season: Harvest prohibited year-round (Prohibited Species) — no open season
rows.notes: Narrowtooth shark (Carcharhinus brachyurus) is on Florida's Prohibited Species list for state waters. It is illegal to harvest, possess, land, purchase, sell, or exchange this species. If caught, it must be released without delay, kept in the water with gills submerged, and only the hook/leader may be cut if quick removal isn't possible — no retention, no size or bag limit applies since harvest is never allowed.

Nassau Grouper is completely closed to harvest in Florida state waters. The species is federally listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act, and FWC prohibits all recreational and commercial harvest. Possession is also prohibited.

Night shark is a prohibited species in Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic). Harvest, possession, landing, purchase, or sale is unlawful year-round. Sharks must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released immediately without delay; if hook removal would delay release, cut the leader/hook as close as possible. This is a Ridgeback shark species also on NOAA's federal Atlantic HMS Prohibited Species list, so the same no-harvest rule applies in adjacent federal Gulf waters.

Nurse shark is classified in FWC's 54-inch fork-length harvestable shark group (with Bull, Spinner, Blue, Oceanic Whitetip, Porbeagle, Common Thresher). Sharks are managed as a combined group for bag limit purposes — 1 shark per harvester per day or 2 per vessel, whichever is less, regardless of species mix. Retained sharks must be landed in whole condition (head, tail, fins attached). Hook-and-line gear only; non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks required with natural bait. Shore-based anglers need the free FWC Shore-Based Shark Fishing permit/course. No recreational closed season currently posted for state-water shark harvest, though FWC closes state waters to shark harvest if adjacent federal waters close.

Oceanic Whitetip Shark is classified as a prohibited species in Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic). No harvest, possession, landing, purchase, sale, or exchange is allowed. Must be released immediately without removing from the water, keeping gills submerged, to maximize survival. This aligns with NOAA federal HMS regulations, which also prohibit retention in all U.S. federal Atlantic, Gulf, and Caribbean waters as the species is listed as Threatened under the ESA.

Opah (Lampris guttatus) is not one of FWC's specifically regulated species (no listing in the Reef Fish, Pelagics, or Coastal Species quick-reference charts) and is therefore classified as an 'unregulated species' under Florida rule. Per FWC's official unregulated-species page, the default recreational harvest limit for any species without species-specific regulations is 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is greater — there is no minimum size, slot, or closed season. This applies the same in Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters (no coast-specific opah rule exists). Note: 'Opah' does appear on FWC's commercial Restricted Species endorsement list, but that pertains only to commercial sale requirements, not recreational bag/size/season.

Slot limit: 11"-22" fork length. Daily bag limit of 2 permit per harvester, but only 1 of the 2 may exceed 22" fork length. A vessel-level cap of no more than 2 permit over 22" per boat per day also applies (in addition to the 2-per-person bag). Gear: hook-and-line only in FL state waters. No closed season currently in effect for recreational permit in Gulf state waters. Special stricter rules apply in the Special Permit Zone (SPZ) in extreme South Florida, which is not part of the broader Gulf state waters covered here.

Pigfish are classified by FWC as an 'unregulated' saltwater species in Florida (state waters, Gulf and Atlantic). No minimum size, maximum size, or closed season applies. The default statutory bag limit for unregulated species is 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is greater; for smaller fish like pigfish the 100 lb by-weight limit effectively applies rather than a strict 2-fish cap. No specific vessel/boat limit is published.

Pinfish are classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' with no species-specific size limit or closed season. Per Florida statute, the default recreational harvest limit for any unregulated marine species is 100 pounds OR 2 fish per harvester per day, whichever is greater (expressed here as 100 lb since pinfish are small bait-sized fish, 2-fish minimum would rarely apply). This rule applies statewide in Florida state waters, Gulf and Atlantic alike — no coast-specific split exists for pinfish.

rows.season: Year-round (open recreational harvest season; no closed season specific to porbeagle in FL state waters)
rows.notes: Porbeagle shark falls in FWC's 54-inch fork-length harvestable group (with bull, nurse, spinner, blue, oceanic whitetip, and common thresher). Bag limit is 1 shark per person per day, with a hard cap of 2 sharks per vessel per day regardless of number of anglers aboard. Shore-based anglers need the free FWC Shore-Based Shark Fishing Permit; all HMS permit holders must have a shark endorsement. Federally, porbeagle is an Atlantic HMS pelagic shark and, per NOAA, must be released alive if a swordfish, tuna, or billfish is aboard at haulback. Sharks must be landed with head, tail, and fins naturally attached.

Pinfish are commonly used as bait in Florida Gulf waters and are generally unregulated for recreational harvest with no size or bag limits under FWC rules. However, this should be verified directly with FWC as regulations can change.

Red grouper is open year-round in Florida Gulf state waters (inside 9 nm). The only closure is in adjacent federal waters seaward of the 20-fathom break, Feb 1–Mar 31, which does not apply to state waters. The 2-fish red grouper bag limit counts toward the 4-fish Gulf grouper/tilefish aggregate bag limit per person per day. Zero bag limit applies to captain/crew of for-hire vessels for Gulf red, gag, and black grouper. Note: Gulf Council voted Jan 28, 2026 (Amendment 62) to eliminate the Feb–Mar federal shallow-water closure and raise red grouper catch limits, but this was not yet in effect as of this rule's implementation and applies to federal, not state, waters.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season in Florida Gulf state waters; seasonal closures apply only in Atlantic state waters)
rows.notes: Gulf state-waters red porgy have NO minimum size limit and NO recreational fish-count bag limit — the limit is a weight-based 100 lbs per harvester per day, per Fla. Admin. Code 68B-14.0035/0036 and current FWC regional fishing-rule summaries. This is distinct from Atlantic state waters, where red porgy has a 14-inch minimum size, a 1-fish/person/day bag limit, and a seasonal closure (open only May 1-June 30, closed the rest of the year). Do not apply the Atlantic rules to Gulf-caught fish.

Sailfish is managed under the Billfish category (with blue marlin, white marlin, roundscale spearfish) with an aggregate bag limit of 1 billfish per person per day, regardless of species. Minimum size is 63" measured lower jaw to fork of tail. Sailfish is an HMS species; Florida's state-water rule mirrors the federal NOAA HMS Atlantic Billfish minimum size and bag limit, so state and federal limits align here. No closed season — open year-round. HMS Angling Permit and 24-hr NOAA landing report (800-894-5528 or hmspermits.noaa.gov) required for any landed billfish.

Sand seatrout has no species-specific FWC regulation and falls under Florida's default 'unregulated species' rule: no minimum size, no closed season, and a default recreational limit of 2 fish or 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is greater. Exceeding this is considered a commercial quantity requiring a saltwater products license.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species - no harvest season)
rows.notes: Sand tiger shark is a Prohibited Species in Florida — no possession, harvest, landing, purchase, sale, or exchange is allowed in Florida state waters (Gulf or Atlantic). Any sand tiger caught must be released immediately with minimal harm. This aligns with the federal NOAA HMS Fishery Management Plan, under which take has been prohibited since 1997.

Sandbar Shark is on FWC's Prohibited Species list statewide (this rule applies equally to Gulf and Atlantic Florida state waters - no coast-specific split for this species). Harvest, possession, or landing is illegal recreationally and commercially. If caught, it must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay (shore anglers) or not brought aboard (vessel anglers). Limited harvest is allowed only under a federal NMFS-observed commercial research fishery permit, which does not apply to recreational anglers.

Scamp is part of the Gulf grouper aggregate bag limit (max 4 grouper of any combination of species per person per day in Gulf state waters). State waters (0-9 nm) are open year-round; note a separate federal-waters closure (Feb 1-Mar 31) applies seaward of the 20-fathom break but does not affect state-water harvest.

Schoolmaster snapper has no closed season in Florida Gulf state waters. 10-inch total length minimum applies to both Atlantic and Gulf. The 10-fish daily bag limit for schoolmaster is not a separate limit — it falls within (counts toward) FWC's overall 10-fish-per-harvester snapper aggregate bag limit that covers all snapper species combined, so effectively an angler cannot exceed 10 total snapper of any mix per day. Special reduced regulations apply if fishing inside Biscayne National Park.

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Sevengill Shark (Heptranchias perlo) is on FWC's Prohibited Species list for state waters statewide (applies to both Gulf and Atlantic coasts). Must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay; retention, landing, or possession is illegal in state waters.
Minimum 12 in total length. Gulf and Atlantic state waters.

Short bigeye (Pristigenys alta) is not one of FWC's individually managed reef fish species (no listing among snapper/grouper/amberjack/tilefish/hogfish rules or the 'Other Reef Fish' chart). It falls under FWC's statewide 'Unregulated Species' category for hook-and-line recreational harvest: no closed season, no minimum/maximum size, and the default statutory bag/possession limit of 2 fish OR 100 lbs per person per day, whichever is greater (the '2' here represents the fish-count floor, not a hard cap if weight is used instead). Note: short bigeye does appear on FWC's commercial Marine Life (aquarium trade) list where its collection is prohibited specifically inside John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park — that restriction applies to marine-life/aquarium collection gear, not general recreational hook-and-line fishing statewide.

Shortfin mako shark may not be harvested, possessed, or landed in Florida state waters (Gulf or Atlantic) at any time. FWC set the recreational bag limit to zero in December 2022 to align with federal Atlantic HMS regulations, which also prohibit all retention of shortfin mako. This is a no-harvest species — catch-and-release only.

Short Bigeye (Pristigenys alta) is not a commonly regulated species under FWC recreational saltwater fishing rules. It may fall under a general unregulated or 'no limit' category, but this cannot be confirmed with high confidence. Verify directly with FWC before publishing.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season / no harvest allowed)
rows.notes: Silky shark is a federally prohibited Atlantic HMS species and is also listed on FWC's prohibited shark species list for Florida state waters. It must be released immediately with minimal harm; gills must remain in the water and it may not be removed from the water, retained, possessed, or landed under any circumstances.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season, harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus griseus) is on Florida's Prohibited Species list for state waters (Gulf and Atlantic). No harvest, possession, landing, purchase, or sale is allowed. If caught, must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay; non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hooks required with natural bait, and a cutting/de-hooking device must be on hand.

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: All sawfish (Smalltooth and Largetooth) are federally listed as Endangered under the U.S. Endangered Species Act and have been protected from harvest in Florida since 1992. It is illegal to harvest, possess, land, purchase, sell, or exchange any sawfish in Florida state waters (Gulf or Atlantic). If accidentally hooked, anglers must not remove the fish from the water and must release it immediately by cutting the line if necessary; report sightings/captures to 1-800-4SAWFISH.

rows.season: Closed - No harvest allowed (prohibited species, year-round)
rows.notes: Smooth hammerhead (Sphyrna zygaena) is classified as a prohibited shark species in Florida state waters. Harvest, possession, or landing is illegal year-round. Must be released immediately without removing from water, with gills submerged, per FWC shark handling rules.

Snowy Grouper counts toward Florida Gulf's 4-grouper aggregate bag limit (combined with other grouper species/tilefish); no minimum size limit applies. This is a state-waters (0-9 nm) regulation for Gulf of Mexico; distinct from Atlantic state waters, where a temporary closure (EO 26-18) is in effect for the remainder of 2026 and no Gulf-specific closure has been issued for snowy grouper in 2026.

rows.season: Closed Oct 15 - Nov 30; open the rest of the year
rows.notes: Minimum 14 in total length. The closure covers gulf, southern, summer and fringed flounder.

Minimum size is 12 inches fork length (not total length). Recreational bag limit is 15 fish per harvester per day in Florida Gulf state waters, with no closed season. No slot/maximum size applies. Legal gear: beach or haul seine, cast net, hook and line, or spear.

Spanish sardine is classified by FWC as an 'unregulated species' in Florida state waters — no species-specific size limit, bag limit, or closed season. Under Florida law, the default recreational take threshold for unregulated species is 2 fish or 100 lbs per person per day (whichever is greater); exceeding that requires a commercial saltwater products license. This default threshold is not a true per-angler 'bag limit' in the managed-species sense, so bagLimit/boatLimit are left null rather than guessed as integers.

Spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) is classified as a Prohibited Species in Florida state waters, meaning no harvest, possession, or landing is allowed under any circumstances. If caught, it must be released immediately with minimal harm, keeping gills submerged and only briefly lifting the head from water to remove a hook if necessary; cut the line/hook if removal would delay release.

For Florida Gulf state waters (all areas outside the Nassau-through-Miami-Dade Atlantic coast rule, which includes the Gulf coast and Monroe County), FWC sets no minimum size limit and a daily recreational bag limit of 100 POUNDS per person (not a fish count) for spot, open year-round. Note: this differs from Florida's Atlantic coast (Nassau through Miami-Dade, excluding Monroe), where a separate 50-fish-per-person bag limit applies (effective Dec 1, 2021) — that Atlantic rule does NOT apply to Gulf waters.

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Spotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari) is designated a protected/prohibited species under Florida Administrative Code 68B-44 (in effect since 1994). Harvest, possession, landing, purchase, sale, or exchange is illegal in Florida state AND federal waters. Any caught while fishing must be released immediately without unnecessary harm — gills must stay submerged and the fish may not be removed from the water. Also prohibited from harvest by all forms of spearing.
Slot 15-19 in total length; one fish over 19 in per vessel, or per person from shore, inside the bag. The bag itself is set by FWC region (2, 3 or 5 per person) — check the region you are fishing.

No minimum size limit. Statewide FWC rule applies to Mugil cephalus (striped mullet) as well as silver, fantail, and redeye mullet. Daily per-person bag limit is 50 fish. Daily vessel limit varies seasonally: 50 fish/vessel Sept 1–Jan 31, and 100 fish/vessel Feb 1–Aug 31 (using the lower Sept–Jan figure here as the current-date applicable boat limit since today is Aug 30, nearing the Sept 1 transition — anglers should verify which seasonal vessel limit is in effect for their exact fishing date). More restrictive seasonal bag limits apply to portions of Pinellas County (5 fish/day, Oct 1–Jan 31) and seasonal night closures apply in portions of Charlotte County. This is a single statewide FWC regulation, not split by Gulf/Atlantic coast.

rows.season: Closed Oct 15 - Nov 30, 2026 (reopens Dec 1, 2026); open year-round outside this closure
rows.notes: FWC regulates all flounder species (Gulf, Southern, Summer, and Fringed flounder) under a single 'Flounder' rule applying to both Gulf and Atlantic state waters, plus adjacent federal waters. As of today (Oct 22, 2026), the annual recreational harvest closure is in effect; season reopens Dec 1, 2026. Legal gear: spears, gigs, hook-and-line, seine, cast net. For-hire captain/crew have a 0 bag limit.

Minimum size is 47 in lower-jaw-fork-length (head attached) OR 25 in cleithrum-to-keel length if head is removed. Bag limit is 1 swordfish per harvester per day; private recreational vessel limit is 4 per vessel regardless of number of anglers aboard, while for-hire (charter/headboat) vessels may possess up to 15. Zero bag/possession limit applies to captain and crew of for-hire vessels. Federal HMS Angling Permit required to fish in federal waters (not required in FL state waters). All landed swordfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours (800-894-5528). Swordfish is an Atlantic HMS species; Florida's state-water rule (FAC 68B-58.004) mirrors the federal recreational limits, so state and federal numbers align.

rows.season: Open now. Closed Dec 1, 2026 – Feb 28, 2027 and May 1, 2027 – Aug 31, 2027.
rows.notes: Managed under the same FWC snook rule as common snook. Swordspine snook reaches about 15 inches, so it never meets the 28-inch slot - in practice it is catch and release. FWC also calls it rare on the west coast.

Tarpon is a catch-and-release only fishery statewide, including Gulf state waters. Harvest is prohibited except when a single tarpon is retained under a $50 harvest tag in pursuit of an IGFA/state record (limit 1 per person per year, 1 per vessel). Tarpon over 40 inches must remain in the water during release. Hook-and-line only; snagging, snatch hooking, and spearing prohibited. Additional gear restriction (no weighted jigs below hook) applies year-round in Boca Grande Pass.

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Tiger sharks are on FWC's prohibited species list for Florida state waters (Gulf and Atlantic). Catch-and-release only; sharks must remain in the water with gills submerged and be released without delay. This has been in effect since Jan 1, 2012 (Ch. 68B-44, F.A.C.) and remains current. A Shore-based Shark Fishing Permit + Shark-Smart course is required if targeting/encountering sharks from shore, and non-offset non-stainless circle hooks are required with natural bait.

Hook and line gear only (no nets or spearing); harvest prohibited using multiple hooks with live/dead natural bait; snatching prohibited. State size/bag regulations also extend into adjacent federal waters. Special rules apply in Biscayne National Park.

Vermilion snapper (beeliner/mingo) in Florida Gulf state waters are managed by FWC. 10-inch minimum total length; 10 fish per person per day aggregate or individual limit. Verify whether this counts within a snapper aggregate or stands alone, as groupings can change annually.

No minimum size limit for wahoo in Florida state waters (Gulf or Atlantic). Regulation applies to Florida state waters only (Gulf state waters extend 9 nautical miles from shore); federally permitted vessels must follow federal Gulf/Atlantic HMS or South Atlantic Dolphin-Wahoo FMP rules even in state waters if applicable.

Bag limit of 100 pounds per day applies as a weight-based limit (not per-fish count) for weakfish in Florida Gulf state waters. Florida's only weakfish-specific size/bag restrictions (12" minimum, 1 fish/harvester) apply solely to the Weakfish Management Area in Nassau County on the Atlantic side near the FL-GA line — this does NOT apply to Gulf state waters. No closed season is published for weakfish in Florida Gulf waters.

White Marlin is a federally managed Atlantic HMS species; Florida FWC regulations mirror NOAA HMS rules and apply in state waters. A Federal HMS Angling Permit is required in federal waters (not required for state waters). Catch reporting to NOAA required within 24 hours of landing.

Yellowfin tuna is an HMS (Highly Migratory Species). Federal NOAA HMS rules govern regardless of state waters. Under current NOAA HMS regulations, the recreational limit is 3 fish per person per day with a 27-inch curved fork length minimum. FWC defers to federal HMS rules for this species. Verify current federal limits at fisheries.noaa.gov/contact/highly-migratory-species.

Yellowmouth grouper is part of Florida's Gulf grouper aggregate bag limit — up to 4 grouper per harvester per day in any combination of grouper species (no more than 4 total, even if mixing species). No separate Gulf state-waters closed season applies to yellowmouth grouper; the Jan 1–Apr 30 shallow-water grouper closure applies only in Atlantic state waters and Monroe County, and a Feb 1–Mar 31 closure applies only in federal Gulf waters seaward of the 20-fathom break, not in Gulf state waters.

Yellowtail snapper has no closed season in Florida Gulf state waters. The 10-fish bag limit is per person per day and counts within the overall 10-snapper aggregate bag limit for all snapper species combined (not an additional 10 on top of other snappers). 12-inch minimum is total length. Reef fish gear requirements (e.g., dehooking tools, venting/descending device) apply.

Almaco Jack has no individual minimum size limit in Louisiana state waters. It falls within a 20-fish aggregate reef fish bag limit shared with Vermilion Snapper, Lane Snapper, Gray Triggerfish, Goldface Tilefish, Tilefish, and Blueline Tilefish (not a standalone 20-fish limit). No closed season is currently in effect for this species in LA state waters.

rows.season: Closed - Prohibited species (no open season, year-round)
rows.notes: Atlantic Angel Shark (Squatina dumeril) is listed as a prohibited shark species under Louisiana Administrative Code Title 76, Part VII §357. Harvest, possession, and retention (recreational or commercial) is unlawful in Louisiana state waters at all times. This mirrors NOAA Atlantic HMS federal prohibited species list.

No closed season and no minimum/maximum size limit for Atlantic Sharpnose Shark in Louisiana state or federal waters. Recreational limit is 1 Atlantic sharpnose shark per person per trip, regardless of trip duration (this is a per-person possession limit, separate from the 1-shark-per-vessel limit that applies to other shark groups). Anglers targeting HMS sharks with rod & reel must have an Atlantic HMS Angling Permit. Finning is prohibited.

rows.season: No open season — retention prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) is listed as a prohibited shark species in Louisiana state waters under La. Admin. Code tit. 76, §VII-357, and is also prohibited under federal NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations (50 CFR 635). If caught, it must be released immediately with minimal injury and never removed from the water; no possession, sale, or retention is allowed recreationally or commercially in any waters.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season — prohibited species)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sand Tiger Shark (Odontaspis noronhai) is listed as a federally prohibited shark species under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations, which LDWF incorporates directly into Louisiana state water rules. It may not be harvested, possessed, sold, or retained recreationally or commercially in LA state or federal waters. If caught incidentally, it must be released immediately with minimal harm and without removing it from the water.

Bigeye Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus nakamurai) is classified as a prohibited shark species in Louisiana. No harvest, possession, purchase, sale, or barter is allowed at any time in state waters. Any specimen caught must be released immediately unharmed. This applies regardless of commercial or recreational permit status.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season — prohibited species)
rows.notes: Bigeye thresher shark is listed as a prohibited species under Louisiana's shark harvest regulations (LAC 76:VII.357) and under NOAA Atlantic HMS rules, which apply concurrently in state waters. Any bigeye thresher caught must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water; it may not be retained, possessed, sold, or landed under any circumstance by recreational or commercial anglers.

Bigeye tuna is a federally-managed Atlantic HMS species; the same federal rule applies in Louisiana state and federal waters. Minimum size is 27 inches curved fork length with no recreational bag/possession limit and no closed season. A federal HMS Angling (or Charter/Headboat) permit is required to target/retain bigeye tuna, and anglers must comply with both LDWF and NOAA HMS rules. LDWF's own saltwater finfish page defers to NOAA for exact current tuna sizes/bag limits, noting these can change often.

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season) - prohibited species, must be released
rows.notes: Bignose Shark is a federally and state-prohibited shark species. LDWF's shark harvest regulations (LAC 76:VII.357) explicitly list bignose shark among prohibited species, and NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations (which apply in all US Atlantic/Gulf waters, including LA state waters) also list Bignose as a prohibited species that must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water. No retention, size, or bag limit applies because harvest is not permitted under any circumstance.

rows.season: Open year-round except closed February 1 – March 31, 2026 in state waters seaward of the 20-fathom (120 ft) boundary
rows.notes: 24" minimum total length. Black grouper falls within the 4-fish daily 'grouper aggregate' shared with speckled hind, red, snowy, yellowedge, yellowfin, yellowmouth, and warsaw grouper, gag, and scamp. Within that aggregate: no more than 1 speckled hind and 1 warsaw grouper per vessel per day, no more than 2 red grouper per person, and no more than 2 gag per person. Closed season Feb 1–Mar 31 applies to black, red, yellowfin, and yellowmouth grouper and scamp in state waters seaward of the 20-fathom line. Charter captain/crew have a zero bag limit for grouper. Rules may differ in adjacent federal (NOAA) waters.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed recreational season currently in effect)
rows.notes: Blacknose shark is managed by LDWF as part of the 'small coastal shark' group (with bonnethead, Atlantic sharpnose, and finetooth). Under LAC 76:VII.357, recreational anglers are limited to no more than one shark per vessel per trip drawn from the combined large coastal/small coastal/pelagic shark groups (blacktip and bull sharks are exempt from this vessel limit and have no bag limit in LA state waters, and sharpnose/bonnethead get a separate 1-per-person allowance) — blacknose does not fall into any of those exemption categories, so it counts toward the single vessel-limit shark. Minimum size is 54 inches fork length for all sharks EXCEPT Atlantic sharpnose, bonnethead, blacktip, and bull sharks — blacknose is not exempted, so the 54-inch minimum applies. Finning is prohibited and sharks must be landed with head/fins intact. The historical April–June closed season was repealed for commercial harvest in Jan 2025; no current LDWF notice indicates a recreational closed season for small coastal sharks.

Blue marlin is a NOAA Atlantic HMS-managed species; federal rules apply in ALL waters, including Louisiana state waters (LDWF does not set separate state limits for billfish). Minimum size is 99 inches lower-jaw fork length (LJFL). Retention limit is 1 billfish per vessel per trip, which may be EITHER a blue marlin OR a white marlin (not one of each). There is no closed season, but U.S. recreational landings of blue marlin, white marlin, and roundscale spearfish combined are capped at 250 fish annually nationwide, and NOAA can restrict retention if that cap is approached. Vessel must have a valid HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit, and any retained billfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours.

rows.season: Closed year-round for targeted/directed fishing; Trophy (73"+) incidental-catch fishery in the Gulf of America closed through December 31, 2026
rows.notes: Atlantic Bluefin Tuna is a federally-managed HMS species. NOAA Fisheries does not allow targeted/directed recreational fishing for bluefin tuna anywhere in the Gulf of America (which the Gulf portion of Louisiana state waters falls under), as this region is designated bluefin spawning grounds. Only incidental catch of 'trophy' bluefin (≥73" curved fork length) while fishing for other HMS was permitted, but NOAA closed the Angling category Gulf of America Trophy Fishery effective through Dec 31, 2026 due to the 2.3-mt subquota being reached. Louisiana LDWF explicitly defers to and is superseded by federal HMS rules for tuna harvest in state waters, and anglers must hold a federal HMS Angling Permit plus LA Recreational Offshore Landing Permit. Net effect: no legal retention of Atlantic bluefin tuna currently in Louisiana state or federal Gulf waters.

Atlantic Bonito is not specifically listed among LDWF's regulated saltwater finfish species (Reef Fish, Highly Migratory Species sharks, or Common Coastal Species like Cobia/Sheepshead). LDWF's finfish page states its general default rule applies to unlisted species.

Bonnethead sharks have no minimum size limit in Louisiana state or federal waters (exempted along with Atlantic sharpnose, blacktip, and bull sharks from the standard 54-inch fork length minimum). Recreational anglers may possess no more than 1 bonnethead shark per person per trip, regardless of trip duration. This is a per-person limit, not an additional per-vessel limit (the 1-per-vessel large coastal shark rule does not apply to bonnethead, which is a small coastal species). Finning is prohibited, and an HMS Angling Permit is required if fishing in/from the federal EEZ.

Caribbean Reef Shark is classified as a prohibited shark species under both Louisiana state regulations (LAC 76:VII.357) and NOAA Atlantic HMS federal rules. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and cannot be retained, possessed, or landed by recreational or commercial anglers in any Louisiana or federal waters. This is a standing (non-seasonal) prohibition.

Caribbean Sharpnose Shark is classified as a prohibited species in Louisiana state waters. No possession, harvest, or retention is allowed recreationally or commercially at any time. This is a state-water prohibition list separate from general HMS shark bag limits.

Louisiana state waters recreational cobia limits: 36-inch total length minimum, 1 fish per person per day, and 2 fish per vessel per day (regardless of number of trips), matching federal Gulf waters limits. These limits took effect April 20, 2023 via LWFC rule change and remain in effect as of Sept 20, 2026 with no closed season identified. Recreational Offshore Landing Permit (ROLP) required to possess cobia in LA waters.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season established for Cubera Snapper in Louisiana state waters, 2026)
rows.notes: Cubera Snapper has no individual size or bag limit; it falls under LDWF's 10-fish aggregate bag limit shared with Mutton, Gray (Mangrove), Schoolmaster, Dog, Mahogany, Yellowtail, Queen, Blackfin, Silk, and Wenchman snappers. LDWF states there are no size limits for species not specifically listed. Possession limit is twice the daily bag limit (per LDWF's standard possession rule). A Recreational Offshore Landing Permit (ROLP) is required to possess snappers in Louisiana. Federal Gulf waters (GMFMC) may set separate rules if fishing beyond 9 nm.
