Finetooth shark is classified by LDWF as a 'small coastal shark' and falls under the general 'Other Sharks' HMS category (all small coastal, large coastal, and pelagic sharks except silky/sandbar). Minimum size is 54 inches fork length. Limit is 1 shark per vessel per trip in aggregate across this whole group (not a per-angler bag limit) — no one may possess more than this regardless of trips/duration. No separate finetooth-specific allowance exists; it shares the pooled vessel limit with blacknose and other small/large coastal/pelagic sharks. Season is open year-round in LA state waters per the current LDWF regulation page and the 2026 (updated Sept 21, 2026) fishing pamphlet, which no longer references the older April 1–June 30 closed season found in 2022–2024 pamphlets.

Galapagos Shark is listed as a prohibited species under Louisiana Administrative Code tit. 76, § VII-357, meaning it may not be harvested, possessed, or sold in Louisiana state waters. This aligns with NOAA's federal Atlantic HMS prohibited species list, which also classifies Galapagos Shark as prohibited and requiring immediate release with minimal injury. No size, bag, or vessel limits apply since retention is never legal.

Golden Tilefish (listed as 'Tilefish') has no closed season or minimum size in Louisiana state waters. It falls within a 20-fish-per-person aggregate daily bag limit shared with Vermilion Snapper, Lane Snapper, Gray Triggerfish, Almaco Jack, Goldface Tilefish, and Blueline Tilefish (with sub-caps of 1 Gray Triggerfish and 10 Vermilion Snapper within that 20). No species-specific sub-limit applies to Golden Tilefish itself, and no separate boat limit is specified.

Goldface tilefish has no minimum size limit and no closed season in Louisiana state waters. It falls within a 20-fish aggregate daily bag limit shared with vermilion snapper, lane snapper, gray triggerfish, almaco jack, tilefish, and blueline tilefish (with no more than 1 gray triggerfish and no more than 10 vermilion snapper counted within that 20-fish aggregate). Possession limit equals the daily bag limit unless otherwise noted.

Goliath Grouper (formerly 'Jewfish') is listed by LDWF under 'Saltwater Species You Cannot Harvest' in Louisiana state waters. Harvest has been prohibited since 1990 and remains so; no recreational season, size, or bag limit exists — any catch must be released immediately unharmed. This mirrors the federal harvest prohibition in Gulf federal waters (Gulf Council). Note: Florida runs a separate limited-permit lottery harvest (Mar 1–May 31) in its own state waters only — this does NOT apply to Louisiana.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational, no closed season currently in effect)
rows.notes: Great Hammerhead is classified as a 'large coastal shark' under LDWF rules (LAC 76:VII.357), not a prohibited species, in Louisiana state waters. Recreational anglers are limited to 1 shark in aggregate from the large coastal/small coastal/pelagic group PER VESSEL PER TRIP (not per angler) — bull and blacktip sharks are exempt from this 1-shark vessel limit and now have no bag limit. Minimum size for retained large coastal sharks (including great hammerhead) is 54 inches fork length; there is no listed maximum/slot size. Hammerhead sharks may not be retained if tuna, swordfish, or billfish are aboard (federal HMS rule applies concurrently). LDWF has eliminated the prior April–June closure that applied to commercial harvest; no current recreational seasonal closure for large coastal sharks was found on official pages as of retrieval date.

34-inch minimum fork length, 1 fish per person per day (daily bag = possession limit). Charter vessel captain and crew may not retain any Greater Amberjack (creel limit is zero for them). This state-waters season mirrors the NOAA federal Gulf recreational season, which closes at 12:01 a.m. on Oct 14, 2026.

Anchor tilefish is grouped under the general 'Tilefish' category (goldface, blackline, anchor, blueline) in Louisiana state waters. It falls within the 20-fish-per-person aggregate bag limit shared with vermilion snapper, lane snapper, gray triggerfish, almaco jack, goldface tilefish, and blueline tilefish (with sub-caps of only 1 gray triggerfish and 10 vermilion snapper within that 20). No minimum size limit applies to tilefish, and no closed season is listed for this species in LA state waters.

rows.season: Year-round in Louisiana state waters, except closed October 15 - November 30, 2026
rows.notes: LDWF does not set a separate regulation for Gulf flounder (Paralichthys albigutta); its recreational 'flounder' rules (listed under 'Southern Flounder' in LDWF publications) apply to all flounder species taken in Louisiana state waters. No minimum/maximum size limit applies. Possession limit equals the daily bag limit (10/person). Annual closure Oct 15 - Nov 30 applies to all gear, recreational and commercial.

Recreational king mackerel in Louisiana state waters is open year-round. Minimum size is 24 inches fork length, daily bag/possession limit is 3 per person. LDWF notes anyone actively fishing may not possess more than the daily take limit, and off-water possession allows up to two days' bag limit under certain conditions.

Lemon shark is classified as a Large Coastal Shark under LDWF rules. It is legal to harvest (not a prohibited species) in Louisiana state waters, open year-round, with a 54-inch minimum fork length and a boat-aggregate limit of 1 shark per vessel per trip (not per angler). Sandbar and silky sharks are excluded from this group and prohibited from recreational harvest; lemon shark is not on the prohibited list. As of the 2026 regulations update, the prior April 1–June 30 seasonal shark closure has been removed from current LDWF guidance, with sharks (other than blacktip/bull, which have no limits) now shown as open year-round in state waters.

Slot limit 14-22 inches fork length. 5-fish daily bag is an AGGREGATE limit shared with Banded Rudderfish (combined total of both species cannot exceed 5 per person/day). Requires a free Recreational Offshore Landing Permit (ROLP) to possess in Louisiana waters. This differs from Greater Amberjack, which has a 34" minimum, 1-fish bag, and seasonal closures.

Longbill spearfish is federally classified as a PROHIBITED SPECIES under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations — it may not be retained, possessed, or landed under any circumstances (recreational or commercial), and must be released immediately without removing it from the water. Louisiana's own billfish harvest rule (LAC Title 76:VII.355) sets minimum sizes only for blue marlin, white marlin, roundscale spearfish, sailfish, and swordfish — longbill spearfish is notably absent, consistent with the federal prohibition (neighboring Mississippi codifies an explicit possession ban on this species). HMS species are managed under NOAA Atlantic HMS rules in all jurisdictions, including Louisiana state waters.

Longfin mako shark (Isurus paucus) is listed as a prohibited species in Louisiana state waters — no recreational or commercial retention is allowed at any size. This aligns with NOAA Atlantic HMS federal rules, which also prohibit longfin mako retention in all U.S. Atlantic HMS fisheries.

Mangrove (Gray) Snapper has a 12-inch minimum total length and no closed season in Louisiana state waters. It counts within the 10-fish snapper aggregate (gray, mutton, yellowtail, cubera, queen, blackfin, silk, and wenchman snapper combined) — no more than 5 of that 10 may be mutton snapper, but there is no individual sub-limit on gray/mangrove snapper, so up to 10 per person per day may be gray snapper if no other aggregate species are kept. Red, vermilion, and lane snapper are managed separately and NOT part of this aggregate.

Narrowtooth Shark (Carcharhinus brachyurus) is classified as a prohibited species in Louisiana state waters — no retention, harvest, or possession is allowed at any time. If caught, it must be released immediately with minimal harm. This aligns with the Louisiana Administrative Code shark harvest regulations and matches NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited shark listings, which apply concurrently.

Night Shark (Carcharhinus signatus) is classified as a PROHIBITED shark species under Louisiana Administrative Code Title 76, §VII-357(B)(4), meaning it may not be harvested, retained, or possessed in Louisiana state waters at any time. This aligns with NOAA Atlantic HMS federal regulations (50 CFR 635), which also list Night Shark as prohibited coast-wide — any caught Night Shark must be released immediately with minimal injury.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season for large coastal sharks in LA state waters)
rows.notes: Nurse shark is classified as a 'large coastal' shark species under LDWF rules. Recreational anglers must retain nurse sharks at a minimum of 54 inches fork length (nurse sharks are NOT among the species exempted from the size limit — only Atlantic sharpnose, bonnethead, blacktip, and bull sharks are exempt). Vessel limit: no more than ONE shark from the large coastal species group (which includes nurse shark) per vessel per trip, regardless of number of anglers aboard — this functions as a per-boat, not per-angler, limit. LDWF eliminated the prior April–June closed season for shark harvest, so the fishery is open year-round in LA state waters absent a new emergency closure. Finning is prohibited; sharks must be landed with head, tail, and fins naturally attached.

rows.season: Closed year-round — retention prohibited (federal rule effective February 2, 2024)
rows.notes: Oceanic Whitetip Shark is a NOAA HMS prohibited species. Federal rule (50 CFR Part 635, effective Feb 2, 2024) bans retention/possession in all U.S. Atlantic waters including the Gulf of Mexico, and applies to all HMS-permitted anglers regardless of state or federal waters. Louisiana's own administrative code still lists it under the 'pelagic sharks' management category, but LDWF's current recreational fishing guidance directs anglers to federal HMS rules and states anglers 'may not possess any... threatened, endangered, or prohibited species.' Sharks must be released in the water with minimal injury; no possession, harvest, or landing is legal.

rows.season: Year-round (Louisiana state waters, subject to real-time closure if the federal Atlantic HMS pelagic/porbeagle group quota closes)
rows.notes: Porbeagle is classified by LDWF as a legal 'pelagic shark' (not a prohibited species) in LAC 76:VII.357. Minimum size is 54 inches fork length (no exemption for porbeagle). Recreational retention is capped at one shark from the pelagic/large-coastal/small-coastal group per VESSEL per trip (not a per-angler bag limit), and finning is banned. An HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit with shark endorsement is required, and NOAA's federal rule requires any porbeagle alive at haulback to be released unharmed if a swordfish, tuna, or billfish is aboard.

Atlantic sailfish is a NOAA HMS-managed billfish; federal HMS minimum size and bag limits apply in Louisiana state waters as well as federal waters (LDWF defers to NOAA for billfish and requires a Recreational Offshore Landing Permit to possess billfish in LA waters). Minimum size is 63 inches lower-jaw fork length (LJFL); bag limit is 1 sailfish per harvester per day, with no defined additional LA-specific vessel limit. An HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit is required to fish for or retain billfish, and any harvested sailfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours.

rows.season: Closed year-round — Prohibited Species (no legal harvest season), 2026
rows.notes: Sand tiger shark (Carcharias taurus) is listed as a prohibited shark species under both Louisiana state regulation (LAC 76:VII.357) and the federal NOAA Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan. It may not be retained, possessed, sold, or landed in Louisiana state waters (or federal waters) under any circumstance. Anglers who hook a sand tiger shark must release it immediately without removing it from the water. This prohibition applies statewide in Louisiana with no distinction by coast.

Sandbar Sharks may not be retained by recreational anglers in Louisiana state waters. Per LDWF and LA Admin Code 76:VII.357, no sandbar or silky shark may be retained by persons fishing under recreational vessel limits; commercial harvest is prohibited unless the fisherman holds a valid federal shark research permit under 50 CFR 635.32(1).

Scalloped Hammerhead is classified by LDWF under the 'Large Coastal Sharks' group (with nurse, smooth hammerhead, bull, spinner, great hammerhead, tiger, lemon, and silky* sharks). In Louisiana STATE waters, this group has a 54-inch minimum fork length and a combined 1-shark-per-vessel-per-trip aggregate limit (not a per-angler bag limit), open year-round, with no possession of silky or sandbar sharks and no prohibited species retained. Finning is illegal. Note: Louisiana's state-water rule differs from the separate FEDERAL HMS hammerhead group (great/scalloped/smooth), which carries its own 78-inch minimum fork length and 1-per-vessel limit in federal waters — anglers crossing into federal waters must follow the stricter federal hammerhead-specific rule.

rows.season: Open year-round in Louisiana state waters, except closed February 1 – March 31 (2026 dates: Feb 1 - Mar 31, 2027 for next cycle) seaward of the 20-fathom (120 ft) curve
rows.notes: Scamp is managed as part of Louisiana's shallow-water grouper (SWG) group (black, red, yellowfin, yellowmouth grouper, and scamp), which share a single closed season each year from Feb 1 - Mar 31 seaward of the 20-fathom break, mirroring the federal Gulf closure. Outside that window, grouper fishing in LA state waters is open year-round. The 4-fish bag limit is an AGGREGATE limit shared across all grouper species combined, not 4 scamp individually. Minimum size is 16 inches total length. Charter vessel captains/crew have a zero bag limit for any grouper species. Recreational Offshore Landing Permit (ROLP) required to possess grouper in LA waters.

Sevengill Shark (Heptranchias perlo, listed by LDWF simply as 'Sevengill Shark') is classified as a prohibited shark species in Louisiana state waters. No recreational or commercial harvest, possession, sale, or retention is permitted at any size, in any quantity, in any season, within or without Louisiana waters.

rows.season: No open season - retention prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Shortfin mako shark retention is prohibited in Louisiana state waters for both recreational and commercial fisheries. LDWF confirmed that as of January 20, 2025, shortfin mako sharks are prohibited from being possessed in any waters, consistent with the federal NOAA HMS zero retention limit in effect since July 2022. Sharks caught must be released.

Sixgill shark (Hexanchus griseus) is listed as a prohibited shark species under Louisiana Administrative Code Title 76:VII.357(B)(4) and the LDWF Saltwater Creel & Size Limits chart. No possession, harvest, or retention is allowed in Louisiana state waters at any time; must be released immediately if caught. This is a statewide rule (no separate Gulf/Atlantic coast distinction applies since Louisiana only has Gulf coastline).

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Smalltooth Sawfish is a federally endangered species (ESA-listed since 2003) and is classified by LDWF as a Threatened/Endangered and Prohibited species. It is illegal to target, harvest, harm, or possess this species in Louisiana state waters. If incidentally caught, it must be released immediately unharmed. Federal ESA prohibitions apply concurrently with LDWF state rules.

Smooth hammerhead is an Atlantic HMS (shark); federal NOAA HMS rules apply in ALL waters, including Louisiana state waters — state jurisdiction does not override. Minimum size is 78 inches FORK LENGTH (not total length). Retention limit is 1 hammerhead shark (of any of the three hammerhead species combined) OR other shark PER VESSEL per trip — this is a boat limit, not a per-angler bag limit, so bagLimit is left null. Hammerhead sharks cannot be retained if a swordfish, tuna, or billfish is on board or has been offloaded. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks required. HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement required.

Snowy Grouper has no individual state season closure in Louisiana; it falls under LDWF's 'grouper aggregate' bag limit shared with speckled hind, black grouper, red grouper, yellowedge grouper, yellowfin grouper, yellowmouth grouper, warsaw grouper, gag grouper, and scamp — 4 fish per person per day combined (with sub-caps of 1 speckled hind/1 warsaw per vessel and 2 red grouper/2 gag grouper per person within that 4-fish total). No minimum size limit applies to Snowy Grouper in LA state or adjacent federal Gulf waters. Gag Grouper has a separate closed season (currently open Sept 1–30, 2026) but this does NOT apply to Snowy Grouper, which may be harvested year-round subject to the aggregate limit. A Recreational Offshore Landing Permit is required to possess grouper species in Louisiana waters. Charter/for-hire captains and crew have a zero bag limit for any grouper species.

rows.season: Year-round in Louisiana state waters, except closed October 15 - November 30, 2026 (reopens December 1, 2026)
rows.notes: No minimum/maximum size limit for Southern Flounder in Louisiana state waters. Daily take and possession limit is 10 fish per person. Annual closed season (no harvest/possession allowed) runs October 15 through November 30 each year for both recreational and commercial sectors, statewide, all gear types. As of today (Oct 14, 2026), the season is open but closes tomorrow.
Size limit is 12 inches minimum fork length. Bag and possession limit are the same (15 per person per day). Regulations may differ in federal waters off Louisiana's coast.

Statewide slot limit of 13-20 inches total length with a 15-fish daily creel; up to 2 of the 15 fish may exceed 20 inches (counted within, not in addition to, the 15-fish limit). Regulation took effect Nov 20, 2023 and is scheduled to sunset Jan 1, 2028 unless modified. Charter guides/deckhands have a zero bag limit while conducting a for-hire trip. This is one statewide rule (LDWF eliminated the previous separate western LA zone regulation).

Striped/hybrid striped bass are managed under Louisiana's freshwater game fish regulations (all state waters, no closed season). No minimum size limit applies, but within the 5-fish daily bag, no more than 2 fish may exceed 30 inches total length (not a true slot limit — larger fish are allowed, just capped at 2 per angler per day).

No minimum/maximum size limit for striped mullet in Louisiana recreational saltwater fishing. Daily take/possession limit is 100 lbs per person per day (weight-based, not a fish count) — confirmed consistently in LDWF's Common Coastal Species table and in LA Admin Code Title 76 §VII-193 for recreational mullet harvest. Recreational harvest has no closed season; only the COMMERCIAL mullet fishery (strike-net) has a season (3rd Monday Oct – 3rd Monday Jan). Possession limit equals the daily bag limit unless otherwise noted.

Tiger shark is managed recreationally as part of Louisiana's 'large coastal shark' group. Per LAC 76:VII.357, recreational anglers are limited to one shark from the large coastal, small coastal, or pelagic group per vessel per trip, and any shark retained under a bag limit (including tiger shark) must be at least 54 inches fork length — this size minimum does NOT waive for tiger sharks (only sharpnose, bonnethead, blacktip, and bull are exempt from the size minimum, and blacktip/bull now have no bag limit in LA state waters as of Jan 2025). No recreational closed season currently exists for tiger shark in Louisiana state waters; the state's shark 'season' references apply to the commercial fishery only. Finning is prohibited. HMS federal rules (NOAA) set the same 54-inch fork-length minimum and 1-per-vessel limit for tiger shark, so state and federal requirements align.

No closed season for tripletail in Louisiana state waters — bag/size limits apply year-round. Minimum 18-inch total length; no maximum (slot) size or possession limit above 2x daily bag. Rule applies whether tripletail are caught within or outside Louisiana waters.

LDWF established Louisiana's first-ever recreational bag and possession limit for Wahoo (5 fish per person, no size limit), effective June 20, 2025, to preempt federal Gulf Council management. Wahoo remains open year-round in LA state waters. A Recreational Offshore Landing Permit (ROLP) is also required to possess Wahoo. Federal Gulf waters (GMFMC) regulations may differ.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season specific to Warsaw Grouper in Louisiana state waters)
rows.notes: Warsaw Grouper has no recreational minimum size limit. It is part of Louisiana's 4-fish-per-person grouper aggregate (with speckled hind, black, red, snowy, yellowedge, yellowfin, yellowmouth grouper, gag, and scamp), but is capped at 1 Warsaw Grouper PER VESSEL per day regardless of number of anglers aboard — this is stricter than the per-person aggregate. Charter/headboat captain and crew bag limit for any grouper is zero. Some other species in the aggregate (gag, black/red/yellowfin/yellowmouth grouper, scamp) have their own closed seasons, but Warsaw Grouper itself is not subject to a closed season under current LDWF rules. Federal Gulf EEZ regulations for Warsaw Grouper differ (commercial IFQ, no directed recreational federal season) and do not apply to LA state waters fishing.

White marlin is designated a saltwater gamefish under LA R.S. 56:327 and its harvest is governed by LAC 76:VII.355, which sets a 66-inch Lower Jaw Fork Length (LJFL) minimum size. Louisiana regulations do not specify a distinct daily bag/vessel limit for white marlin (unlike swordfish, which has an explicit creel limit). As an Atlantic HMS species, federal NOAA Fisheries rules also apply and currently show no per-trip retention limit for white marlin, but total U.S. recreational landings of blue marlin, white marlin, and roundscale spearfish combined are capped at 250 fish annually, and any retention/landing must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours. Anglers must hold a NOAA HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit to retain billfish in LA state or federal waters.

Minimum size is 27 inches Curved Fork Length (CFL). Bag/possession limit is 3 fish per person per day or trip (no separate vessel limit). Louisiana state waters regulations mirror the federal NOAA HMS Atlantic yellowfin tuna rules. Anglers must have a valid federal Atlantic HMS Angling (or Charter/Headboat) permit plus an LDWF Recreational Offshore Landing Permit to possess yellowfin tuna in Louisiana waters, whether inside or outside state territorial waters.

rows.season: Open year-round in Louisiana state waters, EXCEPT closed February 1 - March 31 (annually) seaward of the 20-fathom (120 ft) boundary
rows.notes: Yellowmouth grouper is managed within Louisiana's 4-grouper aggregate bag limit, which also includes speckled hind, black, red, snowy, yellowedge, yellowfin, and warsaw grouper, gag, and scamp. No species-specific minimum size limit is published by LDWF for yellowmouth grouper (unlike black/gag at 24in or red/yellowfin at 20in). A seasonal closure for yellowmouth (along with black, red, yellowfin grouper and scamp) applies Feb 1 - March 31 each year, but only in state waters seaward of the 20-fathom (120 ft) curve; inside that depth it remains open year-round. No more than 1 speckled hind and 1 Warsaw grouper per vessel per day; charter boat captain/crew have a zero bag limit for any grouper species.

No minimum size limit for Almaco Jack in Mississippi state waters. Bag limit is 20 fish per person, but this is a SHARED 20-fish 'reef fish aggregate' limit (combined total, not 20 Almaco Jack alone) that also includes Gray Triggerfish, Vermilion Snapper, Lane Snapper, and all Tilefish species. Almaco Jack is classified as a reef fish, so anglers must have a Mississippi Recreational Offshore Landing Permit (ROLP) to possess it, and fish must be landed with heads/tails intact (may be gutted/gilled) unless a filed float plan applies for trips >24 hrs.

rows.season: No open season - Prohibited species (harvest/possession unlawful year-round)
rows.notes: Atlantic Angel Shark (Squatina dumerili) is listed as a prohibited shark species under MDMR regulations (Title 22, Part 7, Ch. 09, §101.14) - unlawful for commercial fishermen to possess. It is also on the MDMR Recreational Catch Limits page as prohibited from harvest, and is federally prohibited under NOAA Atlantic HMS shark regulations in all U.S. Atlantic/Gulf waters. Sharks must be released with minimal injury; no retention, size, or bag limit applies since take is banned entirely.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season for Banded Rudderfish in Mississippi state waters)
rows.notes: Slot limit: fish must be between 14 and 22 inches fork length (FL). Bag limit is 5 fish per person per day in aggregate, combined with Lesser Amberjack (Seriola fasciata) — not 5 of each species separately. No boat/vessel limit specified for this species.

Basking Shark is listed by MDMR as a Current Shark Species Prohibited from harvest in Mississippi state waters. No retention, landing, or possession is allowed recreationally or commercially. This aligns with NOAA HMS federal prohibited species status, which also applies in all U.S. waters.

rows.season: Year-round closure (no open season, harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sand Tiger Shark (Odontaspis noronhai) is listed as a prohibited shark species in Mississippi state waters — must be released immediately, no possession allowed by recreational or commercial fishermen at any time. This aligns with the federal NOAA HMS prohibited species list, which applies coastwide.

Bigeye Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus nakamurai, listed as Hexanchus vitulus by MDMR) is on Mississippi's list of prohibited shark species — no possession, harvest, or retention allowed for recreational or commercial fishermen in state waters at any time. This aligns with federal NOAA HMS prohibited species status for this shark. If caught incidentally, it must be released immediately.

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Bigeye Thresher Shark is a federally prohibited species under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations and is also explicitly listed as prohibited under Mississippi state regulation. Anglers must release any bigeye thresher shark immediately without removing it from the water, using methods that maximize survival. No possession, retention, or landing is legal for either recreational or commercial fishermen in MS state waters.

Bigeye tuna is a NOAA Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS); federal rules apply in ALL waters including Mississippi state waters and override state regulations per NOAA HMS management. Minimum size is 27 inches curved fork length (CFL), measured along the body contour from jaw tip to tail fork. There is no recreational bag/possession limit for bigeye tuna (unlimited retention, subject to permit and reporting requirements). A valid federal HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit is required to fish for bigeye tuna. Tunas cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded from the vessel.

rows.season: Closed year-round — prohibited species, no open season
rows.notes: Bignose Shark (Carcharhinus altimus) is listed by MDMR as a Prohibited shark species — harvest, possession, and retention are not permitted in Mississippi state waters. This mirrors NOAA HMS federal prohibited species status (Atlantic shark management), which applies uniformly across all U.S. Atlantic/Gulf jurisdictions. Any bignose shark caught must be released immediately with minimal harm.

Mississippi state waters recreational regulations set no minimum size and no daily bag/possession limit for Black Drum, and no closed season is listed for the species (unlike Red Drum, Spotted Seatrout, etc. which have defined size/bag limits on the same table). Note: this applies to recreational harvest in MS state waters only — commercial shrimp trawl fishermen may keep Black Drum for personal consumption only up to a 25 lb cumulative weight cap alongside other bycatch species, per Title 22 Part 3 Rule 8.1(R).

Black Grouper counts within Mississippi's 4-fish grouper aggregate bag limit (shared with Red, Yellowfin, Scamp, and other groupers). Minimum size is 24 inches total length. Unlike Red Grouper and Red Snapper, Black Grouper does not have a separately announced opening/closing order from the MDMR Executive Director, so it remains open year-round in MS state waters under the current administrative rule.

Blackline Tilefish (Caulolatilus cyanops) is treated by MDMR as a Gulf 'reef fish' species. It is NOT listed on MDMR's published Recreational Catch Limits table (which only itemizes inshore/nearshore species like Seatrout, Red Drum, Flounder, Sheepshead, Gray Snapper, Tarpon, Tripletail, Cobia, and mackerels). MDMR's Title 22 Part 3 regs reference Blackline Tilefish only in the context of (a) the list of reef-fish species excluded from the charter-boat two-day bag-limit endorsement, and (b) the general rule that reef fish possession/sale must comply with the NOAA Gulf of Mexico Reef Fish Fishery Management Plan and any state/federal conditions. No MDMR-specific minimum size, bag limit, or closed season for Blackline Tilefish was found — it appears to fall under the general federal Gulf reef-fish framework (often bundled in a large multi-species reef-fish aggregate bag limit) rather than a state-specific numeric limit. Because no explicit MDMR or NOAA per-species number for Blackline/Anchor/Goldface tilefish could be confirmed with confidence, numeric fields are left null per the no-guessing rule.

Blacknose shark falls under MDMR's 'small coastal sharks' management group (with Atlantic sharpnose, bonnethead, finetooth). Mississippi Administrative Code Title 22, Part 7 sets a 25-inch total-length minimum size and a 4-fish aggregate daily bag limit per person for small coastal sharks in state waters; no separate vessel cap is specified for this group (unlike large coastal sharks, which are capped at 1 per person/3 per vessel). No closed recreational season is published for small coastal sharks in MS state waters (commercial shark season runs concurrent with the federal Western Gulf sub-region season, but that is a commercial-only provision). Federally, NOAA HMS rules for blacknose shark (54-inch fork length, 1 fish per vessel, no minimum size for retention limit context) apply only in federal waters beyond MS's 9-mile state boundary and are less restrictive than the state minimum size — anglers in MS state waters must follow the state's 25-inch minimum.

rows.season: Year-round (Mississippi state waters, no closed season for recreational large coastal sharks)
rows.notes: Blacktip shark is classified as a 'large coastal shark' under MDMR Title 22 Part 3 rules. Recreational anglers may possess no more than 1 large coastal/pelagic shark per person per day, and no more than 3 large coastal/pelagic sharks in aggregate per vessel per day, with a 37" total length minimum size. Finning is prohibited. Federal HMS rules (NOAA) also apply and may impose additional restrictions or prohibited species lists; check NOAA HMS Compliance Guide for any federal overlays.

rows.season: Year-round (open access; subject to closure if the coastwide 250-fish combined blue marlin/white marlin/roundscale spearfish annual landings cap is reached, per NOAA HMS status page checked Aug 2026)
rows.notes: Blue marlin is a federal Highly Migratory Species (HMS) — NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations (50 CFR 635.20/635.24) apply in ALL waters, including Mississippi state waters, and override any MDMR state-specific limit. Minimum size is 99 inches lower-jaw fork length (LJFL). Retention limit is 1 Atlantic billfish (blue marlin, white marlin, sailfish, or spearfish combined) per vessel per day/trip — this is a per-vessel/day limit, not a per-angler daily bag. Additionally, combined U.S. recreational landings of blue marlin, white marlin, and roundscale spearfish are capped at 250 fish annually; if that cap is reached, NOAA switches the fishery to catch-and-release only for the remainder of the year. Billfish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is already aboard. HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit required to fish for or retain Atlantic billfish, and all landed billfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours.

rows.season: Year-round — directed/commercial harvest prohibited in Mississippi state waters; recreational retention permitted only as an incidental catch (2026)
rows.notes: Mississippi state law (22 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 3, Ch. 10) makes it unlawful to take, catch, or possess Atlantic Bluefin Tuna in MS state waters EXCEPT as an incidental catch by recreational fishermen. Rule 10.2 caps incidental recreational landings at 1 fish PER BOAT PER WEEK (not per day), and all such landings must be reported to MDMR. Commercial harvest is 'No Take' in MS state waters. Note: Mississippi (along with Connecticut) is explicitly excluded from the list of states where NOAA's federal HMS Atlantic Tunas regulations are automatically applied to state waters, so the state's own (more restrictive) rule governs MS state waters rather than the federal Angling-category daily bag limits that apply coastwide/Atlantic.

Bonnethead is classified by MDMR as a 'small coastal shark' along with Atlantic Sharpnose, Finetooth, and Blacknose. Recreational anglers may possess a 25-inch total length minimum and no more than 4 small coastal sharks in aggregate (not 4 bonnetheads alone) per person per day in Mississippi state waters. No separate closed season applies to recreational small coastal shark harvest in state waters; commercial shark seasons instead follow federal Western Gulf sub-region dates.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational harvest permitted in Mississippi state waters; no closed season published)
rows.notes: Bull shark is classified as a 'Large Coastal' shark under MDMR recreational rules. Recreational anglers may possess no more than 1 large coastal/pelagic shark per person per day, with a vessel cap of 3, and a 37-inch total length minimum. Bull shark is not on MDMR's prohibited shark species list (which includes Sand Tiger, White, Dusky, Sandbar, Silky, etc.), so harvest is legal subject to these limits. Commercial harvest requires a separate MDMR shark endorsement and follows the federal Western Gulf sub-region season; this record reflects RECREATIONAL state-water rules.

Caribbean Reef Shark is a federally and state-prohibited species. It must be released immediately with minimal injury, kept in the water, and cannot be retained, possessed, or landed by recreational or commercial fishermen in Mississippi state waters. This matches NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited species list, which applies uniformly regardless of jurisdiction.

rows.season: Year-round closed to harvest — prohibited species
rows.notes: Caribbean Sharpnose Shark (Rhizoprionodon porosus) is listed by MDMR as a prohibited shark species in Mississippi waters and must be released; no retention is allowed under any circumstance. This is consistent with NOAA's federal Atlantic HMS prohibited shark species list, which also names Caribbean sharpnose as a species that must be released with minimal injury.

Size is 36 inches fork length (not total length). No recreational closed season is specified in current MDMR regulations. Note: A valid Mississippi Recreational Offshore Landing Permit (MS-ROLP) is required to land Cobia in Mississippi. Commercial harvest of Cobia is currently 'No Take' per MDMR Commercial Catch Limits page, and sale of Cobia caught/landed in MS is illegal regardless.

Finetooth Shark is classified as a Small Coastal Shark under MDMR rules. The 25-inch TL minimum size and 4-fish bag limit are an aggregate limit shared with other small coastal species (Atlantic Sharpnose, Blacknose, Bonnethead) — not 4 finetooth alone. No closed season currently published for small coastal sharks in MS state waters; finning is prohibited.

Mississippi state waters recreational Gag Grouper: 24-inch total length minimum. Counts within the 4-fish grouper aggregate bag/possession limit, but only 2 Gag may be retained within that aggregate. Season set annually by MDMR Executive Director order under Miss. Code Ann. § 49-15-15; applies to Mississippi territorial waters.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species — no legal harvest season)
rows.notes: Galapagos Shark is listed by MDMR as a prohibited shark species in Mississippi state waters. Harvest, possession, and retention are not allowed for either recreational or commercial fishermen at any time. This aligns with NOAA Atlantic HMS federal prohibited shark species list, which also applies in the Gulf region.

Goldface Tilefish has no MDMR minimum size limit and is not subject to a species-specific season closure in Mississippi state waters. It is regulated as part of the 20-fish 'reef fish aggregate' bag limit shared with Gray Triggerfish, Vermilion Snapper, Lane Snapper, Almaco Jack, Anchor Tilefish, Tilefish, Blacklined Tilefish, and Bluelined Tilefish (MS Admin Code Title 22, Part 3, Ch. 07, Rule 7.1, item 15). The 20 fish are combined across all listed species, not 20 goldface tilefish alone.

Great Hammerhead (Sphyrna mokarran) is classified as a Large Coastal Shark and is NOT on MDMR's state-prohibited shark species list (which includes Sand Tiger, Whale, Basking, White, Dusky, Bignose, Galapagos, Night, Caribbean Reef, Narrowtooth, Caribbean Sharpnose, Smalltail, Atlantic Angel, Longfin Mako, Bigeye Thresher, Sevengill, Sixgill, Bigeye Sixgill, Sandbar, and Silky). Recreational anglers may possess no more than 1 large coastal/pelagic shark per person and no more than 3 per vessel per day in MS state waters, with a 37-inch TL minimum size. No recreational closed season is published; commercial shark seasons run concurrent with the federal Western Gulf Sub-Region season. Note: a 2024 NOAA federal rule prohibits hammerhead retention only in the U.S. Caribbean Sea — this does NOT apply to Gulf of Mexico/Mississippi waters. Finning is illegal; sharks must be landed with fins naturally attached.

Great White Shark (white shark) is a federally prohibited HMS shark species under the 2006 Consolidated Atlantic HMS FMP — no retention is allowed in any U.S. waters, including Mississippi state waters. MDMR's own recreational catch limits page lists 'White' shark under prohibited species. If caught, it must be released immediately without removing it from the water.

Legal notice from MDMR confirms recreational Greater Amberjack season open Sept 1, 2026 through Oct 14, 2026 in Mississippi territorial waters (season aligns with federal Gulf closure date). Minimum fork length is 34 inches, bag limit 1 fish per angler per day. Note: charter vessel captains and crew are prohibited from retaining a recreational bag limit of Greater Amberjack. Season open in both state and federal waters per MDMR announcement; closes early if Gulf-wide federal quota is met.

No minimum size limit. Anchor Tilefish has no individual bag limit but counts toward the 20-fish Reef Fish Aggregate (combined with Almaco Jack, Goldface Tilefish, Tilefish, Blackline Tilefish, Blueline Tilefish, etc.). No MDMR-specific seasonal closure is listed for this species in MS state waters.
Minimum 12 in total length.

rows.season: Closed year-round — no open season (harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Gulf and Atlantic Sturgeon are listed as protected species in Mississippi. The Gulf Sturgeon is federally listed as Threatened under the Endangered Species Act, and directed fishing has been closed in Mississippi since 1974. MDMR explicitly lists 'Atlantic and Gulf Sturgeon' under Protected Species — it is illegal to catch, keep, or injure sturgeon in MS waters. Any sturgeon caught incidentally must be released unharmed and reported to NOAA Fisheries at 844-788-7491.

Minimum size is 24 inches fork length (FL). Recreational bag limit is 3 King Mackerel per person per day in Mississippi state (territorial) waters. Commercial harvest is capped at 3,000 lbs per vessel/trip/day (federal Western Zone limit adopted by MDMR). No closed recreational season is published for MS state waters; check for in-season federal quota closures if fishing federal waters.

Lane snapper in Mississippi state waters are managed under the aggregate reef fish / snapper grouper complex. The 8-inch minimum size is drawn from training data referencing MDMR rules aligned with Gulf Council framework; however, lane snapper are often counted within an aggregate snapper bag limit rather than a species-specific bag limit. Bag limit could not be confirmed with high confidence and is returned as null. Admin must verify current per-angler and vessel limits directly against the live MDMR source.

Lemon Shark is classified as a 'Large Coastal and Pelagic' shark under MDMR rules. The 1-per-person/3-per-vessel bag limit and 37-inch TL minimum are aggregate limits shared across the entire Large Coastal and Pelagic shark group (Blacktip, Spinner, Bull, Tiger, Lemon, Nurse, Hammerheads, Mako, Porbeagle, Thresher, Blue, Oceanic Whitetip), not species-specific. No closed recreational season is published; harvest is allowed year-round subject to these size/bag limits and finning prohibitions. Commercial harvest of this species requires a separate MDMR shark endorsement and runs concurrent with the federal Western Gulf shark season.

Slot limit is 14-22 inches fork length. Bag limit of 5 fish is an aggregate shared with Banded Rudderfish (Seriola zonata), not 5 Lesser Amberjack individually. No closed season is specified for Lesser Amberjack in Mississippi state waters (unlike Greater Amberjack, which has a separate federal-aligned closure); recreational offshore landing permit (ROLP) required to possess any reef fish species in MS waters, and non-stainless steel circle hooks required when using natural bait for reef species.

rows.season: No open season - Year-round closure (No Take)
rows.notes: MDMR administrative rule prohibits all take/possession of Longbill Spearfish in Mississippi state waters. This has been in effect since at least 2019 and remains current in MDMR's Title 22, Part 3, Chapter 11 rule (current version dated Nov 2024, published July 2025).

rows.season: No open season — retention prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Longfin Mako Shark is a federally prohibited species under NOAA's Atlantic HMS Fishery Management Plan (prohibited since the late 1990s/2000) and is also explicitly listed by MDMR as a prohibited shark species for recreational and commercial harvest in Mississippi state waters. It must be released immediately if caught; retention, possession, or landing is illegal in all U.S. Atlantic and Gulf waters, including Mississippi state waters.

Mahi-Mahi/Dolphinfish is not a state-managed species in Mississippi waters — it does not appear in MDMR's Recreational Catch Limits list or in Title 22 Part 7 Chapter 08 (Recreational Bag, Possession and Size Limits) of the Mississippi Administrative Code, which enumerates specific minimum sizes/bag limits only for Spotted Seatrout, Red Drum, Cobia, Greater Amberjack, and the Snapper species. No closed season, minimum size, or bag limit is currently published by MDMR for mahi-mahi in MS state waters, consistent with third-party charter guides reporting no size/bag restrictions for MS.
Minimum 12 in total length (gray snapper).

rows.season: Closed year-round (no open season — prohibited species)
rows.notes: Narrowtooth Shark (Carcharhinus brachyurus) is listed by MDMR as a prohibited shark species — harvest is not allowed recreationally or commercially in Mississippi state waters. Any narrowtooth shark caught must be released. This aligns with its status as a prohibited species under NOAA Atlantic HMS shark management (federal waters) as well.

rows.season: No open season - Prohibited species (year-round no-harvest)
rows.notes: Night Shark (Carcharhinus signatus) is a federally prohibited Atlantic HMS shark species. It must be released immediately with minimal injury and without removing it from the water. This federal prohibition applies in Mississippi state waters, whose shark seasons run concurrent with federal Western Gulf of Mexico Sub-Region shark seasons per MDMR rule 22-7-09-113.

Nurse shark is classified as a 'large coastal shark' under MDMR recreational rules. Minimum size is 37 inches total length. Recreational anglers may possess no more than 1 large coastal/pelagic shark species per person and no more than 3 per vessel per day (aggregate across that species group, not per-species). Nurse shark is NOT on MDMR's prohibited shark species list, so it is legally retainable if it meets the size limit. Federal NOAA Atlantic HMS rules also apply (nurse shark currently authorized for recreational retention, 1 per vessel per trip federally) — anglers must comply with whichever rule (state or federal) is more restrictive, and must hold an HMS permit if required. No closed season is published for recreational large coastal sharks in MS state waters (commercial shark season runs concurrent with the federal Western Gulf sub-region season, but that does not apply to recreational).

Oceanic Whitetip Shark is a federally protected/prohibited species under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations (50 CFR 635.34) — retention and possession banned in all U.S. Atlantic waters including the Gulf of Mexico since Feb 2, 2024, due to ESA-threatened status. Mississippi state waters follow this prohibition; MDMR's own protected species and recreational catch-limit pages list Oceanic Whitetip Shark among species that must be released unharmed if caught. Any oceanic whitetip caught in MS state or federal waters must be released immediately with minimal harm — 0 bag/possession at all times, no size limit applies since retention is never legal.

rows.season: Year-round (NOAA Atlantic HMS recreational shark fishery is open; no specific closed season for porbeagle)
rows.notes: Porbeagle is an authorized (non-prohibited) recreational HMS shark species. The 1-shark limit is PER VESSEL PER TRIP and is a combined/aggregate limit shared across the whole authorized shark list (e.g., blacktip, bull, tiger, blue, common thresher, porbeagle, etc.) — not 1 porbeagle in addition to other species. Minimum size is 54 in. fork length. Special condition: porbeagle sharks alive at haulback must be released unharmed if a swordfish, tuna, or billfish is on board/possessed on that trip. MDMR requires an HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement to retain any shark, including porbeagle, in Mississippi waters, and Mississippi's saltwater fishing guide explicitly lists porbeagle among species requiring this federal permit. Porbeagle is biologically rare/uncommon in Gulf of America (Mississippi) waters, as it is primarily a cold-water Atlantic species.
Slot 18-30 in total length.

Sailfish is a federally managed Atlantic HMS (billfish); NOAA HMS rules apply in all US waters, including MS state waters, and supersede state-set limits. Minimum size 63 inches measured lower-jaw fork length (tip of lower jaw to fork of tail). The 1-fish daily bag limit is an aggregate limit shared across all Atlantic billfish (sailfish, blue marlin, white marlin, roundscale spearfish) — not 1 of each. Federal HMS Angling Permit required to fish for sailfish in federal waters; not required in MS state waters unless vessel holds one, in which case federal HMS rules must be followed. All landed sailfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours.

rows.season: Closed / Prohibited - No open season for harvest
rows.notes: Sandbar Shark is listed by MDMR as a prohibited species for recreational harvest in Mississippi state waters. Commercially, sandbar sharks may only be possessed by fishermen holding a NMFS research fishery permit (not available to general recreational or commercial harvesters). This aligns with the federal NOAA HMS prohibited species list. All catches must be released.

Scalloped Hammerhead is grouped with other 'Large Coastal and Pelagic Sharks' (Blacktip, Spinner, Bull, Tiger, Lemon, Nurse, Great Hammerhead, Smooth Hammerhead, Shortfin Mako, Porbeagle, Thresher, Blue, Oceanic Whitetip) under MS recreational rules. Limit is 1 shark per person/day from this entire group (not 1 hammerhead specifically) and no more than 3 of this group per vessel/day, 37in TL minimum. No recreational closed season is published for MS state waters; commercial harvest season follows the federal Western Gulf of Mexico shark sub-region season and requires a shark endorsement. This is a Gulf-side MS rule; it is distinct from NOAA Atlantic/Caribbean HMS rules where hammerhead retention is prohibited.

rows.season: Year-round in Mississippi state (territorial) waters, EXCEPT closed February 1 – March 31, 2026 (and annually) seaward of the 20-fathom break, per the shallow-water grouper spawning closure
rows.notes: Scamp is regulated as part of Mississippi's 4-fish 'grouper aggregate' per person per day (along with Black Grouper, Yellowmouth, Rock Hind, Red Hind); there is no scamp-specific sub-limit within that aggregate (unlike Gag, which is capped at 2 of the 4). Minimum size is 16 inches total length. The Feb 1–Mar 31 closure only applies to the portion of MS state waters seaward of the 20-fathom depth contour, mirroring the federal shallow-water grouper closure; inside 20 fathoms, scamp harvest is open year-round subject to size/bag limits. A Recreational Offshore Landing Permit (ROLP) is required to possess any grouper species in MS waters.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season for Schoolmaster Snapper in MS state waters)
rows.notes: Schoolmaster is regulated under MDMR's 12-inch (total length) minimum size group shared with Gray, Cubera, Dog, Mahogany, and Yellowtail Snapper. It also falls within a 10-fish daily aggregate bag limit shared with Gray, Mutton (max 5 of the 10), Yellowtail, Schoolmaster, Cubera, Dog, Mahogany, Queen, Blackfin, Silk, and Wenchman snappers — it is not an individual per-species limit. No MDMR closed season applies to this species (only Red Snapper has a set season in MS state waters).

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species — no open season)
rows.notes: Sevengill Shark (the group including Sharpnose Sevengill, Heptranchias perlo) is on MDMR's list of Prohibited shark species for both recreational and commercial harvest in Mississippi state waters — must be released immediately if caught. This mirrors the NMFS Atlantic/Gulf HMS Prohibited Species list. No possession, minimum/maximum size, or bag limit applies because retention is unlawful at all times.
Minimum 14 in total length.

rows.season: Closed year-round (zero retention limit in effect since July 5, 2022, until further notice)
rows.notes: Shortfin mako shark is an Atlantic HMS species. NOAA Fisheries set a zero retention limit for shortfin mako sharks in all commercial and recreational Atlantic HMS fisheries (including Gulf of Mexico/Mississippi waters) effective July 5, 2022, and this remains in effect. All shortfin mako sharks caught must be released immediately, whether dead or alive at haulback. This federal HMS rule applies in Mississippi state waters as well; MDMR's own prohibited-species list separately bans Longfin Mako, but Shortfin Mako retention is barred under the overriding federal zero-retention rule.

rows.season: Closed year-round (prohibited species — no retention allowed)
rows.notes: Silky shark is a federally prohibited 'ridgeback' shark species under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations and is explicitly listed as prohibited from recreational harvest on MDMR's own recreational catch limits page. Must be released immediately with minimal injury; retention is illegal in both state and federal waters. As an HMS-managed shark, federal prohibition applies regardless of state jurisdiction, and Mississippi's state rules concur.

rows.season: Closed year-round — no open season (harvest prohibited)
rows.notes: Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus griseus) and Bigeye Sixgill are both listed on MDMR's 'Current Shark Species Prohibited from harvest' list for Mississippi state waters, applicable to recreational anglers. Retention (including possession) of this species is unlawful; catch-and-release only. This is Mississippi's single statewide saltwater rule (Mississippi has only Gulf coastline, no separate Atlantic-side rule applies).

Smalltooth Sawfish (Pristis pectinata) is listed as Endangered under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. Take, possession, harassment, harm, pursuit, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capture, or collection is federally prohibited at all times, regardless of state jurisdiction. Any incidental capture must be released immediately with minimum harm. Bag limit of 0 reflects absolute prohibition on retention.

rows.season: Year-round (recreational Atlantic shark fishery is open under an annual HMS Angling/Charterboat permit with shark endorsement, subject to in-season closure if the Large Coastal Shark/Hammerhead quota is met)
rows.notes: Smooth hammerhead is an Atlantic HMS shark, so federal NOAA rules apply in Mississippi state waters too (state jurisdiction does not override). Minimum size is 78 inches fork length. Retention is limited to 1 hammerhead (of the great/scalloped/smooth group) per vessel per trip, counted against the same 1-shark vessel limit shared with other 'large' shark species. Hammerheads cannot be retained if any tuna, billfish, or swordfish is aboard, and vice versa. Vessel must have a valid HMS Angling or Charterboat/Headboat permit with shark endorsement; non-offset, non-stainless circle hooks required. Note: Texas state waters set a different (99 in) state-only minimum size for hammerheads, illustrating why MS anglers should not assume other Gulf states' numbers apply — this record uses the federal HMS standard per the compliance rule for HMS species.
Minimum 12 in total length.

Minimum size is 12 inches fork length (FL), not total length. Gulf Spanish mackerel recreational harvest has no scheduled seasonal closure in Mississippi state waters; NOAA notes the Gulf stock 'does not have a scheduled seasonal closure' and carries a 15-fish recreational daily bag limit that applies to both state and federal Gulf waters. MDMR could close state waters if adjacent federal Gulf waters are closed via an in-season accountability closure, but no such closure is currently in effect.

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Spotted Eagle Ray is a recreationally and commercially prohibited species in Mississippi state waters (must be released if caught, no possession allowed).
Minimum 15 in total length.

Mississippi state regulations do not distinguish 'summer flounder' (Paralichthys dentatus) as a separate managed species from other flounders; MDMR regulates all flounder under the genus 'Paralichthys sp.' as a single group (dominated in MS waters by Southern Flounder). No closed season is published for recreational flounder in MS state waters — it is open year-round subject to the 12-inch minimum size and 10-fish daily bag/possession limit, per MDMR's official catch limits page and Title 22 administrative code.

Swordfish is a federally-managed Atlantic HMS species; NOAA HMS rules apply in ALL waters (state and federal) and Mississippi state regs do not override them. Requires a valid HMS Angling or HMS Charterboat/Headboat permit (covers everyone aboard); all landed swordfish must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours. Minimum size is 47 in lower-jaw fork length (or 25 in cleithrum-to-caudal-keel alternative measurement for shark-damaged fish). Daily bag is 1 fish per person, capped at 4 per recreational (non-for-hire) vessel or 15 per for-hire vessel per day; captain/crew of for-hire vessels have a zero bag/possession limit. Swordfish cannot be retained if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip shark is aboard or has been offloaded. Fishery status (open/closed) can change via NOAA in-season action, so verify live status before app release.

Minimum size is 75 inches FORK LENGTH (not total length) — very few recreationally caught tarpon meet this, so harvest is effectively rare/catch-and-release in practice. Limit is 1 fish PER VESSEL per day, not per angler. Additionally, it is unlawful to remove any Atlantic Tarpon over 40 inches from the water unless the angler intends to harvest it within the legal size/bag limits (i.e., large fish must stay in water for release). Sale of Atlantic Tarpon is prohibited.

Tiger shark is managed as part of the 'large coastal shark' group under Mississippi recreational shark rules (it is NOT on MDMR's prohibited-species list). Recreational anglers may keep 1 large coastal/pelagic shark per person and up to 3 large coastal/pelagic sharks per vessel per day, with a 37-inch total length minimum, in MS state waters. No closed recreational season is published (year-round); this applies to state waters only — commercial harvest instead follows the federal Western Gulf shark sub-region season. Finning is prohibited.
Minimum 18 in total length.

Wahoo does not appear as a listed species with a size, bag, or season restriction on MDMR's Recreational Catch Limits page or in the Title 22 Part 3 finfish size/bag/season rule text located during this search (which explicitly lists Spotted Seatrout, Red Drum, Flounder, Sheepshead, Gray Snapper, Tarpon, Tripletail, Cobia, Spanish Mackerel, King Mackerel, Black Drum, Sand Seatrout, and various snappers, but not Wahoo). Wahoo are a pelagic/offshore species rarely encountered within Mississippi's narrow state territorial waters, and MDMR does not appear to impose a species-specific size or bag limit on it in state waters (unlike Florida's explicit 2-fish/day, no-minimum-size rule, or the South Atlantic Council's federal 2-fish/day Atlantic rule, neither of which applies here). Absent a listed restriction, no closed season is indicated either, so 'Year-round' is used as the default open status. Anglers should still confirm no new MDMR rule changes have been filed since this search (MDMR periodically issues Notices of Intent to amend Title 22 Part 3).

White Marlin is an HMS (Highly Migratory Species) governed exclusively by NOAA HMS federal rules regardless of state jurisdiction. Under NOAA HMS regulations, White Marlin is currently prohibited from retention — catch-and-release only. State-level bag/size limits from MDMR do not apply or override federal HMS rules.

Yellowfin Tuna is an HMS species. Federal NOAA HMS rules apply. Atlantic Tunas regulations (50 CFR Part 635) govern yellowfin tuna: 27-inch curved fork length minimum, 3 fish per person per day bag limit for recreational anglers. Mississippi state waters extend only 3 nautical miles offshore; yellowfin tuna are rarely encountered inside state waters but federal HMS rules still apply regardless of state jurisdiction. Verify current HMS regulations directly with NOAA Fisheries.

rows.season: Year-round (no closed season for Yellowmouth Grouper in Mississippi state waters, 2026)
rows.notes: Yellowmouth Grouper has no minimum size limit in MS state waters but is harvested within a 4-fish 'Grouper Aggregate' that also includes Red, Yellowfin, Black, Scamp, Rock/Red Hind, Yellowedge, Misty, and Snowy Grouper (daily bag of 4 in aggregate, per person). A free Recreational Offshore Landing Permit (ROLP) is required to possess any Grouper species in Mississippi waters. No seasonal closure specific to Yellowmouth Grouper was found on MDMR's current pages (unlike Gag Grouper or Red Snapper, which do have set seasons).

Yellowtail snapper in Mississippi state waters typically follow Gulf reef fish framework rules, but MDMR-specific aggregate snapper-grouper or individual species bag limits for yellowtail snapper in MS state waters could not be confirmed with high confidence from training data. Verify current limits directly with MDMR before publishing.

rows.season: Year-round, 2025-2026 license year (Sep 1, 2025 - Aug 31, 2026); subject to temporary closures during optimum spawning conditions
rows.notes: Alligator gar is a freshwater species; for freshwater finfish caught in Texas public salt waters, statewide freshwater limits apply. Statewide daily bag limit is 1 alligator gar of any size (no min/max length). All alligator gar harvested from public waters (except Falcon International Reservoir) must be reported to TPWD within 24 hours via the 'Texas Hunt & Fish' app or online. TPWD may temporarily close specific areas to alligator gar fishing for up to 30 days when spawning conditions occur (water temps 68-82°F plus moderate flood levels).

Atlantic Angel Shark is a designated Prohibited Shark Species in Texas state waters. It may not be retained under any circumstances and must be released immediately without removing it from the water. This is a year-round, zero-bag-limit prohibition, not a seasonal closure.

Texas state waters daily bag limit for Atlantic sharpnose shark is combined with all other allowable shark species (1 fish total per person per day, 2-shark possession limit). Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for sharks. Only the head may be removed from a retained shark carcass; the rest must remain intact.

rows.season: Year-round (Prohibited species — no open season, zero bag limit)
rows.notes: Basking Shark is on TPWD's prohibited shark species list. It may not be retained (zero bag limit) and must be released immediately without removing it from the water. This applies year-round in Texas state waters.

Bigeye Sand Tiger Shark (Odontaspis noronhai) is listed as a Prohibited Shark Species in Texas state waters. It may not be retained under any circumstances (zero bag limit) and must be released immediately without removing it from the water. This aligns with the federal NOAA HMS Atlantic prohibited species list, which has barred retention of this species since 1997.

rows.season: Year-round (catch and release only — prohibited species)
rows.notes: Bigeye Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus nakamurai) is on TPWD's prohibited shark species list for Texas state waters. It may not be retained under any circumstances and must be released immediately without removing it from the water.

rows.season: Year-round (catch-and-release only; retention prohibited) — valid Sep 1, 2025 through Aug 31, 2026
rows.notes: Bigeye Thresher Shark (Alopias superciliosus) is listed as a PROHIBITED shark species in Texas state waters. It must be released immediately and may not be retained, possessed, or landed. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for sharks in TX state waters. This aligns with NOAA HMS federal prohibited species status for Atlantic sharks as well.

Bigeye tuna is a NOAA Atlantic HMS species; NOAA HMS rules apply in federal waters and are also followed for state-water HMS permitting in the Gulf. 27-inch curved fork length (CFL) minimum size applies per 50 CFR 635.20 (no person may retain a bigeye tuna under 27 inches CFL). There is no recreational bag limit for bigeye tuna (unlike yellowfin's 3/person/day limit). A valid HMS Angling or Charterboat/Headboat permit is required to target bigeye tuna, covering everyone aboard the vessel.

Bignose Shark is a PROHIBITED species in Texas state waters — zero bag limit, no possession allowed. Any bignose shark caught must be released immediately without removing it from the water. This designation is consistent with NOAA's federal Atlantic HMS prohibited shark species list, which also applies in adjacent federal Gulf waters. There is no open season for this species; it may never be retained.

rows.season: Year-round (Sep 1, 2025 - Aug 31, 2026 license year; no closed season listed for Texas state waters)
rows.notes: TPWD's official Grouper Bag & Length Limits page lists no closed season for black grouper in Texas state waters, matching the pattern for other reef fish (e.g., red snapper) that are open year-round in-state. Applies to waters out to 9nm in the Gulf and EEZ waters (9-200nm) when possessed in state waters or landed in Texas. Possession limit is double the daily bag (8) unless otherwise noted. Venting tool/descending device required for reef fish showing barotrauma per Texas DESCEND-Act-aligned rule.

Blacknose shark falls under TPWD's 'Other allowable shark species' category (min. 64 in. total length, no max). Texas has a combined daily bag limit of 1 shark per person per day across ALL allowable shark species (not species-specific), with a possession limit of 2 (double the bag limit). Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when shark fishing in TX state waters.

Blacktip shark is grouped with Atlantic sharpnose and bonnethead under a combined daily bag limit of 1 fish (any allowable combination) for all allowable shark species. Minimum size is 24 inches total length with no maximum. Possession limit is double the daily bag limit (2). Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for sharks in TX state waters (except when using artificial lures). No closed season — shark fishing for allowable species is open year-round in TX state waters.

rows.season: No targeted recreational fishing allowed for Atlantic Bluefin Tuna in the Gulf of America (includes Texas state and federal waters) — year-round 2026. Retention limited strictly to incidentally caught trophy-sized bluefin (≥73" curved fork length) while targeting other HMS species, subject to trophy sub-quota availability.
rows.notes: Atlantic Bluefin Tuna is a NOAA HMS-managed species; federal rules govern retention even in Texas state waters — a federal HMS Angling (or Charter/Headboat) permit is required to keep any bluefin tuna, even in state waters. Per NOAA: recreational daily bag limits for bluefin tuna 'are effective for all areas except for the Gulf of America, where NOAA Fisheries does not allow targeted fishing for bluefin tuna. Retention of bluefin tuna in the Gulf of America is only allowed for incidentally caught trophy-sized bluefin tuna when fishing for other HMS.' Any retained bluefin (school through trophy sizes) must be reported to NOAA within 24 hours via the HMS Catch Reporting app or 888-872-8862. TPWD's own saltwater/federal-waters pages defer to NOAA/HMS rules for this species and do not set separate state numeric limits.

Bonnethead shark: 24-inch minimum total length, no maximum. Daily bag limit is 1 fish in any allowable combination for allowable shark species (including Atlantic sharpnose, blacktip, and bonnethead) — i.e., the 1-shark bag is shared across allowable species, not per-species. Possession limit is double the bag limit (2). Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for sharks in Texas state waters. No closed season; open year-round in state waters (out to 9 nautical miles in the Gulf).

Bull shark falls under TPWD's 'Other allowable shark species' category (min. 64 inches total length, no max). Daily bag limit is 1 shark per person per day in any allowable combination of shark species (not species-specific); possession limit is double the bag limit (2). Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for sharks in Texas state waters. Only the head may be removed; carcass (including tail) must remain intact.

Caribbean Reef Shark is on TPWD's Prohibited Shark Species list. It may not be retained under any circumstances (zero bag limit) and must be released immediately without removing it from the water, per TPWD's Shark Identification and Regulations brochure and Outdoor Annual.

rows.season: Year-round (catch-and-release only) — current period Sep 1, 2025 through Aug 31, 2026
rows.notes: Caribbean sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon porosus) is on TPWD's Prohibited Shark Species list for Texas state waters. It may not be retained (zero bag limit) and must be released immediately without removing it from the water. This mirrors the NOAA Atlantic HMS prohibited shark list as well.

Texas state waters have no closed season for cobia (ling). Minimum size is 40 inches total length with a daily bag limit of 1 fish per angler; no maximum size limit. Possession limit is generally twice the daily bag unless otherwise noted, but confirm current possession rule on the Outdoor Annual page.

Finetooth shark is not one of the named species (Atlantic sharpnose, blacktip, bonnethead, or hammerhead) and is not on TPWD's prohibited shark list, so it falls under the 'Other allowable shark species' category: 64-inch minimum length, no maximum. The daily bag limit of 1 shark applies in aggregate across ALL allowable shark species combined (not 1 per species). Only the head may be removed from any shark carcass; remainder must stay intact. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for sharks in TX state waters.
No daily bag or possession limit on Gafftopsail Catfish in Texas state waters; 14-inch minimum length applies, no maximum length. No closed season is listed for this species (open year-round).

rows.season: Year-round (catch-and-release only; harvest prohibited) — Sep 1, 2025 through Aug 31, 2026
rows.notes: Galapagos shark is on TPWD's Prohibited Shark Species list for Texas state waters (0-9 nautical miles). It must be released immediately without removing it from the water; no minimum/maximum size applies since retention is never legal. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when shark fishing in TX state waters.

rows.season: Closed year-round — Catch & Release Only (no open harvest season)
rows.notes: Goliath Grouper (jewfish) harvest is prohibited in Texas state waters. TPWD lists the species as 'Catch & Release Only' with a daily bag limit of 0 in all official size/bag limit charts. This matches the federal harvest moratorium in place since 1990.

Great Hammerhead is classified by TPWD under the 'Hammerhead (smooth, great, scalloped)' category in Texas state waters (out to 9 nautical miles in the Gulf). Minimum total length is 99 inches with no maximum. The daily bag limit of 1 is shared in the aggregate across ALL allowable shark species (not 1 hammerhead plus other sharks) — i.e., only 1 shark total per angler per day regardless of species. Possession limit is double the bag limit (2) per TPWD general possession rules. Non-offset, non-stainless-steel circle hooks are required when shark fishing in TX state waters. Note: Great Hammerhead is NOT on Texas's prohibited shark list (unlike Florida and federal Atlantic/Caribbean HMS rules, where it is prohibited) — TX state-water regulations differ from federal/other-state rules for this species.

rows.season: Year-round in Texas state waters (2025-2026 regulatory cycle, valid Sep 1, 2025 - Aug 31, 2026)
rows.notes: Texas state waters impose no closed season for greater amberjack — only bag/length limits apply year-round. This differs from federal Gulf waters, where NOAA has closed greater amberjack recreational harvest until the 2026/2027 season begins Sept 1, 2026 due to the stock being overfished. Possession limit is double the daily bag (2 fish) per TPWD's standard rule unless otherwise noted.

rows.season: Open year-round except annual closure Nov 1 - Dec 14, 2026 (reopens Dec 15, 2026)
rows.notes: TPWD's flounder bag and length limits apply collectively to all flounder species, hybrids, and subspecies in Texas state waters — including Gulf flounder, Southern flounder, and fringed flounder — there is no separate Gulf-flounder-specific limit. Daily bag and possession limit is 5 fish with a 15-inch minimum total length and no maximum. The fishery is closed annually Nov 1 through Dec 14 (bag limit drops to 0 during that window) to protect the fall spawning migration; it reopens Dec 15.

rows.season: No open season — harvest prohibited year-round
rows.notes: Sturgeon (Atlantic/Gulf, Acipenser oxyrinchus and subspecies) are listed as threatened under the federal Endangered Species Act and are fully protected nationwide, including in Texas state waters. NOAA Fisheries states it is illegal to fish for, catch, or keep sturgeon, and anglers who accidentally hook one must release it immediately without removing it from the water. No recreational or commercial harvest, possession, or retention is legal in any U.S. waters, including the Sabine River system area where Gulf Sturgeon occasionally occur in Texas.

King mackerel in Texas state waters has a 27-inch minimum length (total length) and no maximum/slot limit. Possession limit is double the daily bag (6 fish) per TPWD general rules. Fish may have head or tail removed but carcass must remain intact/unfilleted for verification. King mackerel is managed under the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council's Coastal Migratory Pelagics plan (not NOAA HMS).

No daily bag or possession limit for lane snapper in Texas waters; only an 8-inch minimum length applies. Applies to aquatic life caught in Texas waters out to 9 nautical miles and EEZ waters landed in Texas.

Lemon shark falls under TPWD's 'Other Allowable Shark Species' group (64-inch minimum total length), distinct from the 24-inch group (Atlantic sharpnose, blacktip, bonnethead) and 99-inch hammerhead group. Daily bag limit is 1 shark per person per day (combined for all allowable shark species), with a 2-shark daily possession limit per angler (not a per-boat limit). Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when shark fishing in TX state waters (except with artificial lures). No closed season is published for shark fishing in Texas state waters.

Longbill spearfish is a federally managed Atlantic HMS billfish. Retention has long been prohibited in both commercial and recreational fisheries — it is not among the billfish species (blue marlin, white marlin, sailfish, roundscale spearfish) for which limited recreational landings are permitted. NOAA HMS compliance guides state harvest of billfishes 'i.e., white or blue marlin, sailfish, roundscale spearfish, and longbill spearfish' is prohibited for commercial purposes, and recreational retention allowances explicitly exclude longbill spearfish. A 2020 Federal Register action noted 'Retention of longbill spearfish is already prohibited.' Since HMS billfish rules are federally set and apply uniformly (TPWD's own saltwater fishing pages defer to federal HMS rules for HMS species and do not list separate state numeric limits for longbill spearfish), anglers in Texas state waters must release any longbill spearfish caught — no bag, boat, or size limit applies because retention is not allowed at all. An HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit is still required to target/possess Atlantic billfish species even in state waters if landing elsewhere applies, though TX state-water billfishing itself does not require the federal permit per FWC-style guidance used regionally.

Longfin mako shark is on TPWD's Prohibited Shark Species list for Texas state waters. It may not be retained under any circumstances and must be released immediately without removing it from the water, using non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks as required for all shark fishing in TX state waters.

rows.season: Year-round (catch and release only — prohibited species)
rows.notes: Narrowtooth shark is classified as a Prohibited Shark Species in Texas state waters. It may not be retained under any circumstances and must be released immediately without removing it from the water. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for sharks in TX state waters.

Night Shark is a Prohibited Shark Species under TPWD regulations — it may NOT be retained (zero bag limit) and must be released immediately without removing it from the water. This matches its federal prohibited status under NOAA Atlantic HMS regulations. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when shark fishing in TX state waters.

rows.season: Year-round (open season for allowable shark species, current regulatory cycle Sep 1, 2025 - Aug 31, 2026)
rows.notes: Nurse shark is classified as an 'Other allowable shark species' in Texas state waters (not on the prohibited list). The daily bag limit of 1 shark is a combined limit across all allowable shark species (any allowable combination), not per-species. Possession limit is double the daily bag (2). Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for shark in state waters (except when using artificial lures).

Oceanic Whitetip Shark is classified as a Prohibited Shark Species by TPWD. It may not be retained under any circumstances and must be released immediately without removing it from the water. This aligns with NOAA HMS federal rules (effective Jan 3, 2024) prohibiting retention/possession of oceanic whitetip sharks in all U.S. Atlantic/Gulf waters, and the species is also ESA-listed as threatened.

Porbeagle is not a TPWD-prohibited shark species, so in Texas state waters it falls under the 'Other allowable shark species' category: 64-inch total length minimum, no maximum. Daily bag is 1 fish for ALL allowable shark species combined (aggregate limit, not species-specific), with a possession limit of 2 (double the daily bag). Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required for shark fishing in TX state waters. Note: Porbeagle is a cold-water HMS species rarely encountered in Texas/Gulf waters; if fishing federal waters instead of TX state waters, NOAA HMS rules apply (1 shark per vessel per trip pooled across authorized pelagic/coastal species, and porbeagles alive at haulback must be released if tuna/swordfish/billfish are aboard).

No daily bag or possession limit on sailfish in Texas waters, but any fish under 84 inches (lower jaw fork/total length) must be released. As an HMS billfish, anglers fishing federal waters need a NOAA HMS Angling permit and must follow release-without-removal-from-water rules if a federal permit is held; TPWD state-water rule does not itself require a federal permit for state-water fishing.

Sand Tiger Shark is a federally/state-listed prohibited shark species in Texas state waters. It may not be retained under any circumstances and must be released immediately without removing it from the water, regardless of size or season.

Sandbar Shark is designated a Prohibited Shark Species by TPWD. It may not be retained under any circumstances (zero bag limit) and must be released immediately without removing it from the water. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for sharks in Texas state waters.

Scalloped hammerhead is classified as an 'allowable' (not prohibited) shark species in Texas state waters, distinct from Florida/federal Atlantic rules where hammerheads are prohibited. Texas requires a 99-inch total length minimum, no maximum. The 1-fish daily bag / 2-fish possession limit is a combined limit across ALL allowable shark species (not species-specific) — i.e., only 1 shark of any legal species may be kept per person per day. Non-offset, non-stainless steel circle hooks are required when fishing for sharks in TX state waters, and only the head may be removed from any retained shark (carcass, including tail, must stay intact).

Sharpnose sevengill shark (Heptranchias perlo, listed by TPWD simply as 'Sevengill') is a prohibited shark species in Texas state waters.
